The 2023 Mathematics Compendium

114 developed treatments with worked examples and proofs, six connecting arguments, and reproducible computational checks.

All 114 revised questions are developed here into mathematical treatments with definitions, a stated result, a derivation or proof, a worked example, and a precise scope. Six connecting arguments organize the material into a more coherent programme. The source bundle contains portable verification scripts and their retained outputs.

The 2023 evidence remains fragmentary. U marks a recovered user question, A an assistant passage without the original user wording, and T a dated topic fragment; none supplies a complete transcript. The historical starting points and their evidence labels come from the earlier table; the mathematical treatments are newly authored expositions and calculations. Classical results and small examples are not claimed as new discoveries. A worked example does not settle every general classification or research question mentioned in its extension.

Reading the proof scope. A written proof, an exhaustive finite computation and a floating-point check are different forms of evidence. Every treatment states its assumptions and limits. The verification ledger records what each script actually checks; it is not a formal proof assistant certificate. General theorems invoked from the literature remain literature dependencies.

Connections and extended developments

S001 · Synthesis

Minimal recurrences connect observations to finite realizations

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

A finite-state linear description and a recurrence for an observed sequence are two presentations of the same algebraic structure. The useful dimension is the reachable and observable dimension, which can be smaller than the dimension of the original matrix. This links the Cayley–Hamilton, observability, Fourier and exact-certificate questions without claiming that every nonlinear model has finite closure.

Definitions and assumptions

Work over a field F. A scalar sequence has a linear representation y_n=cAⁿb with finite-dimensional A, row c and column b. Its infinite Hankel matrix is H=(y_(i+j)) for i,j≥0.

The rank of the infinite Hankel matrix is the supremum of ranks of its finite submatrices. A recurrence of order r means y_(n+r)=Σ_(j=0)^(r−1)a_j y_(n+j) for every n≥0.

Hankel rank equals the minimum linear realization dimension

For a scalar sequence with a finite linear representation, the minimum possible state dimension equals rank H. It also equals the minimum order of an everywhere-valid forward recurrence, with the zero sequence assigned order zero.

Derivation or proof

For any representation H factors as O R, where O has rows cAⁱ and R has columns Aʲb. Therefore rank H cannot exceed the state dimension. Restrict first to the reachable subspace span{Aʲb}, then quotient by its invisible subspace {v:cAⁱv=0 for all i}. The resulting representation is reachable and observable. In a minimal r-dimensional scalar realization, the first r Krylov columns are independent: the first linear dependence would make their earlier span A-invariant and stop further growth. The analogous statement holds for the first r observation rows. Their product is the leading r×r Hankel block, which is consequently invertible, proving rank H≥r. Cayley–Hamilton gives a recurrence of order at most r. Conversely, an order-r recurrence has an r-dimensional companion realization, so no smaller recurrence is possible. These arguments also account for finite transients, which can contribute nilpotent modes.

Worked example

Take y_n=2ⁿ+3ⁿ, generated by A=diag(2,3), b=(1,1)ᵀ and c=(1,1).

The first values are 2,5,13,35,97. The leading 2×2 Hankel matrix is [[2,5],[5,13]], whose determinant is 1. The polynomial (z−2)(z−3)=z²−5z+6 gives y_(n+2)=5y_(n+1)−6y_n. Thus a two-state representation exists and the nonzero Hankel determinant rules out a one-state representation. If instead A=diag(2,−2), then y_n=2ⁿ+(−2)ⁿ has dimension two, while the even subsequence y_(2k)=2·4ᵏ has dimension one.

A short recurrence can be a certificate of exact observable compression. Subsampling can also erase modes, so reduced apparent dimension need not mean that the original dynamics became simpler.

Scope of the result

Finite prefix agreement alone never proves an infinite recurrence without a model-class or order bound. Given any inspected prefix, a sequence that agrees there and changes later is indistinguishable on that prefix. Numerical Hankel rank additionally requires tolerances and perturbation analysis.

Further development

Given an exact matrix family A(θ), determine where the reachable-observable dimension changes by computing rank minors. This is a finite algebraic question for a specified polynomial parameterization. For nonlinear polynomial dynamics, the degree-growth obstruction in M018 identifies an important class where a polynomial closure containing the state coordinate cannot be finite.

S002 · Synthesis

A reversible observation transform preserves Fisher information

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

The Gudermannian can turn an unbounded coordinate into a bounded angle and simplify a formula. An exact reversible change of observation cannot itself create statistical information. This distinction turns the old activation and geometry questions into an analysis of representation, quantization, noise and numerical precision.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X have a regular density p_θ(x), with θ-independent support and square-integrable score s_θ=∂_θlog p_θ. Fisher information is I_X(θ)=E_θ[s_θs_θᵀ].

Let g be a θ-independent differentiable bijection with nonzero Jacobian on its domain. Y=g(X) is the same observation expressed in another coordinate.

Fisher information is invariant under an invertible parameter-independent observation chart

Under the stated change-of-variable and regularity assumptions, I_Y(θ)=I_X(θ). Additional quantization or a parameter-independent noisy channel cannot increase Fisher information when the score-conditioning identity and the usual differentiation conditions hold.

Derivation or proof

The transformed density is q_θ(y)=p_θ(g⁻¹(y))|det Dg⁻¹(y)|. The Jacobian factor is independent of θ, so differentiating its logarithm with respect to θ gives zero. Consequently the transformed score is s_θ(g⁻¹(y)), and change of variables in its second moment proves equality. For a further observation Z produced through a θ-independent channel, differentiation under the integral gives s_Z(Z)=E[s_X(X)|Z]. Conditional Jensen yields E[s_Zs_Zᵀ]⪯E[s_Xs_Xᵀ], since their difference is E[Cov(s_X|Z)]. This is a statement about observations; reparameterizing θ has its own Jacobian transformation law and is a different operation.

Worked example

Let X∼N(μ,σ²) with σ>0 known and take Y=gd(X)=arctan(sinh X), so −π/2<Y<π/2.

The inverse is x=artanh(sin y), with dx/dy=sec y. Therefore q_μ(y)=exp(−(artanh(sin y)−μ)²/(2σ²))sec y/(σ√(2π)). Its μ-score is (artanh(sin y)−μ)/σ², and its squared expectation is 1/σ², exactly the original information. If Y is then rounded into a finite set of bins, the retained information becomes Σ_j (∂_μP_j)²/P_j and is at most 1/σ². The bundled calculation evaluates this finite-bin quantity directly from Gaussian CDFs.

The coordinate transformation is mathematically useful while its statistical information is unchanged. A benefit under a fixed finite-bit or hardware budget is possible, but it must be demonstrated for that budget and distribution.

Exact reversible observations preserve Fisher information. Finite uniform angle bins lose information in a distribution-dependent way. Curves evaluate Gaussian bin probabilities directly; they are illustrative floating-point calculations.

Scope of the result

The theorem does not forbid a transform from improving optimization behavior, finite-precision conditioning or a restricted approximation class. It also does not apply unchanged to a transform depending on an unknown θ. A bounded activation used inside a noninvertible network is not merely an observation chart.

Further development

Compare candidate transforms at a fixed bit budget by optimizing retained information under a declared prior or worst-case parameter range. Include saturation, endpoint roundoff and added sensor noise. This yields a concrete design objective rather than a claim that bounded coordinates are intrinsically more informative.

S003 · Synthesis

Finite observations generate an algebra of distinguishable classes

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

The common core of exact classification, graph signatures and probe selection is the partition induced by the available observations. On a finite state set, that partition has a complete algebraic description. This is stronger and more precise than assigning a complexity score to each state.

Definitions and assumptions

Let Ω be a finite set and f₁,…,f_m:Ω→R be exact observations, with m≥1. States x and y are equivalent when f_i(x)=f_i(y) for every i.

Let A be the unital algebra generated by the f_i under real linear combinations and pointwise products. Its elements are polynomial functions of the observation vector.

The observation algebra is exactly the set of functions constant on observation classes

If the observations induce K distinct classes, then A has dimension K and contains the indicator of each class. If every observation is invariant under a group action, no function in A can distinguish two states in the same orbit.

Derivation or proof

Every polynomial in the observations is constant on each equivalence class, giving one inclusion. For the reverse inclusion choose a linear combination h=Σa_i f_i whose values h₁,…,h_K on the classes are all distinct. Such coefficients exist because equality on any two distinct observation vectors excludes only one proper hyperplane, and finitely many proper hyperplanes cannot cover R^m. The Lagrange polynomial ℓ_j(h)=∏_(k≠j)(h−h_k)/(h_j−h_k) is the indicator of class j. These K indicators span every function constant on the classes and are independent. This also gives a constructive integer choice: take a_i=T^(i−1). Each pairwise equality is a nonzero polynomial in T of degree at most m−1, so among more than (m−1)K(K−1)/2 distinct integers at least one choice avoids all equalities. Group invariance is preserved by sums and products, proving the orbit obstruction.

Worked example

Take Ω={(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)} and first observe f(x,y)=x+y.

The observed values 0,1,1,2 give K=3 classes. Swapping coordinates preserves f, so no polynomial in f can separate (1,0) from (0,1). Add g(x,y)=x. The combined observation separates all four states; h=f+2g takes values 0,3,1,4. Its four Lagrange polynomials recover the four individual state indicators exactly. The verification script checks the indicator table using rational arithmetic.

An ambiguity caused by the observation partition cannot be repaired by increasingly elaborate postprocessing of the same data. A new probe must split the ambiguous class.

Scope of the result

The finite-set hypothesis is essential to this elementary algebraic completeness statement. Exact equality, noisy equality and approximate separability are different questions. A coordinate identity or formal feature space may include states that no physical object realizes.

Further development

For a specified family of admissible probes, define each probe’s covered pairs as those it separates. Minimum-cost separation of a finite target set becomes a weighted set-cover problem on state pairs. The certificate is exact only for that declared target population; it makes no automatic claim about unseen states or faults.

S004 · Synthesis

Heat observations separate exact recovery from stable recovery

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

The heat-kernel questions contain two distinct issues. A compressed signature can lose information exactly, whereas the full kernel can be complete but poorly conditioned for reconstruction. The exact collision in M020 and the bounds below make both statements concrete.

Definitions and assumptions

Let L and M be real symmetric positive semidefinite matrices. At t>0 define K_L(t)=exp(−tL). Matrix norms below are Euclidean operator norms.

For a labeled undirected weighted graph, L is its combinatorial Laplacian. A heat trace, the diagonal of the heat kernel and the full heat kernel are different observations.

Forward heat evolution is Lipschitz while its logarithmic inverse can amplify noise

For t≥0, ||exp(−tL)−exp(−tM)||≤t||L−M||. For t>0, the full positive-definite kernel determines L uniquely by L=−log(K_L(t))/t. If t>0 and ||L||,||M||≤Λ, then ||L−M||≤e^(tΛ)||K_L(t)−K_M(t)||/t.

Derivation or proof

Differentiate F(s)=exp(−(t−s)L)exp(−sM) with respect to s. Since F(t)−F(0)=exp(−tM)−exp(−tL), integration gives exp(−tL)−exp(−tM)=∫₀ᵗexp(−(t−s)L)(M−L)exp(−sM)ds. Each exponential has norm at most one because the generators are positive semidefinite; integrating norms proves the first bound. For positive-definite A and B with eigenvalues at least a>0, the resolvent integral for the logarithm and the identity U⁻¹−V⁻¹=U⁻¹(V−U)V⁻¹ give ||log A−log B||≤||A−B||∫₀∞(a+s)⁻²ds=||A−B||/a. The spectral lower bound for either heat matrix is e^(−tΛ); substitute a and divide by t. The principal logarithm is unique for a positive-definite matrix, which proves exact completeness of the full labeled kernel.

Worked example

The 4×4 rook graph and the Shrikhande graph have the same Laplacian spectrum 0,4 with multiplicity 6, and 8 with multiplicity 9, but different clique numbers.

Both are vertex-transitive, so every diagonal heat value equals (1+6e^(−4t)+9e^(−8t))/16 for every t. Thus even all-time vertex heat signatures cannot distinguish these two graphs. Their full heat matrices do differ up to graph isomorphism, because equality after a vertex relabeling would force equality of their recovered Laplacians. For the full-kernel inverse bound, e^(tΛ)/t is minimized at t=1/Λ when Λ>0 and the absolute kernel-error budget is held fixed.

There can be exact blindness in a compressed signature and severe numerical sensitivity in a complete observation. Completeness and robustness must be evaluated separately.

Scope of the result

The inverse bound applies to exact heat kernels of symmetric positive semidefinite generators with a common norm bound. An arbitrary noisy matrix need not remain positive definite; reconstructing a nearest valid generator is a separate constrained problem. The time 1/Λ minimizes this particular upper bound, not every practical estimator’s risk.

Further development

Combine the exact observation partition with perturbation bounds: first determine which states are distinguishable in principle, then select times and probes that provide a specified margin under the declared noise model. This avoids optimizing a highly precise score on a fundamentally incomplete signature.

S005 · Synthesis

Positivity conservation entropy and spectra share one graph update

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

A reaction–diffusion discretization becomes much more informative when its algebraic and probabilistic properties are checked together. For a finite undirected graph, one elementary step provides mass conservation, positivity, an entropy inequality and an explicit stability boundary.

Definitions and assumptions

Let a_ij=a_ji≥0, a_ii=0 define a connected finite weighted graph, with degrees d_i=Σ_j a_ij and d_max>0. Let L=diag(d)−A and P_h=I−hL.

For row probability vectors p, the update is p↦pP_h. The uniform distribution u is stationary whenever P_h is doubly stochastic.

An explicit step is a Markov update precisely within its positivity range

For 0≤h≤1/d_max, P_h is nonnegative and doubly stochastic, so it conserves probability and cannot decrease Shannon entropy. At h≤1/(2d_max), all eigenvalues of P_h are nonnegative. For h>0 in that latter range, every zero-sum vector contracts in Euclidean norm by at most 1−hλ₂(L), where λ₂ is the spectral gap.

Derivation or proof

Off-diagonal entries of P_h are h a_ij≥0, diagonal entries are 1−h d_i and each row sums to one. Symmetry gives column sums one. With φ(s)=s log s and φ(0)=0, Jensen applied to each column gives φ((pP)_j)≤Σ_i P_ij φ(p_i); summing and using row sums proves Σφ(pP)≤Σφ(p), which is the entropy statement. Symmetric diagonalization gives eigenvalues 1−hλ_i(L). The bound λ_max(L)≤2d_max follows from xᵀLx=Σ_(i<j)a_ij(x_i−x_j)²≤2Σ_i d_i x_i². Therefore h≤1/(2d_max) makes all update eigenvalues nonnegative. On the orthogonal complement of constants, the largest is 1−hλ₂. Squaring gives the corresponding residual-energy contraction.

Worked example

For a periodic one-dimensional grid with diffusion coefficient D and mesh size Δx, the nearest-neighbor generator has degree 2D/Δx².

The condition h≤1/d_max becomes r=DΔt/Δx²≤1/2, the usual positivity condition for the explicit stencil. Taking r≤1/4 also makes every Fourier multiplier nonnegative. At the endpoint r=1/2 on an even cycle, the alternating mode has multiplier −1 and does not decay: positivity and conservation hold, but convergence to equilibrium can fail through periodicity. A two-state swap gives the simplest example: p=(1,0) alternates with (0,1), preserving zero Shannon entropy.

A valid nonnegative conservative update need not be a strictly mixing update. The spectral calculation identifies the missing hypothesis and quantifies convergence once it is supplied.

Scope of the result

Reaction terms, directed edges, nonuniform stationary measures and adaptive time steps need additional analysis. Entropy monotonicity for the uniform measure does not automatically transfer to arbitrary dynamics; a relative entropy against the correct stationary measure is often the relevant quantity.

Further development

Design a discretization or graph update to satisfy a joint contract: mass, positivity, symmetry, entropy and a specified decay rate. Then verify each property algebraically before measuring prediction performance.

S006 · Synthesis

Whitening turns sensor questions into projection geometry

Classical framework with a proved synthesis and worked example

The squared-residual, covariance and observation questions admit an exact common model for Gaussian mean changes. In this model one can calculate precisely what a linear sensor panel preserves and what it loses. The same calculation gives a robust margin and an impossibility statement for universal dimension reduction.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X∼N(μ+δ,Σ), where the baseline μ and positive-definite covariance Σ are known and δ is an unknown mean shift. Let B be a k×d matrix of full row rank and observe Y=BX.

Whiten the shift as d₀=Σ^(−1/2)δ. Define C=BΣ^(1/2) and the orthogonal projection P=Cᵀ(CCᵀ)⁻¹C onto the row space of C.

A linear panel retains exactly the projected noncentrality

The statistic T_B=(Y−Bμ)ᵀ(BΣBᵀ)⁻¹(Y−Bμ) has a noncentral χ²_k law with noncentrality λ_B=||P d₀||². Full observation has λ_full=||d₀||². Hence λ_B≤λ_full, with equality exactly when d₀ lies in the retained row space. If k<d, some nonzero shifts have λ_B=0.

Derivation or proof

Write X−μ=Σ^(1/2)(Z+d₀) with Z standard normal. Multiplying by (CCᵀ)^(−1/2)C gives a k×d matrix with orthonormal rows. It maps Z to a standard k-dimensional normal, while the squared norm of the transformed shift is d₀ᵀCᵀ(CCᵀ)⁻¹Cd₀=||P d₀||². This proves the distribution and noncentrality formula. The Pythagorean identity ||d₀||²=||P d₀||²+||(I−P)d₀||² proves the inequality and equality condition. If k<d, the projection has a nontrivial kernel, giving a nonzero invisible shift. For perturbations d=d₀+e with ||e||≤ε, triangle inequality gives ||Pd||≥max(||Pd₀||−ε,0). Equality is attained by choosing e opposite to Pd₀ within the retained subspace, or by cancelling it completely when ε is large enough. Thus the exact worst-case noncentrality is max(||Pd₀||−ε,0)².

Worked example

Take Σ=I₃ and let B retain the first two coordinates. Then P=diag(1,1,0).

A shift δ=(3,4,0) has λ_full=λ_B=25. A shift δ=(0,0,5) also has λ_full=25 but λ_B=0: the selected panel sees the null distribution exactly. For the first shift with whitened uncertainty radius ε=2, the worst-case retained noncentrality is (5−2)²=9, attained by perturbation e=(−6/5,−8/5,0). Under the null, T_B∼χ²₂, with mean 2 and variance 4; the full statistic has three degrees of freedom. Comparing only raw residual scores without this calibration can be misleading.

Exact optimization for a declared finite list of shifts is useful and checkable. Preserving every possible shift while reducing dimension is impossible in this model. Robustness can be expressed as a proved geometric margin rather than a hope that selected probes generalize.

Scope of the result

Known Gaussian covariance, mean-shift alternatives and linear measurements are strong assumptions. Estimated baselines change calibration, non-Gaussian tails can invalidate χ² laws and nonlinear features need their own analysis. The noncentrality comparison alone is not a universal theorem about every detector at every significance level.

Further development

For a finite target family {d_j}, choose a minimum-cost panel subject to max(||P_B d_j||−ε_j,0)²≥τ_j. Solve a small instance exactly and report every target and uncertainty set. This produces a concrete experimental-design certificate whose scope is visible.

S007 · Synthesis

Exact finite polynomial closure for triangular maps and its resonance strata

A complete theorem for the specified triangular family with exact examples; no novelty claim

The univariate degree-growth obstruction in M018 has a substantial positive counterpart. Every triangular polynomial map T(x,y)=(ax,by+p(x)) admits an exact finite linear feature representation containing the original coordinate functions. Its smallest such space can be classified completely by collisions among the eigenvalues a^k. Repeated nonlinear eigenvalues reduce the required feature count, while resonances with b determine the only possible nontrivial Jordan chain. The same calculation yields an exact iterate formula and a criterion for removing the forcing by a polynomial fiber translation. An invertible coupled counterexample demonstrates why this is a theorem about a specified family, not a universal finite-closure principle.

Definitions and assumptions

Work over F=R or C with the polynomial ring F[x,y]. Let a,b∈F and p(x)=Σ_(k=0)^d c_kx^k, with zero coefficients omitted from its support. The Koopman operator is U_Tf=f∘T.

A feature space is an F-linear subspace W of polynomials with U_TW⊂W. It is not required to be closed under pointwise products. A finite-dimensional algebra containing x would already be impossible because it would contain every x^n.

Require W to contain 1,x,y. Let q(x)=Σ_(k≥2)c_kx^k, S={k≥2:c_k≠0}, Λ={a^k:k∈S}, and v_λ(x)=Σ_(k∈S,a^k=λ)c_kx^k for λ∈Λ.

On the diagonal subspace E=span{1,x,v_λ:λ∈Λ}, group all terms of p by their eigenvalue: p_μ(x)=Σ_(k≥0,a^k=μ)c_kx^k. For k=0 use a^0=1, including a=0. Missing groups mean the zero polynomial.

Minimal feature dimension, resonance normal form and exact iterates

The unique smallest invariant linear feature space containing 1,x,y is W_min=span{1,x,y,v_λ:λ∈Λ}, and dim W_min=3+|Λ|. Its action is U1=1, Ux=ax, Uv_λ=λv_λ and Uy=by+p. Put z=y+Σ_(μ≠b)p_μ/(b−μ). Then Uz=bz+p_b and Up_b=bp_b. Consequently U|W_min is diagonalizable exactly when p_b=0; if p_b≠0 it has precisely one size-two Jordan block at b, with every other block of size one. Writing D={1,a,b}∪Λ as a set, its minimal polynomial is ∏_(μ∈D)(t−μ), multiplied by one further factor (t−b) when p_b≠0. Its characteristic polynomial, with multiplicities retained, is (t−1)(t−a)(t−b)∏_(λ∈Λ)(t−λ).

For n≥0 the exact state iterate is x_n=a^n x and y_n=b^n y+Σ_μ C_n(b,μ)p_μ(x), where C_0=0 and C_n(b,μ)=Σ_(j=0)^(n−1)b^(n−1−j)μ^j. For b≠μ this is (b^n−μ^n)/(b−μ); for b=μ≠0 it is n b^(n−1). The convolution sum is the definition at b=μ=0 and removes any 0^0 ambiguity: C_1=1 and C_n=0 for n≥2.

Derivation or proof

The proposed space is invariant because each v_λ is a polynomial eigenfunction, while Uy=by+c_0+c_1x+Σv_λ belongs to it. Every invariant W containing 1,x,y must contain q=Uy−by−c_0−c_1x and hence U^jq for every j. The distinct-eigenvalue decomposition is U^jq=Σ_(λ∈Λ)λ^jv_λ. Its first |Λ| rows form a Vandermonde matrix with nonzero determinant, including when one eigenvalue is zero. Therefore W contains each v_λ. Equivalently, applying the Lagrange spectral projector ∏_(ν≠λ)(U−νI)/(λ−ν) to q extracts v_λ. This proves minimality. The nonlinear group polynomials have disjoint nonempty monomial supports of degree at least two, so they are mutually independent and independent of 1,x,y. Thus the dimension formula follows even if a nonlinear eigenvalue coincides with 1 or a; that coincidence does not permit discarding the nonlinear vector.

The restriction to E is diagonal in the displayed basis, though its eigenvalues may repeat. Decompose p into its E-eigencomponents p_μ. Direct calculation gives U(y+h)−b(y+h)=p+(U−b)h. Taking h=Σ_(μ≠b)p_μ/(b−μ) cancels every nonresonant component and leaves p_b. If p_b=0, z is an additional eigenvector independent of E and completes an eigenbasis. If p_b≠0, z maps to p_b under U−b and p_b maps to zero, giving a Jordan chain of length two. No chain can be longer because E is diagonal. Replacing a basis of E_b by one containing p_b leaves exactly one such chain and all remaining vectors as eigenvectors. The characteristic and minimal polynomial formulas now follow, including the case in which b equals several listed diagonal eigenvalues.

The iterate formula follows by solving y_(n+1)=b y_n+p(a^n x) and expanding the forcing into p_μ(a^j x)=μ^j p_μ(x). Induction produces the convolution sum; multiplying it by b−μ telescopes to b^n−μ^n. Resonance makes every term of the sum equal b^(n−1), which explains the factor n. Finally a polynomial fiber change H(x,y)=(x,y+h(x)) removes p entirely exactly when c_k+(a^k−b)h_k=0 for every coefficient k. This is possible precisely when all resonant c_k vanish, equivalently p_b=0, and the displayed h supplies it. All such h differ by a polynomial satisfying h(ax)=bh(x), so resonant eigenfunctions describe the freedom in the coordinate change. This is a criterion for that specified class of coordinate changes, not a classification of arbitrary polynomial conjugacies.

Worked example

The twelve exact replay cases include generic real eigenvalues, a=0, a=1, a=−1, affine forcing, zero forcing and the complex fourth root of unity a=i. All coefficients and all calculations are rational or Gaussian-rational. The following examples expose different structural regimes.

For a=2, b=4 and p=x²+x³, Λ={4,8}, so W_min=span{1,x,y,x²,x³} has dimension five. The b=4 component is x² and creates a size-two Jordan chain. Taking z=y−x³/4 gives Uz=4z+x². The exact iterate is y_n=4^n y+n4^(n−1)x²+(8^n−4^n)x³/4 for n≥1. This is a nonlinear map with a finite exact linear feature evolution, and the resonant term has the predicted n factor.

For a=−1, b=1 and p=x²+2x³+3x⁴, the even powers form v_+=x²+3x⁴ and the odd power forms v_−=2x³. Dimension is five rather than the six obtained by retaining every monomial separately. The shifted coordinate z=y+x³ satisfies Uz=z+v_+, so the minimal polynomial is (t−1)²(t+1). For a=0, b=0 and p=3+2x+x²+2x⁵, the single nonlinear group is q=x²+2x⁵, dimension is four, and z=y−3 satisfies Uz=2x+q and U²z=0. This is the zero-eigenvalue Jordan case, not a reason to discard q.

For a=i and p=x²+x⁶+2x³+3x⁷+x⁴+x⁸, six nonlinear monomials collapse into the three residue groups modulo four, so dimension is six. Their eigenvalues are −1,−i,1. Choosing b=−1 creates a resonant chain; choosing b=2 does not. Conversely, a=2,b=3,p=3+2x+x²+x³ has no resonance: z=y+3/2+2x−x²−x³/5 gives the actual two-coordinate linear dynamics x′=2x,z′=3z. Nevertheless any invariant linear space required to contain the original y still needs the nonlinear readout features and has dimension five.

For contrast, the coupled invertible map G(x,y)=(y,y²−x) has inverse G^(−1)(x,y)=(x²−y,x). If Y_n=U_G^n y, then Y_0=y, Y_1=y²−x and Y_(n+1)=Y_n²−Y_(n−1). Induction gives total degree 2^n with leading monomial y^(2^n); the lower-degree subtracted term cannot cancel it. The Y_n are therefore linearly independent, so no finite invariant polynomial feature space containing y exists. Invertibility by itself neither guarantees nor obstructs finite closure.

Finite closure, feature dimension, eigenvalue collision and Jordan resonance are separate questions and all are decidable for the triangular family. The verifier independently forms polynomial compositions and exact ranks, checks closure and generation, verifies every asserted Jordan relation and minimal-polynomial factor, and compares eight iterates with the closed formula in twelve cases. The coupled-map calculation illustrates the proved degree-growth obstruction rather than relying on a fitted approximation.

Scope of the result

The classification holds for the specified triangular polynomial family over R or C and for invariant linear spaces containing 1,x,y. It does not classify all polynomial systems, all finite smooth feature embeddings or all nonlinear conjugacies. A different observation requirement, nonlinear output recovery, restriction to a finite orbit or quotient relations among states can change the minimal representation problem. At an exact root of unity the dimension can drop, while parameters arbitrarily close to that stratum retain the generic dimension and may produce ill-conditioned Vandermonde coordinates. Exact algebraic dimension therefore does not imply robust numerical recoverability.

Further development

Parameter strata are explicit. For fixed nonzero nonlinear support S, real a outside {0,1,−1} gives |Λ|=|S|. At a=0 or a=1, every nonlinear term belongs to one group, so a genuinely nonlinear p gives dimension four. At a=−1 the count is the number of occupied parities, giving dimension four or five. Over C, a≠0 that is not a root of unity gives distinct nonlinear eigenvalues. If a has finite multiplicative order h, group exponents by their residue modulo h and count the occupied residues. Coefficient hyperplanes c_k=0 change the support. For a fixed finite degree, collision loci satisfy a^k=a^l for some supported distinct exponents, so the possible collision strata form a finite union of zero and root-of-unity loci. When the nonlinear support has at most one exponent, there are no pairwise collision strata. Jordan resonance occurs exactly when (b=1 and c_0≠0), or (b=a and c_1≠0), or (b=a^k for at least one supported k≥2). Because these components use independent monomials, they cannot cancel each other when eigenvalues coincide. These statements classify the exact dimension and Jordan strata of this family. A useful further investigation is a perturbation analysis near a collision or resonance, rather than an unsupported claim that nearby numerical features share the lower-dimensional exact closure.

S008 · Synthesis

An exact robust Gaussian sensor panel with a strict greedy gap and a blind direction

Constructed finite model proved and exhaustively certified

This worked design turns the projection formula in S006 into a complete exact optimization problem. Six coordinate channels, six declared mean-shift centers, nonuniform costs and six uncertainty balls give a unique cost13 optimum. A fully specified gain-per-cost greedy rule instead costs16. Every channel participates in an inclusion-minimal feasible panel, no single channel is cost-dominated, and none of the six fault constraints is implied by the others. A deliberately withheld direction is nevertheless invisible to the optimum panel. All of these claims concern this constructed mathematical instance, with no empirical dataset or application-performance claim.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X∼N(μ+d+e,I₆), with a known baseline μ and deterministic mean shift d+e. A coordinate panel S⊆{A,B,C,D,E,F} observes the selected coordinates. Its centered squared statistic T_S=Σ_{i∈S}(X_i−μ_i)² has a noncentral χ²_|S| law with noncentrality λ_S(d+e)=Σ_{i∈S}(d_i+e_i)². The empty panel is allowed in the finite enumeration but cannot meet the positive target.

The six costs and coverage sets are A:(6,{1,3,5}), B:(7,{1,2,3}), C:(6,{4}), D:(6,{2,3,5,6}), E:(7,{2,4,5,6}), F:(4,{1,6}). Define the six rational centers by d⁽ʲ⁾_i=2 when channel i covers target j and zero otherwise. Thus d⁽¹⁾=(2,2,0,0,0,2), d⁽²⁾=(0,2,0,2,2,0), d⁽³⁾=(2,2,0,2,0,0), d⁽⁴⁾=(0,0,2,0,2,0), d⁽⁵⁾=(2,0,0,2,2,0), and d⁽⁶⁾=(0,0,0,2,2,2).

For each center, the declared uncertainty set is the full Euclidean ball ||e||₂≤1 in six-dimensional whitened coordinates. Feasibility means inf_{||e||≤1}λ_S(d⁽ʲ⁾+e)≥1 for every j=1,…,6. Costs add across selected channels. Noncentrality is the declared design criterion; panels of different sizes have different null degrees of freedom and require their own significance calibration.

The greedy heuristic starts with no channels. At each step it chooses the unused channel maximizing the number of newly satisfied target constraints divided by its cost; ties would be settled alphabetically. It stops when all six constraints are satisfied. There are no maximizing ties along the path in this instance.

Exact robust-margin reduction and a unique finite optimum

For any orthogonal coordinate projection P_S and ε≥0, inf_{||e||≤ε}||P_S(d+e)||²=max(||P_Sd||−ε,0)². Consequently the declared ε=1,target1 problem is feasible exactly when every center has selected energy at least4. The unique minimum-cost panel is {A,E}, of cost13. Greedy selects D,F,C and has cost16, a strict ratio16/13. The optimum is blind to the withheld center d*=2e_D, whose full-observation noncentrality is4.

Derivation or proof

Triangle inequality and ||P_Se||≤||e|| give ||P_S(d+e)||≥max(||P_Sd||−ε,0). If ||P_Sd||>ε, choose e=−εP_Sd/||P_Sd||. If ||P_Sd||≤ε, choose e=−P_Sd. Both perturbations are allowed and attain the bound, including the zero case. For positive target1 and ε=1, the inequality max(√λ−1,0)²≥1 is equivalent to λ≥4. Every nonzero center coordinate is2, so the energy condition is equivalent to selecting at least one channel from that target’s coverage support. The statistical robustness problem has therefore reduced exactly, without approximation, to this declared weighted set-cover instance.

The panel A,E covers all targets and costs13. Any feasible panel containing C needs at least two additional channels: no pair C plus one other channel covers all six targets. The cheapest possible two other channels cost4+6, so such a panel costs at least16. A feasible panel not containing C must contain E, because only C and E cover target4. At total cost at most13, E can be accompanied by at most one other channel, since the two cheapest remaining costs are4 and6. E alone fails; E,F misses target3; E,D misses target1; E,A succeeds and costs13; E,B exceeds the budget. Thus A,E is the unique feasible panel at cost at most13. This gives an analytic optimality and uniqueness certificate in addition to the enumeration.

Initially D has gain/cost4/6=2/3, uniquely larger than E’s4/7 or any other ratio. After D, the missing targets are1 and4. F supplies target1 at ratio1/4, uniquely beating A’s1/6 and the other choices. After D,F only target4 remains; C’s1/6 beats E’s1/7. Greedy therefore returns D,F,C of total cost16. No claim is made that this heuristic is worst possible, or that the example estimates its usual behavior.

For the withheld vector2e_D, P_{A,E}d*=0. Its selected Gaussian law is exactly the same as the baseline law. Hence every test using only those observed coordinates, including repeated independent samples, has the same rejection probability under this alternative as under the null. Full observation retains norm2 and worst-case noncentrality(2−1)²=1 under the same unit uncertainty. More generally, any rank-k linear panel with k<6 has a nonzero kernel. Selecting an appropriately scaled shift in that kernel proves that no such panel can preserve all mean-shift directions. This is an information obstruction, not a failure of the finite optimization certificate.

Worked example

The portable supplement_verify.py enumerates every one of the2⁶=64 coordinate panels. It records the selected channels, integer cost, six integer center energies, covered-target list and feasibility flag. It also records the exact greedy candidates at every step, inclusion-minimal panels and witnesses that each target constraint is necessary.

There are34 feasible panels. The optimum A,E has center energies(4,4,4,4,8,4). Its six exact worst-case noncentralities are(1,1,1,1,9−4√2,1). For the five energy4 centers, subtracting one unit in their sole active retained coordinate attains1. For target5, subtract(1/√2,1/√2) in coordinates A,E; this perturbation has norm1 and attains9−4√2. Greedy D,F,C has center energies(4,4,4,4,4,8), and its minimum robust margin is also1 for the declared targets, at the higher cost16. A withheld center2e_D has selected noncentrality0 in A,E but4 in D,F,C and the full panel. For the simple Gaussian center alternative, the selected Kullback–Leibler divergence from baseline is half the selected noncentrality, so it is zero for the withheld direction in the optimum panel.

To see that the six channels and six constraints are substantive, inspect the additional exact witnesses. No channel has its entire target set contained in that of another channel of equal or smaller cost. Each channel belongs to at least one inclusion-minimal feasible panel. For each target j, selecting all channels that do not cover j satisfies the other five targets and fails exactly j. Thus no target constraint is implied by the other five. The verifier checks all these finite properties rather than relying on a picture of the incidence matrix.

The finite optimum is exact, has a strict cost advantage over the stated greedy rule, and remains unable to guarantee unlisted directions. The constructive counterexample is compatible with all the declared-target certificates. Exact optimization, robustness to a specified ball, detector calibration and universal observability are distinct questions that can now be stated and checked separately.

Scope of the result

This is a deliberately constructed six-channel Gaussian location model with known identity covariance and additive deterministic mean uncertainty. Its costs, centers and radius are mathematical inputs, not measured quantities. The objective constrains worst-case noncentrality; it is not an empirical accuracy guarantee, and equal noncentralities in different degrees of freedom do not by themselves imply equal test power. Estimated covariance, covariance-changing faults, temporal dependence, nonlinear sensors and unmodeled shifts need separate analysis. The withheld vector demonstrates a scope boundary and does not invalidate optimality for the declared family. The general robust-margin formula is classical projection geometry, and the small exact instance is an illustrative certificate rather than a claim of new general optimization theory.

Further development

Replace identity covariance by a fixed rational positive-definite matrix Σ and let each nonempty panel measure specified linear combinations with a full-row-rank matrix B. Then BΣBᵀ is invertible and λ_S=dᵀK_Bd, where K_B=Bᵀ(BΣBᵀ)⁻¹B; state the uncertainty ball in whitened coordinates. When B and Σ are rational, K_B is rational. The Euclidean orthogonal projector in whitened coordinates is instead P=Σ^(1/2)K_BΣ^(1/2), which need not be rational: for Σ=diag(1,2) and B=(1,1), K_B is the all-ones matrix divided by3, whereas P=[[1,√2],[√2,2]]/3. Redundant measurement rows require a separately stated pseudoinverse and observation-rank convention. For finitely many candidate full-row-rank panels, exhaustive enumeration still certifies the optimum, although robust thresholds can involve algebraic numbers. A further exact task is to classify the parameter cells in costs or radii where the optimal panel changes, while retaining the nullspace impossibility for any universal dimension reduction.

S009 · Synthesis

Exact tree synchronization certificates and observable phase information

Full nondegenerate tree branch classification and quantitative bounds proved here; rational examples verified; no general cyclic or global-convergence claim

A finite tree makes the nonlinear locking problem unusually exact: every edge flow is fixed by a cut sum, the cohesive phase differences follow by arcsine, and stability is certified by a positive weighted Laplacian. The same calculation separates dynamic stability from observability. Relative-phase measurements lose common phase and common frequency, while even a stable synchronized star has exact nonlinear motions invisible to a center-only sensor. The locking criterion is classical; the derivation, rational certificate, sensitivity bounds and observation examples here are an explicit synthesis, not a claim of a newly discovered synchronization theorem.

Definitions and assumptions

Let T=(V,E) be an undirected connected tree with n≥2 vertices, arbitrarily oriented edges and incidence matrix B∈R^(n×(n−1)). A column has −1 at its tail and +1 at its head. Every edge has coupling K_e>0.

Use the symmetric Kuramoto equation θ̇=ω−B diag(K)sin(Bᵀθ), componentwise sine. Since 1ᵀB=0, mean frequency is Ω=(1/n)1ᵀω. In the rotating frame set b=ω−Ω1, so 1ᵀb=0 and θ̇=b−B diag(K)sin(Bᵀθ).

General phase states lie on (R/2πZ)^n modulo the diagonal common-phase circle. A cohesive lift has δ=Bᵀθ with |δ_e|<π/2. Fixing 1ᵀθ=0 removes the common-phase direction locally. For 0<γ<π/2 one can instead impose the closed bound |δ_e|≤γ.

For each oriented edge e, remove it and let H_e be the component containing its head. Define the cut flow f_e=Σ_(i∈H_e)b_i. At a locked state the flow equation is Bf=b.

The linearization at a cohesive locked state is η̇=−L_wη, where L_w=B diag(w)Bᵀ and w_e=K_e cosδ_e=√(K_e²−f_e²)>0. Let λ₂ denote the least positive Laplacian eigenvalue.

Necessary and sufficient tree locking, local stability, boundary sensitivity and observability

If every |f_e|<K_e, there are exactly 2^(n−1) locked equilibria on the phase torus modulo common phase. Each edge independently selects arcsin(f_e/K_e) or π−arcsin(f_e/K_e), modulo 2π. An equilibrium with q negative edge cosines has exactly q unstable linear directions on the phase quotient; there are C(n−1,q) such equilibria. Thus precisely one branch, with all edge cosines positive, is locally exponentially stable and cohesive. A state with |δ_e|≤γ<π/2 exists exactly when |f_e|≤K_e sinγ for every edge. If any |f_e|>K_e there is no locked equilibrium; if exactly r edges saturate and the others are strictly feasible, the count becomes 2^(n−1−r) and the quotient Hessian has r zero directions. For the stable branch, edge-flow sensitivity is ∂δ_e/∂f_e=1/w_e. The rate bounds are min_e(w_e)λ₂(BBᵀ)≤λ₂(L_w)≤n w_e/[s(n−s)] for every edge separating s and n−s vertices. A full relative-phase panel leaves only common phase unobservable and a uniform natural-frequency shift unidentifiable; a restricted center-only star sensor can miss additional exact nonlinear trajectories.

Derivation or proof

First prove the cut formula. A connected tree has n−1 edges and B has full column rank. One elementary proof removes a leaf: a zero-divergence flow has zero flow on its only incident edge, and induction removes all edges. The column image is contained in 1⊥ and has dimension n−1, so it equals 1⊥. Thus Bf=b has exactly one solution. Summing the divergence equation over H_e cancels every internal edge and leaves +f_e at the unique crossing edge, giving the displayed cut sum. Conversely those sums produce the unique solution; this can also be constructed by repeatedly eliminating leaves. No nonlinear approximation has been made.

At an equilibrium, f_e=K_e sinδ_e. Strict cohesion forces |f_e|<K_e and gives the unique principal value δ_e=arcsin(f_e/K_e). On a tree, any collection of real edge differences lifts to node phases: choose a root phase and integrate differences along the unique root-to-node path. There are no cycle-sum compatibility conditions. Subtracting the node mean fixes the chosen gauge. This proves sufficiency and uniqueness modulo common phase. Replacing the interval by [−γ,γ] gives precisely |f_e|≤K_e sinγ because sine is strictly increasing there. For a graph with cycles, the integration step can fail even when individual edge bounds hold, so this proof must not be extended merely by reusing its inequalities.

For the full branch classification, consider phase differences modulo 2π rather than restricting to the principal interval. Each strict scalar equation sinδ_e=f_e/K_e has exactly two distinct circle solutions, with cosines of opposite sign. A tree integrates every edge assignment uniquely modulo common phase, so there are exactly 2^(n−1) equilibria. On 1⊥ the linear map T=Bᵀ is an isomorphism. The quotient Hessian quadratic form is x↦(Tx)ᵀdiag(K_e cosδ_e)(Tx), and Sylvester’s law of inertia therefore gives exactly one negative direction per negative edge cosine, one positive direction per positive cosine and one zero direction per saturated edge. The dynamics has the negative of this Hessian as its Jacobian, so q negative cosines give q unstable eigenvalues. Choosing the q negative branches among n−1 edges gives C(n−1,q). All-positive cosines give the unique local minimum; every other nondegenerate branch is a saddle or the all-negative repeller. If r edges saturate, each of those sine equations has only one circle solution, giving 2^(n−1−r) equilibria with r extra linear zero directions. These boundary statements classify the algebraic count and Hessian inertia only; higher-order behavior at a zero eigenvalue is not inferred.

For local stability, differentiate the vector field. Its negative Jacobian is L_w. For every x, xᵀL_wx=Σ_e w_e(Bᵀx)_e². With positive w and connected T, this vanishes exactly when x is constant. Hence the common-phase eigenvalue is zero and every mean-zero eigenvalue is positive. This proves transverse linear stability, and the nonlinear conclusion follows directly from a local gradient estimate. On a mean-zero cohesive lift define U(θ)=−bᵀθ−Σ_e K_e cos((Bᵀθ)_e); the rotating-frame dynamics is −∇U. Around a strict cohesive equilibrium choose a sufficiently small convex ball inside a domain |δ_e|≤γ<π/2. Its Hessian is bounded below on 1⊥ by mI with m=cosγ·λ₂(B diag(K)Bᵀ)>0. If x=θ−θ*, then d||x||²/dt≤−2m||x||² in that ball. The vector field points inward on its boundary, so sufficiently near initial states stay there and converge at least as e^(−mt). This is a local argument; no invariance or attraction of the entire cohesive domain has been assumed.

Differentiate arcsin(f_e/K_e) while holding K_e fixed to get ∂δ_e/∂f_e=1/√(K_e²−f_e²)=1/w_e. Because f_e is a linear cut sum of b, this also gives exact frequency sensitivities. Holding the other flows fixed and changing only f_e shifts the phases by a constant on each component of the cut. In the mean-zero gauge, the two constants differ by dδ_e; therefore ||∂θ/∂f_e||₂=√(s(n−s)/n)/w_e. Thus sensitivity diverges as an edge saturates, even though the equilibrium remains locally stable before the boundary.

The rate estimates quantify the same boundary. The inequality L_w≽w_min BBᵀ gives λ₂(L_w)≥w_min λ₂(BBᵀ) by the Rayleigh principle on 1⊥. For the upper bound, use a test vector equal to (n−s)/n on a component of size s and −s/n on the other. Its only nonzero edge difference is one across the removed edge, its squared norm is s(n−s)/n and its energy is w_e. Its Rayleigh quotient is n w_e/[s(n−s)], proving the bound. If one bridge weight tends to zero, the convergence rate therefore tends to zero; the tree is dynamically approaching disconnection in its linearized restoring force.

For observability, let A=−L_w and C=Bᵀ. Then ker C=span{1}, A1=0, and the unobservable linear subspace ⋂_(j≥0)ker(CA^j) is exactly span{1}: the j=0 kernel already gives an upper bound, while common phase survives every power. For sine measurements the local derivative is diag(cosδ*)Bᵀ, whose diagonal factor is invertible under strict cohesion, so the same conclusion holds. Adding an absolute phase measurement e_rᵀ makes the stacked instantaneous observation injective. Separately, replacing ω by ω+c1 changes a solution to θ(t)+ct1 and leaves every relative-phase output unchanged. Relative data can identify b but cannot determine Ω without a time or phase reference.

A stronger blindness example does not rely on common phase. Take a star with center 1 and identical coupling k>0, equal natural frequencies removed by a rotating frame, and at least two leaves. Put θ₁(t)=0, θ₀(t)=a(t), θ₂(t)=−a(t), and all other leaf phases zero, where ȧ=−k sin a. The center receives sin a+sin(−a)=0, and each leaf equation is satisfied. For |a₀|<π, a(t)=2 arctan(tan(a₀/2)e^(−kt)) is an exact solution converging to synchronization. Its center output is identically zero, just as for the equilibrium, so arbitrarily close nonequilibrium states are not identifiable from that output. At linear order, leaf vectors with zero center and zero leaf sum form an (n−2)-dimensional invisible eigenspace with eigenvalue −k. Adding a measurement of one displaced leaf or one of its incident edges detects this particular pair motion, while measuring every edge difference detects all mean-zero states. Thus local convergence and local observability are independent properties even within an exactly solvable stable family.

Worked example

Use vertices 0,1,2,3 with edges oriented 0→1, 1→2, 1→3. Let Ω=2, b=(−1/2,1/6,1/3,0), ω=(3/2,13/6,7/3,2), couplings K=(5/6,13/15,1/2), and cut flows f=(1/2,1/3,0). These are rational input data.

The incidence equation is Bf=(−f₀,f₀−f₁−f₂,f₁,f₂)=b. The edge sines are s=(3/5,5/13,0), and choose positive cosines c=(4/5,12/13,1). The exact unit phasors are z₀=1, z₁=(4+3i)/5, z₂=(33+56i)/65 and z₃=(4+3i)/5. Their head-tail ratios have precisely those rational real and imaginary parts. Equivalently, choose phases (0,α,α+β,α), where α=arctan(3/4) and β=arctan(5/12), before subtracting the mean. All edge differences are principal and even satisfy |sinδ_e|<4/5, a strict certificate for the cohesive bound γ=arcsin(4/5).

The Hessian weights are w=Kc=(2/3,4/5,1/2). Every principal cofactor of the stable weighted tree Laplacian equals their product 4/15, and its kernel is exactly the common-phase line. The unweighted four-node star has λ₂=1, so the transverse rate obeys 1/2≤λ₂(L_w)≤2/3, the upper bound using the leaf-3 cut. These bounds and the rational Laplacian entries can be checked without evaluating any inverse trigonometric function. Flipping any subset of the three edge cosine signs, while leaving the sine values fixed, constructs all eight phase-locked branches with rational phasors. Their unstable dimensions have counts 1,3,3,1 for indices 0,1,2,3; the stable branch is the sole index-zero case.

Now retain K and the first two flows but replace f₂ by q∈(−1/2,1/2). This changes b to (−1/2,1/6−q,1/3,q). The third weight is w₂(q)=√(1/4−q²), which is always the minimum weight. Consequently w₂(q)≤λ₂(L_w(q))≤(4/3)w₂(q), while dδ₂/dq=1/w₂(q) and the mean-zero phase sensitivity norm is √3/(2w₂(q)). Thus λ₂ times the edge-phase sensitivity stays between 1 and 4/3, while the rate vanishes and sensitivity diverges at either saturation boundary. The rational parametrization q=t/(1+t²), w₂=(1−t²)/(2(1+t²)) for 0≤t<1 supplies exact examples arbitrarily close to the boundary.

The nonlinear equilibrium, its positive Hessian and its cut-flow certificate are explicit. The parameter family proves a quantitative relation between critical slowing and ill-conditioned phase reconstruction. The separate exact star trajectory proves that a stable network can still be invisible to an inadequate observation panel.

Scope of the result

The theorem covers symmetric positive couplings on a finite tree and a specified principal cohesive lift. It does not assert global convergence, attraction from arbitrary phases, robustness to noise or delays, or sufficiency of edge bounds on general cycles. At a saturated edge |f_e|=K_e the positive-weight and exponential-stability proof fails; existence at the closed π/2 boundary does not restore its missing rate. The rational verifier certifies finite examples and exact identities, not the general theorem in a proof assistant. The tree-locking criterion is established literature; no novelty claim is made for it.

Further development

The completed operational consequence is a two-stage certificate: first verify Bf=b and edge feasibility to certify a cohesive equilibrium; then verify the rank of the actual observation map on the mean-zero state space. For a full edge panel the residual blindness is exactly common phase, whereas a center-only symmetric-star panel fails even for exact nonlinear trajectories. If a graph contains cycles, an additional cycle-compatibility problem must be solved before reusing this certificate design.

S010 · Synthesis

The complete one-magnon Gaudin family and its scalar equations

Classical rank-one structure developed into a proved finite-sector theorem with exact rational and exceptional certificates

The two-site calculation extends to an explicit theorem for every number of spin-1/2 sites in the one-magnon sector. Simple critical points of one polynomial give a complete joint eigenbasis. For distinct real sites these critical points necessarily interlace and are simple, so this sector has no missing regular Bethe states apart from the explicitly retained uniform descendant. A three-site rational example is solved on the entire eight-dimensional tensor space, and the complex discriminant-zero locus exhibits a genuine Jordan degeneration.

Definitions and assumptions

Let n≥2, take pairwise distinct complex sites z₁,…,z_n and put p(x)=∏_i(x−z_i). The one-magnon space has basis e_j, meaning that only spin j is down.

Use Ω_ij=(1/2)h_i h_j+e_i f_j+f_i e_j and H_i=Σ_(j≠i)Ω_ij/(z_i−z_j). Define E_i⁰=(1/2)Σ_(j≠i)1/(z_i−z_j) and the uniform vector u=Σ_j e_j.

For w not equal to a site, define a_j(w)=1/(w−z_j), B(w)=Σ_j a_j(w)=p′(w)/p(w), and v(w)=Σ_j a_j(w)e_j. The scalar equation uses u_w(x)=p′(x)/(2p(x))−1/(x−w) and V_w=u_w²−u_w′. The symbol u_w is a scalar connection coefficient and is distinct from the uniform vector u.

Critical points give a complete spectral decomposition under the stated simple-root condition

If p′ has n−1 distinct roots w₁,…,w_(n−1), the vectors u,v(w₁),…,v(w_(n−1)) are a basis of the one-magnon space. Their H_i eigenvalues are E_i⁰ and E_i(w)=E_i⁰+a_i(w), respectively. For distinct real sites, the hypothesis always holds: exactly one critical point lies in each consecutive-site interval. For every critical w, V_w=(3/4)Σ_i(x−z_i)^(−2)+Σ_iE_i(w)/(x−z_i), with no pole at w. Its scalar equation has a rational-over-sqrt(p) fundamental pair of Wronskian one.

Derivation or proof

The action on a pair of sites is explicit: Ω_ij e_i=−e_i/2+e_j, Ω_ij e_j=e_i−e_j/2, while Ω_ij e_k=e_k/2 if k differs from both. Therefore, for k≠i, the kth component of H_i v(w) is E_i⁰a_k+(a_i−a_k)/(z_i−z_k)=(E_i⁰+a_i)a_k. Its ith component equals E_i⁰a_i−a_iΣ_(j≠i)a_j=(E_i⁰+a_i)a_i−a_iB(w). At a critical point B=0, this is the claimed eigenvector. Directly H_i u=E_i⁰u. For any fixed i, the n displayed eigenvalues are distinct because the map w↦1/(w−z_i) is injective and never zero. They therefore give a basis, proving completeness within this finite sector without assuming it. In particular the H_i are simultaneously diagonal in that basis. For real ordered sites, Rolle’s theorem supplies at least one root of p′ in each of n−1 disjoint gaps. Since deg p′=n−1, these are all its roots, each simple. The vectors are orthogonal: uᵀv(w)=B(w)=0 and v(w)ᵀv(v)=[B(w)−B(v)]/(v−w)=0 for distinct critical roots. Their squared norm is −p″(w)/p(w), which is positive for real sites and nonzero whenever the critical root is simple. Thus P_w=v(w)v(w)ᵀ/[−p″(w)/p(w)] and P₀=uuᵀ/n give explicit spectral projectors.

For the scalar equation, a physical site z_i has u_w=1/[2(x−z_i)]+E_i(w)+O(x−z_i), so V_w has double coefficient 3/4 and simple residue E_i(w). At x=w, write u_w=−1/(x−w)+B(w)/2+O(x−w); the double pole cancels and the simple residue is −B(w), hence zero at a Bethe root. Since V_w decays at infinity, its partial fractions are exactly the asserted expression. One solution is y₁=(x−w)/sqrt(p(x)). Reduction of order gives y₂=y₁∫p(x)/(x−w)² dx. Taylor expansion at w has no linear term because p′(w)=0, so an explicit numerator is q₂(x)=−p(w)+Σ_(m=2)^n p^(m)(w)(x−w)^m/[m!(m−1)]. Then y₂=q₂/sqrt(p), and y₁y₂′−y₁′y₂=1. Both solutions are regular at the apparent point w. Their only multivalued factor is a common square root, so the resulting monodromy is scalar and projectively trivial. This is a concrete scalar-oper statement with all normalizations fixed.

Worked example

Take three sites z=(0,1,8/3), and separately study z=(0,1,t) as a complex parameter family.

For z=(0,1,8/3), p′ has roots 2 and4/9. Their highest one-magnon coefficient vectors are (1/2,1,−3/2) and (9/4,−9/5,−9/20), giving Hamiltonian triples (−3/16,6/5,−81/80) and (25/16,−8/5,3/80). Each generates a two-dimensional spin doublet under total lowering. The vacuum generates a quartet with triple (−11/16,1/5,39/80). The verifier constructs all eight rational eigenvectors and all three full 8×8 Hamiltonians, verifies joint eigenvector relations and rank eight, and checks both scalar differential equations through identically zero residual polynomials and Wronskians. As another independent exact example, four sites (−7,−1,1,7) have critical roots (−5,0,5), so their complete four-dimensional one-magnon diagonalization and three scalar solution pairs remain rational.

For z=(0,1,t), p′=3x²−2(1+t)x+t and its root discriminant is 4(t²−t+1). The exceptional sites are t=(1±i√3)/2. They are distinct from 0 and1, but the two Bethe roots coalesce at w=(1+t)/3. Here B(w)=B′(w)=0. Differentiating the exact off-shell relation gives (H_i−E_i(w))v′(w)=−a_i(w)²v(w). The right side is nonzero, and v′ is independent of v because distinct sites prevent all a_j from being equal. Together with u these vectors span the three-dimensional sector, so each H_i has a size-two Jordan block there. The checker works exactly in Q(t) with t²−t+1=0 rather than relying on near-coincident numerical eigenvalues.

The finite real-site completeness theorem is closed under its stated assumptions. The three-site complex exceptional locus is also explicit, and its loss of diagonalizability is certified by generalized eigenvectors. The scalar-oper formula survives there, but it cannot by itself distinguish the generalized direction in a nonreduced spectral problem.

Scope of the result

The general theorem covers one-magnon states and the uniform descendant, not every magnetization sector for arbitrary n. The full eight-dimensional completeness statement applies only to the explicitly checked three-site example. General higher-rank Gaudin opers, arbitrary representations and a global Langlands correspondence require additional theory. Projectively trivial scalar monodromy here follows from the explicit fundamental pair, not from a broad assertion that all ODEs associated with a spin system have trivial monodromy.

Further development

S014 completes the distinct-complex-site one-magnon Jordan classification, including arbitrary critical multiplicities and a closed characteristic formula. For multi-magnon sectors the Bethe equations include root-root interactions. A disciplined next step is to compute a finite highest-weight multiplicity space independently, then compare regular, singular and generalized Bethe vectors with its exact joint spectrum. The exceptional-point calculation shows why a scheme-level spectrum may contain information that a set of distinct eigenvalues loses.

S011 · Synthesis

Minimum induced subgraph order and the sharp heat observation margin

Exact finite classification and analytic margin proved

The rook–Shrikhande collision can be pushed beyond merely producing two graphs with the same spectrum. For this pair, every permutation-invariant induced-subgraph count through order three agrees, all eleven four-vertex pattern counts are classified, and a single labeled off-diagonal heat observation has a sharp optimal time and a sharp worst-case error threshold. These are different observation classes and must not be conflated.

Definitions and assumptions

For a finite simple graph G and an unlabeled k-vertex graph H, N_H(G) is the number of k-element subsets of V(G) whose induced graph is isomorphic to H. Dividing by C(|V(G)|,k) gives the distribution obtained by uniform vertex-subset sampling.

The feature panel through order d is the vector of all N_H(G) for all unlabeled H with at most d vertices. This vector is invariant under relabeling G.

The two candidate graphs R and S are the sixteen-vertex rook and Shrikhande graphs from M020. Their vertices are assigned the known coordinate labels in Z₄².

For the separate labeled observation problem, observe y=(exp(−tL))_{uv}+η at t>0, with known u=(0,0), v=(0,2) and adversarial error |η|≤ε.

A feature-class lower bound and an optimal labeled experiment

The feature panels through order three coincide for R and S; the order-four panels differ, so four is the minimum distinguishing order within this feature class. Their K₄ counts are eight and zero. For the known labels u,v, the heat-entry difference is d(t)=(e^(−4t)−e^(−8t))/4. It has unique maximum 1/16 at t*=log(2)/4. At that time the candidate observations are 5/64 and 1/64. Uniform identification under the stated bounded-error model is possible exactly when ε<1/32.

Derivation or proof

For any strongly regular graph with parameters (v,k,λ,μ), the number of edges is vk/2 and the triangle count is vkλ/6. Each vertex contributes C(k,2) neighbor pairs; subtracting its kλ/2 neighbor-neighbor edges counts induced three-vertex paths centered there, so their total is v[C(k,2)−kλ/2]. For an edge, the vertices adjacent to neither endpoint number v−2k+λ, giving (vk/2)(v−2k+λ) induced single-edge triples. Subtract these three classes from C(v,3) to obtain the independent triples. With (16,6,2,2), these counts are respectively triangles32, paths144, single-edge triples288 and independent triples96. The vertex, edge, nonedge and empty-set counts also agree. Therefore every function of the specified feature panel of order at most three agrees; no decision rule using only that panel can separate the pair. A four-clique occurs on each row and each column of the rook graph, giving eight. The exhaustive canonical certificate finds none in Shrikhande, proving that order four suffices. It classifies all 1,820 four-subsets in each graph rather than checking only one witness.

For the heat formula, both adjacency matrices satisfy A²=4I+2J. On the constant vector the heat operator acts by one; on the adjacency eigenvalues +2 and −2 it acts by a=e^(−4t) and b=e^(−8t). Solving for its coefficients in span{I,A,J} gives K_t=((a+b)/2)I+((a−b)/4)A+((1−2a+b)/16)J. The aligned pair is an edge of R and a nonedge of S, so their difference is (a−b)/4. Put x=e^(−4t)∈(0,1): d=x(1−x)/4=1/16−(x−1/2)²/4. This proves the unique maximum and its time without numerical optimization. At x=1/2, the common nonedge value is 1/64 and adding the edge coefficient gives 5/64.

Under either hypothesis the possible noisy values form a closed interval of radius ε around its candidate value. These intervals are disjoint exactly when 2ε<1/16. The midpoint threshold 3/64 then separates them for every permitted error. At ε=1/32 both hypotheses can produce the midpoint: subtract 1/32 from 5/64 or add 1/32 to 1/64. No deterministic or randomized classifier can guarantee correct identification from that indistinguishable observation. Larger error budgets also contain this ambiguity.

Worked example

Canonicalize a labeled four-vertex graph by enumerating all twenty-four vertex permutations and taking the smallest six-edge bit mask. First enumerate all sixty-four labeled four-vertex graphs to obtain the complete set of eleven canonical classes; then classify every four-subset of R and S.

The counts in canonical-mask order are empty24/16, one-edge-plus-two-isolates288/336, path-plus-isolate576/480, star0/32, triangle-plus-isolate96/128, two-disjoint-edges216/192, four-path288/384, triangle-with-pendant288/192, four-cycle36/12, diamond0/48 and four-clique8/0, where each pair is rook/Shrikhande. Each column sums to 1,820. These exact distributions are stored in supplement_checks.json. At the optimal heat time the shared diagonal is 25/64, the edge value5/64 and nonedge value1/64; 25/64+6(5/64)+9(1/64)=1 verifies the row-sum normalization.

The pair is completely indistinguishable by induced pattern counts of orders zero through three, yet every four-vertex class count differs. A labeled heat entry is a different feature and can separate the same aligned candidates with one scalar observation.

The optimal time for separating one aligned graph pair differs from the time minimizing a full-kernel inverse-error bound. The left margin has exact maximum 1/16; the right normalized bound has exact minimum e. These are distinct objectives.

Scope of the result

The minimum-order statement is restricted to the declared induced-subgraph count panels; it is not a universal lower bound on all graph invariants, sensors, computational algorithms or sample counts. The heat threshold assumes exact time control, fixed known vertex correspondence, the two stated candidate graphs and the bounded-error model. It proves neither recovery of an unknown unlabeled graph nor uniform stability of taking a matrix logarithm. An unknown vertex permutation can change which pair is an edge and must be included as a nuisance parameter in a different problem. The continuous optimum t*=log(2)/4 is exact; numerical time selection incurs a separate margin loss.

Further development

The exact loss from a known mistiming t=t*+h is 1/16−d(t)=(e^(−4h)−1)²/16. If the actual time is observed but the design must tolerate |h|≤δ<t*, the worst same-time gap is [1−(e^(4δ)−1)²]/16, and a threshold adjusted to the observed time works for errors less than half that gap. If the actual time is unobserved, that bound alone is insufficient: each hypothesis ranges over different possible times. Put l=e^(−4δ)/2 and u=e^(4δ)/2. Over that interval, the least rook entry is (1+2u−3u²)/16, while the greatest Shrikhande entry is (1−l)²/16. The uniformly separating interval gap is therefore Δ=[2(u+l)−3u²−l²]/16, when positive, and the admissible bounded error is ε<Δ/2. These extrema follow because the Shrikhande entry decreases in x and the rook entry is concave; the difference of its endpoint values has sign (u−l)[2−3(u+l)]<0. For δ=log(3/2)/4, the exact candidate-set endpoints are 13/256 and 1/36, giving Δ=53/2304 and ε<53/4608. Thus calibrated deviation and an unobserved timing nuisance are genuinely different robustness problems. No version of these bounds establishes uniform unlabeled graph recovery.

S012 · Synthesis

Singular quadratic duality requires an observation quotient

Classical convex duality proved with a complete finite-dimensional classification and exact certificates

A pseudoinverse cannot simply replace an inverse inside every constrained-energy formula. Zero-energy input directions can generate nonzero observed outputs, and these free outputs must be quotiented out before applying the usual minimum-energy expression. The same geometry explains the finite domain of the Fenchel conjugate, the divergent part of ridge regularization, and changes in rank or active constraints. This supplies an algebraic complement to the positive-definite projection calculation in S006; it is a classical result developed here, not a claim of a new duality theorem.

Definitions and assumptions

Work in finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces. Let Q=Qᵀ≥0 be n×n, f(x)=xᵀQx/2, N=kerQ and R=N⊥=rangeQ. The Moore–Penrose inverse Q⁺ inverts Q on R and is zero on N.

For B:Rⁿ→Rᵐ and output z∈Rᵐ, define the output space W=BN generated at zero energy. Let P be the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto W⊥ and put H=PBQ⁺BᵀP. This H is symmetric positive semidefinite.

The equality-constrained value is v(z)=inf{f(x):Bx=z}, with value +∞ if infeasible. Inequalities are not part of this general formula; the separately stated parameter example includes x≥0 and has its own KKT certificates.

The Fenchel conjugate is f*(y)=sup_x(yᵀx−f(x)). For ε>0, the ridge energy is f_ε(x)=xᵀ(Q+εI)x/2. Its conjugate is finite everywhere.

Conjugate domain, ridge limit and complete equality-constrained value

The conjugate is f*(y)=yᵀQ⁺y/2 for y∈R, and +∞ otherwise. Writing y=y_R+y_N, the ridge conjugate is f_ε*(y)=y_Rᵀ(Q|_R+εI_R)⁻¹y_R/2+||y_N||²/(2ε). Thus it tends to f*(y), with an explicit 1/ε divergence off R. The equation Bx=z is feasible exactly when Pz∈rangeH, equivalently z∈rangeB. When feasible, v(z)=(Pz)ᵀH⁺(Pz)/2. Its unique minimum-energy R-component is r*=Q⁺BᵀP H⁺Pz. Choose n*∈N with Bn*=z−Br*. All minimizers are r*+n*+(N∩kerB). A dual optimizer is λ*=H⁺Pz; the dual admissibility condition is Bᵀλ∈R, equivalently λ∈W⊥. If feasibility fails, the dual is unbounded above along an explicitly separating direction.

Derivation or proof

First split x=r+n orthogonally with r∈R and n∈N. Since Qn=0, yᵀx−f(x)=y_Rᵀr−rᵀQr/2+y_Nᵀn. If y_N≠0, choosing n=t y_N and sending t→+∞ proves that the supremum is infinite. If y_N=0, Q is positive definite on R, and completing the square there gives the unique maximizing r=Q⁺y and value yᵀQ⁺y/2; any null component of x is allowed. Diagonalizing Q separately on R and N yields the ridge formula. If Q has smallest positive eigenvalue a, then on R the finite ridge error obeys 0≤f*(y_R)−f_ε*(y_R)≤ε||y_R||²/(2a²). No such finite uniform limit exists for a fixed nonzero y_N because its contribution is exactly ||y_N||²/(2ε).

Next write Bx=Br+Bn. A null component can supply precisely W, so the constraint is equivalent to PBr=Pz. On R set u=(Q|_R)^(1/2)r and C=PB(Q|_R)^(−1/2), interpreted as a map from R to W⊥. The energy is ||u||²/2 and the quotient constraint is Cu=Pz. Since H=CCᵀ, rangeH=rangeC: their orthogonal complements both equal ker Cᵀ, because aᵀHa=||Cᵀa||². Thus feasibility is exactly the stated range test. For a feasible right side, the least-norm solution is u*=CᵀH⁺Pz. Indeed Cu*=HH⁺Pz=Pz, and u* lies in range Cᵀ, orthogonal to every feasible increment in kerC. Pythagoras proves uniqueness and the value ||u*||²/2=(Pz)ᵀH⁺Pz/2. Returning to r gives the displayed formula. The residual z−Br* lies in kerP=W, so a suitable n* exists. Strict convexity on R fixes r*, while all permissible null components differ by N∩kerB.

For the dual, use L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀ(z−Bx). Taking the infimum over x gives d(λ)=λᵀz−f*(Bᵀλ). The finite-domain condition says λ annihilates BN: nᵀBᵀλ=0 for every n∈N. Therefore λ=Pλ and d(λ)=λᵀPz−λᵀHλ/2. At λ*=H⁺Pz, stationarity and feasibility give Qx*=Bᵀλ*, Bx*=z, and primal and dual values agree. This proves strong duality directly without relying on an unstated constraint qualification. If Pz is outside rangeH, let a be its nonzero projection onto kerH∩W⊥. Then Bᵀa lies in R and aᵀHa=0 forces Bᵀa=0. The dual ray λ=ta has d(ta)=t||a||²→+∞, while aᵀz≠0 proves Bx=z impossible. These are both an infeasibility certificate and a dual-geometry explanation.

The simpler expression zᵀ(BQ⁺Bᵀ)⁺z/2 is valid without the quotient when BN={0}, together with the feasibility condition z∈range(BQ⁺Bᵀ). Dropping either condition can give a wrong finite value. The case Q=0 is covered: every feasible output is free, H=0 and the value is zero, while infeasible outputs have value +∞.

Worked example

First use Q=diag(2,0,3), B=[[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] and z=(1,0). Then examine the parameter family Q_t=diag(1,t,0), b_a=(1,1,a), equality b_a x=1, and, as a distinct program, the extra constraint x≥0, for t≥0 and a∈R.

In the two-output example N=span(e₂), W=span((1,1)) and P=[[1,−1],[−1,1]]/2. Direct exact multiplication gives H=(5/24)[[1,−1],[−1,1]] and H⁺=(6/5)[[1,−1],[−1,1]]. Therefore λ*=(6/5,−6/5), r*=(3/5,0,−2/5), n*=(0,2/5,0), and x*=(3/5,2/5,−2/5). Its energy and dual value are both 3/5. The raw matrix BQ⁺Bᵀ=diag(1/2,1/3) would instead give the incorrect naive value one. An independent elimination sets x=(1−s,s,−s), giving energy 1−2s+(5/2)s², whose unique minimizer is s=2/5. This verifies both the quotient formula and the counterexample without using pseudoinverse numerical software.

For the parameter family with equality only, Q_t has rank two for t>0 and rank one at t=0. If t>0 and a≠0, x=(0,0,1/a) is feasible and has zero energy. If t>0 and a=0, the minimum is t/[2(1+t)], attained at x₁=t/(1+t), x₂=1/(1+t), with arbitrary x₃. At t=0 the free second coordinate makes the minimum zero for every a. The raw pseudoinverse expression gives t/[2(1+t)] for every a when t>0 and gives 1/2 at t=0. Thus it is wrong on entire parameter strata, not merely at an isolated numerical accident.

Now impose x≥0. For t>0,a>0, the unique minimizer is (0,0,1/a), with energy zero. For t>0,a=0, all minimizers are (t/(1+t),1/(1+t),s), s≥0, with value t/[2(1+t)]. For t>0,a<0, the unique minimizer is (t/(1+t),1/(1+t),0), with the same positive value. To certify the latter two branches choose λ=t/(1+t), ν=(0,0,−aλ) and stationarity Q_t x−λb_a−ν=0. For a≤0, ν≥0, and complementary slackness holds; at a=0 its third multiplier vanishes. For a>0 choose λ=0,ν=0 at the zero-energy minimizer. At t=0 every feasible vector with x₁=0 is optimal: if a>0 this is the segment x₃∈[0,1/a], x₂=1−ax₃; if a≤0 it is the ray x₃≥0, x₂=1−ax₃. These zero-energy branches also have λ=ν=0 certificates. For example t=2,a=−1 has constrained optimum (2/3,1/3,0), value 1/3 and ν₃=2/3, whereas its equality-only optimum (0,0,−1) has value zero.

For every listed nonnegative candidate, convexity makes these KKT certificates globally sufficient: for any other feasible x=x*+h, the objective difference equals hᵀQ_th/2+νᵀx≥0. This is a proof for all real parameters in the declared strata; the verifier replays representative rational points and checks feasibility, stationarity, nonnegative multipliers, complementarity and primal–dual agreement exactly. As a→0 from above at fixed t>0, the zero-energy minimizer escapes to infinity while the value jumps upward at a=0. The discontinuity comes from loss of uniform control of null directions, not from a failure of the theorem.

The dual must discard observed outputs that can be supplied without energy, by restricting multipliers to their annihilator. Inequalities can prevent use of those directions, which is why a linear nullspace quotient alone is not a formula for an inequality-constrained problem. Rank, output compatibility and active constraints form separate strata. This makes the relation to M062 and M093 precise and complements S006 without conflating zero energy, zero variance and missing statistical information.

Scope of the result

Everything here is finite-dimensional with a symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratic form and exact equality constraints. In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space the range need not be closed and minimizers or bounded pseudoinverses may fail to exist. An indefinite Q can make the primal unbounded below. The nonnegative parameter family is solved separately by KKT; the quotient formula does not automatically incorporate general inequalities. A ridge limit is a declared regularization, not a justification for deleting divergent terms or for replacing inverses by pseudoinverses without range tests.

Further development

For rational parameter-dependent Q and B, produce exact rank strata, bases for kerQ and BkerQ, compatibility equations for Pz and KKT active-set certificates. Preserve both the domain conditions and the optimizer set at boundary parameters. In a statistical application specify whether Q describes energy, precision or covariance before transferring these algebraic formulas into a measurement claim.
