S013 · Synthesis

An exact exceptional point and its two-sheeted spectral cover

Finite parameter-family classification and exact Jordan/projector certificates; no novelty claim

The three-site sl₂ Gaudin family has an explicit exceptional locus where two highest-weight eigenlines coalesce. At that locus a genuine Jordan block replaces the two eigenvectors. Nearby spectral projectors diverge although their sum stays constant. Analytic continuation of the eigenvalue labels exchanges the two lines. This is spectral-cover monodromy in a parameter, not monodromy of a KZ connection or of the scalar differential equation in its spatial variable.

Definitions and assumptions

Use the one-magnon sector and normalization of S010, with sites z=(0,1,t), t≠0,1. Put p_t(x)=x(x−1)(x−t), D(t)=t²−t+1 and w±=(1+t±sqrt(D))/3.

For D≠0, let v± have components 1/(w±−z_j), and E_i±=E_i⁰+1/(w±−z_i). The uniform vector is u=(1,1,1)ᵀ and the highest-weight projection is Q=I−uuᵀ/3.

Transpose is the complex bilinear transpose, not the Hermitian adjoint. For complex t the resulting spectral projectors need not be orthogonal for the standard Hermitian norm. Their divergence is compatible with Q remaining bounded.

Jordan degeneration, projector cancellation and spectral-label exchange

The only critical-root collisions in this family occur at t₀=(1±i√3)/2, the simple zeros of D. At t=t₀, w₀=(1+t₀)/3 and v₀=v(w₀) satisfy (H_i−E_i)v₀=0 and (H_i−E_i)v′₀=−a_i²v₀, where a_i=1/(w₀−z_i). Thus each H_i has a size-two Jordan block on im Q. For D≠0, P±=∓p_t(w±)v±v±ᵀ/(2sqrt(D)), and P++P−=Q exactly. As t approaches t₀ on either local sheet, sqrt(D)P+→−p_(t₀)(w₀)v₀v₀ᵀ/2 and sqrt(D)P− has the opposite limit. A loop encircling just one zero of D exchanges P+ and P−.

Derivation or proof

Differentiating p_t gives p′=3x²−2(1+t)x+t, so the critical roots have the displayed quadratic formula. Its discriminant vanishes precisely at the two stated sites, and D′(t₀)=2t₀−1≠0. At the collision B=p′/p and B′ both vanish at w₀, while p(w₀)≠0 because the physical sites are still distinct. The off-shell identity from S010 is H_i v(w)=E_i(w)v(w)−a_i(w)B(w)e_i. Differentiating in w at fixed t₀ eliminates both residual terms and gives the generalized-eigenvector relation, with E_i′=−a_i²≠0. If v′ were proportional to v, all a_j would have to be equal, contrary to distinct sites. Both vectors have coordinate sum zero; with u they span the full sector. Therefore the block is genuinely Jordan, not a repeated diagonal eigenvalue.

At a simple critical root the bilinear square is v(w)ᵀv(w)=−p″(w)/p(w). Since p″(w±)=±2sqrt(D), the projector formula follows. The eigenvectors u,v+,v− form a bilinear-orthogonal basis when D≠0, so their projectors sum to I and P++P−=Q. The numerator of P+ tends to a nonzero rank-one matrix, giving divergence proportional to |D|^(−1/2) in any fixed finite-dimensional matrix norm. With ε=sqrt(D), one has t−t₀=O(ε²), w±=w₀±ε/3+O(ε²), and p_t(w±)=p_(t₀)(w₀)+O(ε²). Thus P±=∓p₀v₀v₀ᵀ/(2ε)−p₀(v′₀v₀ᵀ+v₀v′₀ᵀ)/6+O(ε). The divergent terms cancel. In fact Q=−p₀(v′₀v₀ᵀ+v₀v′₀ᵀ)/3 at the exceptional point. The finite surviving nilpotent is N_i=(H_i−E_i)Q=(p₀a_i²/3)v₀v₀ᵀ. It is nonzero and N_i²=0 because v₀ᵀv₀=0.

Finally D=(t−t₀)(t−t₁). A sufficiently small loop around t₀ winds D once around zero because t₁ lies outside. Analytic continuation of sqrt(D) therefore changes sign, exchanging the two roots, eigenvalues and projectors. This proof concerns the two-sheeted algebraic spectral cover; it introduces no connection or parallel-transport operator.

Worked example

Perform the exceptional calculation exactly in K=Q(τ), τ²−τ+1=0, taking t₀=τ and w₀=(1+τ)/3.

The supplemental verifier constructs all three 3×3 Hamiltonians over K. It checks their commutators, the eigenvector and generalized-eigenvector identities, rank(u,v₀,v′₀)=3, the constant-projector formula and N_i=(p₀a_i²/3)v₀v₀ᵀ with N_i≠0 and N_i²=0. These are exact algebraic calculations, independent of numerical eigenvalue separation. Additional complex-number evaluations approach the exceptional point along D=ε² and check the leading projector coefficient and cancellation. A separately tracked square root around a small parameter loop exchanges the two labels, agreeing with the analytic winding argument.

This closes the finite three-site exceptional-point question: location, Jordan structure, projector blowup, cancellation and label exchange are explicit. The exact field certificate carries the algebraic result; numerical paths illustrate its limiting and continuation behavior.

Numerical continuation of the exact quadratic Bethe-root formula around a simple discriminant point exchanges the two root labels. This illustrates spectral-cover continuation, not KZ connection holonomy. The source script checks endpoint exchange and the polynomial residual to 1e-12.

Scope of the result

For real distinct sites, D=(t−1/2)²+3/4 is positive and cannot reach this exceptional locus; the real-site orthogonal projectors therefore do not develop this singularity. The result does not classify every higher-site exceptional locus. Spectral-cover label exchange, spatial scalar-ODE monodromy and KZ connection monodromy are three different constructions and must not be identified.

Further development

S014 completes the distinct-site one-magnon answer: each multiplicity-m root of p′ gives exactly one size-m Jordan block, and the commuting spectral algebra retains its nilpotent direction. Further work should address multi-magnon sectors or collisions of the physical sites, where the present hypotheses and one-coordinate construction do not apply unchanged.

S014 · Synthesis

Complete complex one-magnon Jordan classification

Proved finite-sector classification with exact Gaussian-rational examples; classical framework, no global novelty claim

The simple-critical-point qualification in S010 can be removed. For arbitrary distinct complex spin-1/2 sites, multiplicities of the roots of p′ determine all Jordan block sizes in the one-magnon sector. One explicit local coordinate turns the Bethe vector’s derivatives into a Jordan chain of the correct length. The chains exhaust the sector, and every Hamiltonian generates the same finite commuting algebra after polynomial interpolation.

Definitions and assumptions

Retain p(x)=∏_(j=1)^n(x−z_j), H_i and E_i⁰ from S010, with all physical sites distinct. A critical root w_r has multiplicity m_r as a root of p′. Since p has simple roots, p(w_r)≠0; Σ_r m_r=n−1.

Fix any Hamiltonian index i. At w_r write a=1/(w_r−z_i), use local coordinate q=1/(w−z_i)−a, and define w(q)=z_i+1/(a+q). Expand v(w(q))=Σ_(k≥0)V_(r,k)q^k near q=0.

A length-m Jordan chain for H−E is a list V₀,…,V_(m−1) with (H−E)V₀=0 and (H−E)V_k=V_(k−1) for k≥1. No factorial is missing: V_k is the Taylor coefficient, equivalently the kth derivative divided by k!.

Critical multiplicity equals Jordan length for every H_i

On the n-dimensional one-magnon space, each H_i has one uniform-descendant block of size one and eigenvalue E_i⁰, together with exactly one block of size m_r and eigenvalue E_i(r)=E_i⁰+1/(w_r−z_i) for each distinct critical root w_r. Consequently H_i is diagonalizable exactly when p′ is squarefree, and its minimal polynomial equals its characteristic polynomial of degree n. With A_i=H_i−E_i⁰I, one has A_j=A_i[I+(z_i−z_j)A_i]⁻¹. The characteristic polynomial is χ_Hi(λ)=u^n p′(z_i+1/u)/p′(z_i), u=λ−E_i⁰, interpreted by polynomial expansion. The unital algebra generated by the H_j is C[H_i], isomorphic to C×∏_r C[q]/(q^(m_r)).

Derivation or proof

The exact off-shell identity is H_i v(w)=(E_i⁰+a_i(w))v(w)−a_i(w)B(w)e_i, with B=p′/p. At a multiplicity-m critical root, B(w) vanishes to order m. The local coordinate q is valid because a_i′(w_r)=−a²≠0, and its inverse is the displayed rational function. Moreover E_i(w(q))=E_i(r)+q exactly. Thus (H_i−E_i(r))v(w(q))=q v(w(q))+O(q^m). Equating Taylor coefficients through q^(m−1) gives the claimed chain. It is independent: if a linear relation has highest nonzero coefficient at V_k, applying (H_i−E_i(r))^k leaves that coefficient times V₀, a contradiction because V₀≠0. Distinct critical roots have distinct E_i(r), since w↦1/(w−z_i) is injective; none equals E_i⁰. Their generalized eigenspaces and the uniform vector are therefore independent. Their dimensions total 1+Σm_r=n, so they form a complete basis and no larger or additional block can exist.

For any other j, put d=z_i−z_j and A=1+da. This A is nonzero because w_r is not a physical site. In the same coordinate, a_j(w(q))=(a+q)/(A+dq)=a_j(w_r)+Σ_(ℓ≥1)c_jℓ q^ℓ, where c_jℓ=(−d)^(ℓ−1)/A^(ℓ+1). The off-shell remainder still has order m. Hence H_j on the chain is E_j(r)I+Σ_(ℓ=1)^(m−1)c_jℓ N^ℓ, with NV_k=V_(k−1). Its linear coefficient is c_j1=A^(−2)≠0, so its nilpotent part is N times an invertible polynomial in N and has the same Jordan length and generalized-eigenspace flags. Equivalently these jets give A_j=A_i(I+dA_i)⁻¹ on each block and on the uniform vector. The denominator is invertible: its critical eigenvalues are (w_r−z_j)/(w_r−z_i), all nonzero, and its uniform eigenvalue is one. An inverse of this finite matrix is polynomial in A_i, giving C[H_i] as the entire generated algebra. Finally χ=u∏_r(u−1/(w_r−z_i))^(m_r); substituting the factorization p′(x)=n∏_r(x−w_r)^(m_r) gives the displayed polynomial formula. The degree-n minimal polynomial and the Chinese remainder theorem yield the algebra decomposition. This proves the entire finite-sector classification, including its nonsemisimple cases.

Worked example

Take four physical sites (1,−1,i,−i), so p=x⁴−1 and p′=4x³. Fix i to be the site z_i=1.

There is one critical root w=0 of multiplicity three. Its chain coefficients are V₀=(−1,1,i,−i), V₁=(1,1,−1,−1), V₂=(0,2,−1−i,−1+i). The uniform vector and these three vectors have rank four. The eigenvalues are E_j⁰=3/(4z_j) and E_j=−1/(4z_j). In particular H_i has characteristic and minimal polynomial (λ−3/4)(λ+1/4)³. On Q=I−uuᵀ/4, N=(H_i+I/4)Q obeys N³=0 and N²≠0. All equations are checked exactly in Q(i).

A mixed-multiplicity example uses eight distinct sites ±1,±i,±2,±2i, giving p=(x⁴−1)(x⁴−16)=x⁸−17x⁴+16 and p′=4x³(2x⁴−17). The critical multiplicities are three at zero and one at each of four nonzero roots. Thus each H_i has block sizes 3,1,1,1,1,1, including the uniform block. At base site1, E_i⁰=37/60 and E_i(0)=−23/60. If q=λ−37/60, its characteristic polynomial is (λ−37/60)(λ+23/60)³[17q⁴−2(q+1)⁴]/15. The verifier independently calculates the full 8×8 characteristic polynomial by trace/Newton identities over Q(i), checks this factorization and the length-three chain. The four remaining factors have distinct roots because the map w↦1/(w−1) is injective on the four simple roots of 2w⁴−17.

The multiplicity-three and mixed examples verify higher Jordan lengths and coexistence of simple and nonsimple blocks. The arbitrary-n result is supplied by the proof, not extrapolated from those matrices.

Scope of the result

This classification concerns the one-magnon sector for distinct physical sites and the stated spin-1/2 quadratic Gaudin Hamiltonians. It does not settle multi-magnon completeness, higher representations, collisions of physical sites, or a global Langlands correspondence. The direct-product algebra is a finite spectral algebra, not a claim that a general moduli space has been constructed.

Further development

In multi-magnon sectors, root-root interactions and admissibility conditions prevent this one-coordinate argument from being transferred unchanged. An appropriate next problem is to seek an equally explicit off-shell jet construction on a fixed small multiplicity space and compare it against an independently computed joint Jordan form.

M001 · 2023-01-23 · Foundations · historical evidence A

Separate the meanings of Q

Definitions resolved with a structural obstruction

The original notation can be repaired completely at the level of objects. Robinson arithmetic Q is a first-order theory, Q_p is a valued field of characteristic zero, F_p[[q]] is a formal power-series ring of characteristic p, and D_q is an operator depending on a numerical or formal parameter. A proposed connection must name the relevant category and map; the shared letter Q supplies neither.

Definitions and assumptions

Robinson Q consists of axioms in the language of zero, successor, addition and multiplication; it is not a number field.

Q_p is the completion of Q for |x|_p=p^(−v_p(x)); Z_p is its valuation ring.

F_p[[q]] consists of formal series Σa_n q^n. Its q-adic topology measures vanishing order, not numerical size.

D_q f(x)=(f(qx)−f(x))/((q−1)x), initially for q≠1 and x≠0.

Characteristic obstructs a claimed field identification

There is a canonical dense embedding Q→Q_p and a compatible reduction system Z_p→Z/p^nZ. There is no unital ring homomorphism Q_p→F_p[[q]], or in the reverse direction. In particular these objects cannot be identified by renaming their parameters.

Derivation or proof

A unital homomorphism sends an integer n·1 to the same n·1. In characteristic p, p·1=0, whereas p is nonzero and invertible in Q_p. If φ:Q_p→F_p[[q]] were unital, then 1=φ(p p^(−1))=φ(p)φ(p^(−1))=0, a contradiction. In the reverse direction, applying φ to p·1=0 would give p·1=0 in Q_p, also impossible. The dense embedding Q→Q_p instead preserves characteristic and the field operations. The reductions from Z_p preserve ring operations but have nontrivial kernel p^nZ_p, so they are quotients rather than embeddings. This distinction already eliminates several possible informal identifications without requiring a difficult theorem.

Worked example

Compare a rational number, a p-adic approximation and a formal series.

The rational 1/3 maps into Q_7 and can be approximated by compatible residues modulo 7^n. The formal series (1−q)^(−1)=1+q+q²+⋯ belongs to F_7[[q]] because its coefficients satisfy a formal multiplication identity. Its formal variable q is not automatically the prime 7 or a neural-network parameter.

A corrected dictionary gives legitimate arrows and a proof that one tempting arrow cannot exist.

Scope of the result

An arithmetic theory can be interpreted in structures, and equal-characteristic local fields can resemble mixed-characteristic fields in selected respects. The characteristic obstruction does not rule out every model-theoretic or categorical comparison; it rules out the specified unital ring identifications.

Further development

For every later use of q or Q, record its type, admissible values and morphisms. A meaningful bridge should transport a named theorem, not merely an expression.

M002 · 2023-01-23 · Arithmetic · historical evidence A

p-adic completion with certified digits

Simple-root lifting proved and calculated

A useful p-adic computation is a compatible sequence of exact congruences with a precision guarantee. The essential advantage in this example is that a simple solution modulo p determines one branch at every higher precision; decimal proximity has no role in the argument.

Definitions and assumptions

v_p(x) is the exponent of p in a nonzero rational x, and |0|_p=0.

An approximation x_n modulo p^n certifies a p-adic ball x_n+p^nZ_p.

A simple root modulo p satisfies f(x_1)≡0 and f′(x_1) not≡0 modulo p.

Unique next digit in a Hensel lift

For f∈Z_p[x], a simple root x_n modulo p^n has exactly one lift x_n+t p^n modulo p^(n+1), with t∈{0,…,p−1}. The compatible lifts converge to a unique root in x_1+pZ_p.

Derivation or proof

Taylor expansion gives f(x_n+t p^n)≡f(x_n)+t p^n f′(x_n) modulo p^(n+1); all terms of degree at least two are divisible by p^(2n), hence by p^(n+1). Dividing by p^n reduces the lift equation to f(x_n)/p^n+t f′(x_n)≡0 modulo p. The derivative is a unit, so this linear equation has one digit t. Repeating constructs a compatible inverse-limit element. Completeness gives a limit α; polynomial continuity gives f(α)=0. If two roots share the residue x_1, the same unique-digit argument forces agreement modulo every p^n and therefore equality. A finite calculation consequently certifies a ball containing the unique branch, not an approximate real root.

Worked example

Lift x²−2 from the root 3 modulo 7.

At precision 7², write x=3+7t. Dividing f(x) by 7 gives 1+6t≡0 modulo 7, hence t=1 and x=10 modulo 49. Next x=10+49t gives 2+6t≡0, hence t=2 and x=108 modulo 343. Directly, 108²−2=34·343. The verifier continues the uniquely selected digits through precision 7^6.

The result is a root α∈Z_7 with α≡108 modulo 343, with a proof that no other root in 3+7Z_7 has those initial conditions.

Scope of the result

If f′ vanishes modulo p, uniqueness and existence require a different argument; the simple-root calculation cannot be recycled unchanged. This example establishes an arithmetic algorithm, not a general computational speedup over real methods.

Further development

Develop Newton lifting with precision doubling and an independent residual valuation; compare digit lifting and Newton lifting on the same branch.

Mathematical references: R015

M003 · 2023-01-23 · Dynamics · historical evidence A

Affine dynamics on Z_p

Complete fixed-point and attraction classification for the stated family

The affine family can be settled exactly. The hypotheses a,b∈Z_p ensure that f(x)=ax+b maps Z_p into itself and never expands p-adic distance. Attracting, neutral and translational behavior can then be distinguished without metaphor.

Definitions and assumptions

A fixed point solves f(x*)=x*.

Attraction means f^n(x)→x* in the p-adic metric for nearby initial states.

Congruence modulo p^N means two states cannot be distinguished at N-digit precision.

Affine fixed points and orbit differences

If a≠1, a fixed point in Z_p exists exactly when b/(1−a)∈Z_p, equivalently b=0 or v_p(b)≥v_p(1−a), and is then unique. If a=1, b=0 makes every point fixed and b≠0 gives none. For |a|_p<1 the unique point attracts every state; for |a|_p=1 no distinct state converges to a fixed point.

Derivation or proof

The fixed-point equation is (1−a)x=b, which gives the classification because Q_p is a field and membership in Z_p is exactly nonnegative valuation. Subtract two trajectories: f^n(x)−f^n(y)=a^n(x−y). Taking norms gives |a|_p^n|x−y|_p. This converges to zero precisely in the nonunit case, while for a unit it remains constant whenever x≠y. When |a|_p<1, 1−a is a unit, so every b supplies an integral fixed point. For a≠1, direct induction gives f^n(x)=a^n x+b(1−a^n)/(1−a). Congruent initial states remain congruent at every step, since multiplication by a∈Z_p cannot lower their agreement precision.

Worked example

Take p=7, a=7 and b=1.

The fixed point is −1/6∈Z_7. Starting from x_0=0 gives x_n=1+7+⋯+7^(n−1), and x_n−x*=7^n/6. Its valuation is exactly n. Thus n iterations supply n correct base-seven digits. In contrast a=8,b=1 has no fixed point in Z_7 because (1−8)x=1 would require v_7(x)=−1.

The same affine notation yields global contraction in one case and a provable integral fixed-point obstruction in the other.

Scope of the result

Neutral maps may have rich periodic structure modulo p^N; constant separation does not mean every orbit is constant. This classification is for affine maps on Z_p, not arbitrary nonlinear p-adic dynamics.

Further development

Classify neutral affine cycles modulo p^N, then identify which cycle properties stabilize as N grows. Use gcd divisibility as an independent finite checker.

M004 · 2023-01-23 · Probability · historical evidence A

A valid probability model and identifiable parameters

Range failure proved and a finite-design model specified

The original product can be analyzed before any modeling claim is made. A formula is a probability only on an admissible domain, and fitted coefficients are meaningful only when the observation design can distinguish them.

Definitions and assumptions

For the original expression P(x,y)=(1+x)(1−y), assume x,y∈[0,1].

For the alternative logistic model let z=(1,x,y), η=z·β and σ(η)=1/(1+e^(−η)).

A finite design matrix X has rows z_i and identifies β when distinct coefficients give distinct modeled probability vectors.

Exact admissible domain and logistic identifiability

On [0,1]² the product lies in [0,1] exactly when y≥x/(1+x). A logistic model yields probabilities strictly between zero and one for every finite β. At a fixed design, its coefficient vector is identifiable exactly when X has full column rank.

Derivation or proof

Nonnegativity of the product is automatic on the square. The upper bound is (1+x)(1−y)≤1, equivalent to y≥x/(1+x) because 1+x>0. The point (1,0) violates it with P=2. For the logistic family, σ is a strictly increasing bijection R→(0,1). Thus equal probability vectors are equivalent, after applying logit, to Xβ=Xβ′. Full column rank makes this imply β=β′; a nonzero null vector otherwise supplies indistinguishable coefficients. For independent Bernoulli observations the log likelihood is Σ[y_iη_i−log(1+e^η_i)]. Its Hessian is −XᵀWX with W diagonal and positive at finite β. Full rank gives strict concavity, but does not guarantee that a finite maximizer exists: complete separation can send the optimum to infinity.

Worked example

Use the three design points (0,0),(1,0),(0,1).

Their augmented rows form an invertible 3×3 matrix. β=(0,log3,−log3) gives probabilities (1/2,3/4,1/4). Taking logits yields (0,log3,−log3), from which β is uniquely recovered by solving the linear system. Repeating only the first point would identify β_0 but leave the other two coefficients free.

The example separates probability range, structural identifiability and existence of an estimator—three questions the original toy formula left unresolved.

Scope of the result

Choosing a logistic family does not establish empirical truth, independence or adequate calibration. Identifiability is conditional on the design and model; it is not a performance guarantee.

Further development

Add a specified observation model and investigate design conditioning or separation before optimizing the likelihood.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M005 · 2023-01-23 · Cryptography · historical evidence A

Specify a hard problem before using arithmetic complexity

A toy encryption proposal is explicitly broken

Sophisticated number systems do not themselves supply one-wayness. A mathematically assessable proposal must say what an adversary receives, what recovery problem is being claimed difficult, and how problem instances are distributed.

Definitions and assumptions

A toy modular scheme publishes a prime p and nonzero multiplier a and maps a message x to y=ax modulo p.

Correctness of a private recovery algorithm is different from hardness of public recovery.

An instance distribution specifies which public parameters, secrets and observations occur; worst-case difficulty alone need not control that distribution.

Public linear arithmetic is publicly invertible

For the stated toy map, every message is recovered from public data using x=a^(−1)y modulo p. Extended Euclid computes a^(−1), so adding large notation or expressing the same arithmetic p-adically cannot turn this construction into a secret inversion problem.

Derivation or proof

Since p is prime and a is nonzero modulo p, gcd(a,p)=1. The extended Euclidean algorithm produces integers u,v with ua+vp=1. Reducing modulo p gives ua≡1, and multiplying y=ax by u recovers x≡uy. This is a deterministic polynomial-time attack in the bit length of p. More generally, a public invertible linear transformation over a field is inverted by linear algebra. If its matrix is hidden but an oracle permits arbitrary message queries, querying the coordinate basis recovers its columns. Neither attack needs to search the message space or exploit implementation defects. They attack the mathematical specification itself.

Worked example

Take p=101, a=7 and observed y=35.

Euclid gives 7^(−1)≡29 modulo 101, since 7·29=203≡1. Therefore x≡29·35≡5. The verifier recovers x using only these public quantities. A larger prime changes the input size but not the kind of attack.

The construction is correct as a reversible encoding and fails as a claimed secret arithmetic trapdoor.

Scope of the result

This example does not establish security or insecurity of an unrelated fully specified cryptosystem. A different map might pose a genuinely different problem, but its hardness must be argued independently of the prestige of its geometric or arithmetic vocabulary.

Further development

For any proposed replacement, give generation, evaluation, recovery, correctness and an explicit public attack model. Test algebraic simplifications on small instances before attaching a security claim.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M006 · 2023-02-02 · Analysis · historical evidence A

Zeno through a convergent series and a time law

Convergence and endpoint behavior proved

Infinitely many subdivisions do not determine elapsed time. Once both the distance increments and the time increments are stated, the mathematical ambiguity disappears: an infinite event sequence can accumulate at a finite time, or it can continue for an infinite duration.

Definitions and assumptions

Let distance increments be d_n=2^(−n), with milestones x_N=Σ_(n=1)^N d_n.

Let positive time increments be τ_n and milestone times t_N=Σ_(n=1)^N τ_n.

A finite accumulation time exists exactly when the positive time series converges.

Finite distance does not fix finite elapsed time

The distances sum to one. Choosing τ_n=2^(−n) reaches milestones at t_N=1−2^(−N) and admits the continuous extension x(1)=1. Choosing τ_n=1/n instead takes infinite total time while approaching the same spatial limit.

Derivation or proof

For the geometric sum, multiply S_N=1/2+⋯+2^(−N) by two and subtract to obtain S_N=1−2^(−N). Given ε>0, choose N>log₂(1/ε); then 0<1−S_N<ε, proving convergence. With equal distance and time increments, the piecewise linear motion is simply x(t)=t on [0,1), so continuity supplies the endpoint x(1)=1. In the harmonic-time model, the subsequence of times diverges because each block from 2^k+1 through 2^(k+1) contributes at least 1/2. A continuous piecewise linear interpolation still approaches spatial position one, but only as t→∞. The number of labeled milestones is identical in both descriptions; its cardinality does not decide the total time.

Worked example

Compare the first N milestones in the two parametrizations.

Both have spatial coordinate 1−2^(−N). In the first model the remaining time is 2^(−N). In the second, any finite milestone leaves an infinite tail Σ_(n>N)1/n. Their different conclusions follow from different time assignments, not from a contradiction in summing the same distances.

The revised question separates convergence, continuity and parametrization, each of which can be proved with elementary estimates.

Scope of the result

A mathematical parametrization does not assert that a physical device can execute an unbounded rate of discrete operations. The continuous trajectory requires no such discrete mechanism; a physical implementation would add its own constraints.

Further development

Study rectifiable curves with infinitely many segments and ask separately whether a chosen parametrization has bounded speed, finite length and a continuous endpoint.

M007 · 2023-02-20 · Algebra · historical evidence A

Octonions with a declared multiplication convention

Nonassociativity exhibited and Moufang law certified by all coefficients

An analogy involving octonions becomes mathematics once multiplication, regrouping and the surviving identities are explicit. The real octonions are a division algebra but not an associative algebra; consequently their nonzero elements form a Moufang loop rather than a group.

Definitions and assumptions

Represent an octonion as a pair (a,b) of quaternions with product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−conj(d)b, da+b conj(c)).

Use the quaternion convention ij=k, jk=i, ki=j. Set e1=(i,0), e2=(j,0), e3=(k,0), e4=(0,1), e5=(0,i), e6=(0,j), e7=(0,k).

The associator is [a,b,c]=(ab)c−a(bc). The Euclidean norm on R⁸ is multiplicative.

Under this convention [e1,e2,e4]=2e7. Nevertheless the associator is alternating, and the Moufang identity (ab)(ca)=a((bc)a) holds for all real octonions. In particular any two elements generate an associative subalgebra, the classical alternative-algebra theorem.

The displayed associator follows directly from e1e2=e3, e3e4=e7, e2e4=e6 and e1e6=−e7. For an independent finite certificate of alternation, expand the trilinear associator in the basis 1,e1,…,e7. The verifier checks all 512 triples and confirms [a,b,c]+[b,a,c]=0 and [a,b,c]+[a,c,b]=0 at every coefficient. Bilinearity of multiplication then proves alternation for arbitrary real coordinates. The Moufang residual is quadratic in a and linear in b and c. It is therefore enough to check a on each basis vector and each pairwise sum of basis vectors, with b and c on basis vectors: polarization recovers all squared and mixed coefficients. All 2304 evaluations vanish exactly. This finite coefficient certificate verifies the full identity, not merely a random sample.

Worked example

Regroup e1,e2,e4 and compare the two results.

The left grouping gives (e1e2)e4=e7 and the right gives e1(e2e4)=−e7. Their difference has norm two. If the third factor instead belongs to the associative quaternion algebra generated by e1,e2, regrouping makes no difference.

The example demonstrates both a genuine failure and a precise replacement law. No philosophical interpretation is needed for either statement.

Scope of the result

Other octonion tables may change basis signs and the displayed associator sign. The convention must travel with every numerical example. Alternativity does not authorize arbitrary reassociation of three unrelated factors.

Further development

Use the explicit coefficient tensor as an exact algebraic input when investigating invariant subalgebras, automorphisms or defect loci.

For octonions define d(a,b,c)=||(ab)c−a(bc)||.

Let n=||a||||b||||c||. Norm multiplicativity gives ||(ab)c||=||a(bc)||=n.

Evaluate the normalized defect on a maximally nonassociative basis triple and an associative quaternion triple.

For (e1,e2,e4), d=2. For (e1,e2,e3), both products equal −1, so d=0. The two calculations sit at opposite endpoints of the proved interval. The normalized quantity δ=d/(||a||||b||||c||) is consequently dimensionless on nonzero triples and ranges through values in [0,2].

This does not classify every zero-defect triple or every orbit of the automorphism group. A zero associator for one triple alone should not be promoted to a statement that an entire generated algebra is associative.

The derivatives satisfy T′=f, f′=−2fT and d/dz=(1−T²)d/dT when applied to polynomials in T.

For a wave u(x,t)=A f(κ(x−ct−x0)), primes on u below denote spatial derivatives.

Use κ=1, x0=0.

Then u=2sech²(x−4t). Its maximum is two at x=4t and its spatial integral is four, since ∫sech²z dz=tanh z. The profile is localized and translates with speed four. A version with amplitude six and the same width would not solve this normalization of KdV.

The identity repair now produces a complete exact check, conserved profile mass and a falsifiable relationship among width, height and speed.

Changing the sign or coefficient of the nonlinear term changes the amplitude relation. This calculation verifies an explicit family and is not a classification of all solutions or a stability proof.

Set θ=gd(x)=arctan(sinh x), mapping R bijectively to (−π/2,π/2).

The inverse is x=asinh(tanθ)=artanh(sinθ), with dx/dθ=secθ.

Since cosθ is positive in that range, the elementary identities follow by resolving a right triangle with tangent sinh x. The differential operator is ∂_x=cosθ∂_θ; applying it twice gives the stated second derivative. The ordinary change-of-variables theorem supplies dx=secθdθ. Transform u(x)=Asech²x.

The angular profile is U(θ)=Acos²θ. Retaining the measure gives ∫u dx=A∫cosθdθ=2A, matching the direct calculation A[tanh x]_(−∞)^∞. If one integrated Acos²θ against dθ without the Jacobian, the answer would instead be Aπ/2 and would describe a different measure.

The transformation simplifies a profile while preserving its integral only when the derivative and measure factors are carried along.

For a moving coordinate θ=gd(κ(x−ct)), time differentiation also contributes θ_t=−cκcosθ. A stationary spatial formula cannot simply be inserted into a time-dependent PDE without this extra chain rule.

Fix KdV as u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0.

Choose σ=+1, k=2, l=1 and δ=0.

The line wave is an exactly verified two-dimensional solution with a clear localization limitation.

At x=t=δ1=δ2=0 choose k1=2 and k2=1.

The sphere of radius r has area ω_(d−1)r^(d−1). If its flux is Φ, then Φ=ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)F(r), yielding F(r)=Φ/(ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)). Equivalently, away from a source, the radial divergence is r^(1−d)∂_r(r^(d−1)F), which must vanish. For the projection, differentiate the displayed map X(u,v), take Euclidean inner products of its two coordinate derivatives and obtain a diagonal pullback metric with both diagonal entries 4/(1+r²)². Taking the square root of the determinant supplies the stated area factor. This second calculation concerns how one surface is charted, not how a physical flux changes across a family of spheres.

Worked example

Compare the large-distance factors in their own variables.

A three-dimensional radial flux decays as physical radius R^(−2). The stereographic area density decays as chart radius r^(−4). These statements do not contradict each other: R labels different spheres in a physical space, whereas r labels positions within a chart of one unit sphere. Identifying them would discard the very geometric distinction being calculated.

The original question now has a derivation of each factor and a concrete reason the coordinate formula does not imply the conservation law.

A projected representation of a conserved field can of course be constructed. It must transform the field and the integration measure together; conservation is then transported, not created by projection.

Compare q=1/2 and q=2 at x=2.

Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field, A:V→V and C:V→Y linear, with outputs y_n=CA^n x.

Its degree is at most dim(V/N); for a scalar observable with an observable quotient it equals that quotient dimension.

For scalar output, the row span of C,CA,… on the quotient has full dimension by observability. A polynomial of smaller degree would make every later row a combination of fewer initial rows, contradicting full dimension. This last equality need not hold for multiple outputs: A=I with C=I observes an n-dimensional state but has universal polynomial z−1.

Take A=diag(1,2,3) and C=(1,1,0).

The invisible space is span(e3). On the two-dimensional quotient the minimal polynomial is (z−1)(z−2), so y_(n+2)−3y_(n+1)+2y_n=0 for every initial state. The full characteristic polynomial has a redundant factor z−3. If the particular initial state is e1, its individual sequence satisfies the shorter recurrence y_(n+1)=y_n.

A recurrence fitted to one finite prefix may be accidental. The quotient argument proves a recurrence for all times under the stated model; finite fitting alone does not.

Starting at zero, the variation-of-constants formula x(t)=∫_0^t e^(A(t−s))Bu(s)ds lies in R because that subspace is A-invariant and contains imB. Adding a state in R∩N never changes any subsequent output, including under common future inputs, so the quotient preserves the response. Conversely, all reachable quotient states are generated by the projected input, and an invisible quotient class would have a representative in N, hence in R∩N, so it is zero. These properties characterize the usual minimal finite-dimensional realization. Replacing the zero initial condition by arbitrary initial states changes the target: visible but unreachable modes can now contribute.

Take A=diag(−1,−2,3), B=(1,0,1)^T and C=(1,1,0).

R=span(e1,e3), while N=span(e3). The minimal driven state therefore has dimension one and transfer function 1/(s+1). The internally unstable e3 mode is reachable but invisible. The e2 mode is visible but unreachable; it matters for initial condition e2, producing e^(−2t), but not for zero-initial driven responses.

The example has reachable rank two and observable rank two, yet minimal driven order one. Merely taking either rank misses the intersection.

A stable transfer function does not establish internal stability when an unstable canceled mode remains. No empirical sensor claim follows without a correct state and observation model.

Exact finite closure and a polynomial obstruction

Definitions and assumptions

A subspace W of observables is Koopman-invariant for a map f when p∈W implies p∘f∈W.

For the periodic heat equation u_t=u_xx, trigonometric modes are eigenfunctions of the generator ∂_xx.

For the obstruction, work with real polynomials as functions on an interval, and let f have degree d≥2.

Derivation or proof

If W contains x and is invariant, it contains x∘f=f, then f∘f, and inductively every iterate f^(∘n). Their degrees are d^n because the nonzero leading coefficient of a composition cannot cancel. Polynomials with distinct degrees are linearly independent: in any finite linear combination the largest degree has a coefficient contributed by exactly one summand, so that coefficient must vanish, and descending induction eliminates the rest. Compare the logistic map and a nonlinear PDE stencil.

Compare dense p=1/2 with p=c/n and compare W with a covariance matrix.

Write r=√(t²+ε²). For r>0, set P±=(I±H/r)/2.

Direct multiplication gives H²=(t²+ε²)I. Therefore its minimal polynomial divides λ²−r² and, for r>0, P±²=P±, P+P−=0, P++P−=I and HP±=±rP±. The spectral gap formula follows. For ε=0, H commutes with σz, so each coordinate axis is an invariant symmetry sector. The εσx perturbation does not commute with σz and permits those sectors to mix. Thus protection is a statement about an operator relation, not a verbal appeal to symmetry.

Worked example

Set ε=1/5 and let t run through −1,0,1.

The gaps are 2√26/5, 2/5, 2√26/5. The trace remains zero and the determinant is −(t²+1/25), so an eigenvalue cannot pass through zero at any real t. At ε=0, the determinant at t=0 vanishes and both eigenvalues coincide. The projector formulas explicitly cease to apply at that degenerate point because r=0.

A perturbation that changes a commutation relation can open a gap whose size is computed without approximation.

This static spectral calculation does not determine transition probabilities during a time sweep. Those depend on a time law, an initial state and the dynamical equation; replacing the minimum gap by a guessed transition rate is unjustified.

An affine map is T(x)=Mx+b. It is a coordinate isomorphism when M is invertible.

Substitute x into the second affine map and collect terms to obtain the composition law. Differentiate the frame relation using the product rule once and twice. The Ṁ and M̈ terms vanish only for a fixed linear frame; ḃ and b̈ vanish only for a fixed translation. Thus even a stationary world point may have nonzero coordinate velocity in a rotating or translating frame. This is a change in the description of motion, not a newly derived external force.

Let R be rotation by 90 degrees in the plane and T translation by (1,0). Also take a free path x(t)=x₀+vt.

RT sends the origin to (0,1), whereas TR sends it to (1,0), exhibiting noncommutativity. In a constant affine frame, the free path becomes y(t)=Mx₀+b+(Mv)t, still affine in time. For a rotating frame M(t)=R(ωt), a stationary x=(1,0) is described by y=(cosωt,sinωt), with acceleration −ω²y. The derivative terms account for that coordinate acceleration exactly.

The same geometric transformation may be used in a dynamical model, but its time dependence and reference-frame meaning must be stated.

An arbitrary invertible linear map need not preserve Euclidean lengths or kinetic-energy expressions. Those require transforming the metric as well. Singular affine maps are projections rather than reversible coordinate changes.

Cascade two independent binary symmetric channels with flip probability 0.1, and compare with X=Z, Y=Z for a fair common cause Z.

Information is a precisely calculable statistical quantity; assigning a mechanism requires additional assumptions or interventions.

For every sufficiently small λ, g+λδg stays positive. Both aggregate quantities remain G=6 and B=6, so identical C,I,V₀ produce exactly the same V(t) despite different channel conductances. Independently, α=0.2 and β=0.3 give q∞=0.4 and time constant 2 in the chosen time units. These are direct solutions, not fitted physiological claims.

State-domain validity and parameter identifiability are distinct mathematical requirements. A model may satisfy the first while failing the second under a limited observation protocol.

Scope of the result

The frozen-gate reduction is not a proof that the full nonlinear Hodgkin–Huxley model is unidentifiable under every experiment. Voltage dependence, varied inputs and additional observations can break this obstruction.

Further development

Specify a voltage-clamp or current-clamp input family, derive sensitivity equations and determine whether the added protocols remove the null directions demonstrated here.

M055 · 2023-07-18 · Decision theory · historical evidence U

Decision thresholds and genuine strategic equilibria

Finite models solved explicitly

An uncertain state of nature does not automatically supply a second strategic player. The distinction can be made concrete by solving a one-agent decision and a separately defined coordination game.

Definitions and assumptions

In a decision model, nature selects state S with prior p and T with prior 1−p. Action B has payoffs M and −c, while action N has zero in either state, with M,c>0.

In a two-player coordination game, each chooses B or N. Payoffs are (2,2) at (B,B), (1,1) at (N,N), and (0,0) at mismatched choices.

Decision thresholds and genuine strategic equilibria

In the decision problem B is optimal exactly when p≥c/(M+c), with indifference at equality. In the coordination game both (B,B) and (N,N) are Nash equilibria; there is also a mixed equilibrium where each chooses B with probability 1/3.

Derivation or proof

Expected utility of B is pM−(1−p)c=p(M+c)−c, while N gives zero, yielding the threshold. In the game, a player facing B obtains 2 by B and 0 by N; facing N, the player obtains 1 by N and 0 by B. Thus both coordinated profiles resist unilateral deviation. If the opponent chooses B with probability q, the expected payoff from B is 2q and from N is 1−q. Equality gives q=1/3; this mutual indifference verifies the mixed equilibrium.

Worked example

Choose M=9 and c=1 in the decision model.

The action threshold is p=0.1. At p=0.05, B has expected payoff −0.5 and N is better; at p=0.2, B has expected payoff 1 and is better. No opponent changes strategy in this calculation. In the game, the mixed-equilibrium payoff is 2/3, lower than either coordinated pure payoff; these outcomes depend on the explicitly chosen bimatrix, not on the decision table.

The word equilibrium becomes meaningful only after strategic actors and their payoff dependence are specified.

Scope of the result

These are illustrative finite-utility mathematical models and do not validate any metaphysical premise or uniquely prescribe behavior. A zero-sum interpretation would require yet another payoff structure.

Further development

Add explicit private information or a perturbation of payoffs and determine whether the equilibrium set or the decision threshold changes continuously.

M056 · 2023-07-18 · Decision theory · historical evidence U

Infinite utilities through controlled finite limits

Limit-order obstruction exhibited

Replacing very large payoffs by infinity can destroy the expectation being optimized. Finite truncations reveal when a conclusion is robust and when it depends on the order in which utility scales and probabilities approach their limits.

Definitions and assumptions

Take two states with probabilities p and 1−p. For truncation M>0, action A has payoffs (M,−M), action B has (−M,M) and action C has (0,0).

Expected utilities are UA=M(2p−1), UB=−UA and UC=0. Every finite model is well defined.

Infinite utilities through controlled finite limits

At fixed p≠1/2 the better of A and B is determined by the sign of 2p−1. At p=1/2 all three actions tie for every M. But sequences of priors with the same limiting value 1/2 can produce opposite strict preferences that persist as M→∞.

Derivation or proof

Choose p_M=1/2+a/M for fixed a and sufficiently large M so the prior is valid. Then UA=M(2a/M)=2a and UB=−2a. If a>0, A strictly wins; if a<0, B strictly wins; if a=0, all tie. All these priors converge to 1/2. Hence the limiting prior alone does not determine the limiting decision problem. Directly assigning payoffs +∞ and −∞ with both states of positive probability would require subtracting two infinite contributions, leaving an undefined expectation rather than a usable optimization objective.

Worked example

For M=100 take priors 0.51,0.49 and 0.50.

The respective expected payoffs of A are 2,−2 and 0, while B has the opposite values. Repeating with M=1000 and priors 0.501,0.499,0.500 gives exactly the same three outcomes. This is an exact algebraic example of a nonuniform limiting operation. The earlier finite wager threshold c/(M+c) instead tends to zero at fixed c, but that conclusion depends on its asymmetric payoff structure.

A claim involving infinite utilities needs a declared finite approximation, probability assumptions and a limit argument; otherwise an asserted optimum may not exist as a defined mathematical object.

Scope of the result

This example shows sensitivity of one family of limits, not that every model with unbounded utility is inconsistent. Extended-valued expectations are legitimate when their positive and negative parts are not simultaneously infinite.

Further development

Specify a utility function and a class of probability measures under which expectations are well defined, then use uniform-integrability conditions to justify exchanging limits and optimization.

M057 · 2023-07-28 · Probability · historical evidence A

A Cauchy model has no ordinary mean or variance

Classical result developed and worked

The useful revision is a complete separation between symmetry, existence of a mean, and concentration of an estimator. The Cauchy family gives an exact example in which averaging independent observations does not improve the distribution of the sample mean. This is a classical stability calculation, not a conclusion about any particular empirical dataset.

Definitions and assumptions

A Cauchy law with location μ and scale γ>0 has density γ/[π((x−μ)²+γ²)]. Its characteristic function is φ(t)=exp(iμt−γ|t|). Independence multiplies characteristic functions.

Exact failure of sample-mean concentration

If X₁,…,Xₙ are independent Cauchy(μ,γ), then their arithmetic mean is again Cauchy(μ,γ), for every positive integer n. Neither E[X] nor Var(X) exists as an ordinary finite moment.

Derivation or proof

The positive and negative parts of the centered first-moment integral each diverge logarithmically because x/(1+x²) has a logarithmic antiderivative. Symmetric truncation cancels these divergences, but that principal value is not a Lebesgue expectation. For the mean, independence gives E exp(itΣXⱼ/n)=φ(t/n)ⁿ=exp(iμt−γ|t|). Uniqueness of characteristic functions identifies the law. Thus no finite-variance central-limit estimate can be invoked. The same tail calculation gives a divergent second moment.

Worked example

Take standard Cauchy observations and ask whether the mean is within one unit of zero.

For every n, P(|X̄ₙ|≤1)=F(1)−F(−1)=1/2, using F(x)=1/2+arctan(x)/π. The probability remains one half even when n increases. In contrast, the population median is μ and independent sample quantiles can consistently estimate it because F is continuous and strictly increasing there.

A stable distribution can make an apparently reasonable estimator permanently noisy. Quantile estimation and distribution fitting must be evaluated under their actual assumptions.

Scope of the result

This does not establish that observations are Cauchy, that every heavy-tailed law lacks a mean, or that all robust estimators have the same behavior. Dependence would also change the characteristic-function multiplication.

Further development

For a specified tail exponent, determine which absolute moments exist, then compare mean, median and trimmed estimators using exact or justified asymptotic distributions.

M058 · 2023-07-28 · Dynamics · historical evidence A

Feedback instability is a mechanism to specify

Classical result developed and worked

Feedback questions become testable once an update matrix and a measured norm are fixed. Eigenvalues determine asymptotic decay in finite dimension, but they do not bound all finite-time amplification. A two-dimensional Jordan block makes the distinction completely explicit.

Definitions and assumptions

A discrete linear system is xₙ₊₁=Axₙ. Spectral radius ρ(A) is the largest eigenvalue modulus. The Euclidean amplification at step n is the induced norm ||Aⁿ||₂. A real matrix is normal when AAᵀ=AᵀA.

Exact transient amplification in an asymptotically stable system

For A=aI+bN with N=[[0,1],[0,0]], N²=0 and 0<a<1, Aⁿ=aⁿI+n aⁿ⁻¹bN. Although ρ(A)=a<1 and Aⁿ→0, intermediate norms can be arbitrarily large as |b| increases.

Derivation or proof

The binomial theorem applies because I and N commute and every power Nᵏ with k≥2 vanishes. Only the terms k=0 and k=1 survive. The scalar sequences aⁿ and n aⁿ⁻¹ both tend to zero, proving asymptotic stability. Acting on e₂ yields Aⁿe₂=(n aⁿ⁻¹b,aⁿ), so its Euclidean norm supplies a lower bound on ||Aⁿ||₂. At a fixed step n this lower bound grows linearly in |b| without changing either eigenvalue.

Worked example

Choose A=[[1/2,4],[0,1/2]] and initial state e₂.

At one step the output is (4,1/2), with norm √65/2>4. At two steps the output is (4,1/4), although the eigenvalues remain 1/2. The exact formula predicts eventual decay after this transient. The corresponding continuous example A_c=[[-1,4],[0,−1]] has exp(tA_c)=e^(−t)[[1,4t],[0,1]].

A stability statement and a peak-amplification statement answer different questions. A mechanism for a large transient can be proved without asserting any probability distribution for external shocks.

Scope of the result

The calculation assumes a fixed finite matrix. Nonlinear saturation, delayed feedback, time-varying matrices and stochastic inputs require additional models. A large matrix norm does not by itself imply a particular event occurs.

Further development

Optimize supₙ||Aⁿ|| over a parameter family, then compare Euclidean bounds with a quadratic Lyapunov norm that contracts at every step.

M059 · 2023-08-29 · Linear algebra · historical evidence A

Frobenius energy across disjoint blocks

Classical result developed and worked

A multiscale norm construction needs a bookkeeping theorem. The Frobenius norm behaves like a Euclidean norm on the list of matrix entries, so squared energies add over disjoint blocks. Overlapping descriptions need multiplicity corrections instead of an unqualified addition rule.

Definitions and assumptions

For a real or complex matrix A, ||A||_F²=Σᵢⱼ|aᵢⱼ|²=Tr(A* A). A block here means a subset of entry indices; blocks may have irregular shapes. A partition uses every entry exactly once.

Partition additivity and the overlap correction

If entry blocks B₁,…,B_m partition the indices, then ||A||_F²=Σ_b||A|B_b||_F². If they cover entries with multiplicities cᵢⱼ, the uncorrected sum is Σᵢⱼcᵢⱼ|aᵢⱼ|².

Derivation or proof

Expand every block norm as a sum of squared moduli and interchange two finite sums. The coefficient of a given entry is exactly the number of blocks containing it. For a partition that number is one. When every covered entry has positive multiplicity, assigning weight 1/cᵢⱼ to that entry within each occurrence restores the original energy. The argument needs no independence or probabilistic assumptions. An equivalent Hilbert-space statement uses orthogonal coordinate projections P_b and the identity ΣP_b=I.

Worked example

Let A=[[1,2],[3,4]]. Partition it by rows, then deliberately count its first row twice.

The complete squared Frobenius norm is 1+4+9+16=30. Row energies are 5 and 25, adding to 30. Repeating the first row gives 35, exposing five units of double counting. Dividing the two first-row occurrences by multiplicity two restores 30. By contrast, the unsquared norms √5+5 do not equal √30.

Disjoint block decomposition preserves total squared energy. It does not automatically make values comparable across blocks of different cardinalities.

Scope of the result

When comparing differently sized systems, one must choose total energy, mean squared entry, an operator norm or a dimensionless normalization. Those choices encode different questions. Orthogonal-coordinate arguments also do not apply unchanged to arbitrary overlapping learned features.

Further development

For nonorthogonal feature maps F_b, study frame bounds a||x||²≤Σ||F_bx||²≤b||x||² and determine whether a tight-frame normalization can preserve the intended energy.

M060 · 2023-08-29 · Probability · historical evidence A

Population weights versus amplitude weights

Classical result developed and worked

The distinction between probability weights and amplitude weights can be settled before any elaborate multiscale model is built. The former defines an expected square; the latter first attenuates the signal and then squares it. They agree only under special circumstances.

Definitions and assumptions

Let p_i≥0 with Σp_i=1 and let a_i be real or complex values. Expected square is E|A|²=Σp_i|a_i|². Entrywise amplitude weighting by p gives ||p⊙a||₂²=Σp_i²|a_i|².

Probabilistic weighting is implemented by square-root amplitudes

The probability-weighted squared magnitude equals ||diag(√p_i)a||₂². Weighting the amplitudes by p_i instead yields a different quadratic form. Since 0≤p_i≤1, the second is no larger than the first.

Derivation or proof

Expand the Euclidean norm after applying the diagonal matrix. Each squared coefficient is (√p_i)²=p_i. The ordinary amplitude weight p_i is squared by the norm, producing p_i². The inequality follows term by term from p_i²≤p_i. Equality requires p_i(1−p_i)|a_i|²=0 for every i: nonzero signals can occur only at weights zero or one, apart from degenerate cancellations that are impossible in this nonnegative sum.

Worked example

Use values a=(2,4) and probabilities p=(1/4,3/4).

Expected square is (1/4)4+(3/4)16=13. Squared probability-amplitude weighting gives (1/16)4+(9/16)16=37/4=9.25. The weighted mean is 7/2, so the variance is 13−(7/2)²=3/4. None of these three quantities is a substitute for the others.

A correct implementation starts by deciding whether the data describe sampling frequencies, deliberate attenuation or an averaging measure. The square-root representation then supplies a precise matrix formula.

Scope of the result

If some weights vanish, the resulting quadratic form is only a seminorm on the full coordinate space. Importance weights need not sum to one, while signed weights need not produce a positive quadratic form at all.

Further development

For a general positive measure μ, formulate the same distinction as an L²(μ) norm versus a weighted amplitude map, and establish invariance under a change of sampling representation.

M061 · 2023-08-29 · Linear algebra · historical evidence A

Covariance inequalities with finite moments

Classical result developed and worked

Covariance optimization is legitimate only after existence of the required moments is established. Once variables are square integrable, covariance becomes a positive semidefinite Gram matrix in an L² space, and the familiar bounds follow from one short argument.

Definitions and assumptions

For square-integrable X and Y, Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−EX)overline(Y−EY)]. For a real random vector Z, its covariance matrix Σ has entries Cov(Z_i,Z_j). Positive semidefinite means wᵀΣw≥0 for every w.

|Cov(X,Y)|²≤Var(X)Var(Y). For a finite square-integrable real vector, Var(wᵀZ)=wᵀΣw. If both variances are positive, equality in the scalar bound occurs precisely when the centered variables are proportional almost surely.

Derivation or proof

Centered variables are elements of the Hilbert space L². Cauchy–Schwarz gives the bound. Alternatively, for real variables, nonnegativity of E[(X−EX−t(Y−EY))²] for every real t forces the discriminant of this quadratic in t to be nonpositive. Expanding the centered weighted sum proves the matrix identity and hence positive semidefiniteness. Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz identifies linear dependence in L², where two representatives differing only on a null set are equivalent.

Worked example

Let X be equally likely to be −1 or 1, and let Y=2X.

Both means vanish. Variances are 1 and 4, covariance is 2, and Σ=[[1,2],[2,4]] has determinant zero. The combination 2X−Y vanishes almost surely, so its variance is zero. This explains the singularity structurally rather than treating it as a numerical failure.

A singular covariance matrix records an exact L² dependency. It can be essential information for a constrained quadratic calculation.

The Cauchy example M057 is outside these hypotheses; finite-sample covariance numbers do not create a population covariance that fails to exist. For complex variables, conjugation must be retained. Estimated matrices may require a separate analysis of sampling error.

Further development

Characterize which dependencies are preserved under an observation map and how eigenvalue perturbation bounds distinguish a true null direction from one introduced by finite precision.

M062 · 2023-08-29 · Convex optimization · historical evidence A

A quadratic program with singular cases included

Classical result developed and worked

The positive-definite inverse formula is only one branch of the quadratic-program problem. The singular case admits a clean complete classification, and inequality constraints can change the optimizer even when the matrix is nonsingular. These are mathematical statements about quadratic forms, not practical allocation recommendations.

Definitions and assumptions

Let Σ be a symmetric positive semidefinite real matrix and c≠0. Minimize wᵀΣw subject to cᵀw=1. Write Σ⁺ for its Moore–Penrose inverse and kerΣ for its nullspace.

Complete equality-constrained PSD classification

If some z∈kerΣ has cᵀz≠0, the minimum is zero and all minimizers are the feasible null vectors. Otherwise c∈rangeΣ, q=cᵀΣ⁺c>0, the minimum is 1/q, and all minimizers are Σ⁺c/q+z with z∈kerΣ.

Derivation or proof

In the first case, z/(cᵀz) is feasible and has zero objective; positive semidefiniteness rules out a lower value. In the second case, c is orthogonal to the nullspace and hence lies in the range. Set w₀=Σ⁺c/q. It is feasible and Σw₀=c/q. For any feasible w=w₀+h, cᵀh=0, so the cross term 2hᵀΣw₀ vanishes and the objective is 1/q+hᵀΣh. Equality holds exactly when h∈kerΣ. This also proves uniqueness precisely when the feasible tangent space contains no nonzero null vector.

Worked example

Compare a diagonal matrix, a rank-one matrix, and a nonnegative constraint.

For Σ=diag(1,4), c=(1,1), w*=(4/5,1/5) and the minimum is 4/5. For Σ=11ᵀ, every feasible w has objective one. For Σ=[[1,2],[2,9]], the unrestricted optimizer is (7/6,−1/6) with value 5/6; imposing w≥0 gives (1,0) with value one. Its KKT multiplier for the second coordinate is positive.

Nullspaces, budgets and inequality constraints must be handled together; merely replacing an inverse by a pseudoinverse does not cover every singular case.

Scope of the result

If Σ is indefinite the convex proof fails and the objective may be unbounded below along feasible directions. Additional bounds or penalties define different programs.

Further development

For rational inputs, produce exact KKT and nullspace certificates, then study the parameter loci where the active set or nullspace changes.

M063 · 2023-08-16 · Quantum mathematics · historical evidence A

Open-system dynamics must preserve physical states

Classical result developed and worked

An open-system equation must preserve the convex set of density operators, including when an auxiliary system is attached. An exactly solvable qubit channel provides a stronger check than inspection of trace alone. Its Kraus form supplies complete positivity directly.

Definitions and assumptions

A density operator is a positive semidefinite matrix ρ with trace one. A map is completely positive when its tensor product with the identity map on any finite auxiliary system preserves positivity. Set ℏ=1.

Exact amplitude-damping semigroup

For H=0 and L=√γ |0⟩⟨1| with γ≥0, the Lindblad equation sends ρ=[[a,b],[b*,d]] to [[a+(1−q)d,√q b],[√q b*,qd]], where q=e^(−γt), t≥0. This defines a trace-preserving completely positive semigroup.

Derivation or proof

Direct matrix multiplication in LρL†−{L†L,ρ}/2 gives ḋ=−γd, ḃ=−γb/2 and ȧ=γd, which solve to the displayed formula. Define K₀=diag(1,√q) and K₁=√(1−q)|0⟩⟨1|. Their adjoint squares sum to I, and ΣK_jρK_j† reproduces the solution. Tensoring each K_j with an auxiliary identity shows complete positivity. Since q(t+s)=q(t)q(s), composition satisfies the semigroup law.

Worked example

Start from |+⟩⟨+|, so a=d=b=1/2.

At q=1/4 the output is [[7/8,1/4],[1/4,1/8]], with trace one and determinant 3/64>0. More generally detρ(t)=q detρ(0)+q(1−q)d²≥0, giving an additional two-by-two positivity check. As t tends to infinity the state approaches |0⟩⟨0|.

The exact solution verifies what the mathematical generator does. It does not establish that this generator describes any proposed physical mechanism.

Scope of the result

A reduced microscopic model can require weak-coupling, coarse-graining or Markov assumptions before it has this form. Trace preservation alone is weaker than positivity, and positivity alone is weaker than complete positivity. Negative-time inversion is not a physical damping channel.

Add a specified Hamiltonian or dephasing operator and test whether an exact solution, a spectral decomposition of the generator, or a controlled splitting error is available.

Compare the stated discrete interpolation with a continuous model using λ=0.0005.

The latter target time is log(10¹²/77000)/0.0005≈32758.92083, about 8.18905 units earlier. Substituting t*=32767.109878086 back into the original formula recovers 10¹² to the working floating-point precision. The previously reported value near 11788 does not satisfy the equation.

Let E:Rⁿ→R be differentiable. A mobility K(x) is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix. The dynamics ẋ=−K(x)∇E(x) uses the chosen Euclidean coordinates; positive-definite K defines a corresponding metric interpretation.

The chain rule gives Ė=∇Eᵀẋ, and positive semidefiniteness gives the sign. For the coordinate change, ∇_yẼ=S⁻ᵀ∇_xE and ẏ=Sẋ=−SKSᵀ∇_yẼ. Substitution recovers the same scalar energy derivative. Take E(x)=xᵀAx/2 with symmetric A positive semidefinite, and K=I.

Then ẋ=−Ax and Ė=−xᵀA²x. A finite weighted-graph heat equation has this form with A equal to the graph Laplacian, while the scalar equation ẋ=−x is its one-dimensional instance. A constant component in the Laplacian nullspace is preserved rather than dissipated, which shows the difference between nonincrease and convergence to a unique state.

M066 · 2023-09-01 · Functional analysis · historical evidence A

Bessel versus Parseval

Classical result developed and worked

The missing distinction in the original inequality list is completeness. Bessel’s inequality is an exact statement about projection error; Parseval’s equality appears when the chosen orthonormal family spans the relevant Hilbert space. A residual formula makes the practical meaning immediate.

Definitions and assumptions

Use an inner product linear in its first argument. For an orthonormal family e₁,…,e_m, define P_mx=Σ⟨x,e_j⟩e_j. Its span is a closed finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space H.

Projection residual and completeness criterion

For every x, ||x||²=Σ_{j=1}^m|⟨x,e_j⟩|²+||x−P_mx||². For a countable orthonormal family, the infinite coefficient sum is at most ||x||². Equality for every x holds exactly when its closed linear span is H.

Derivation or proof

The residual is orthogonal to every e_j because taking its inner product with e_j subtracts the same coefficient. Pythagoras therefore splits the norm into projection and residual, and orthonormality gives the coefficient sum. Finite partial sums are increasing and bounded, so their limit exists. The partial projections form a Cauchy sequence, with squared differences equal to sums of omitted squared coefficients. Their limit projects onto the closed span. Equality means the residual projection onto the orthogonal complement vanishes. If equality holds for all x, that complement is zero and the span is dense.

Worked example

Take x=(2,3,6) in R³ and initially observe only e₁,e₂.

The observed squared coefficient sum is 4+9=13, total squared norm is 49, and residual squared norm is 36. Adding e₃ removes the residual exactly. Omitting e₃ never becomes harmless merely because the first two coefficients were calculated to high precision.

This is both an approximation certificate and a statement of what the measurement family cannot see.

An infinite orthonormal family need not be complete. For nonorthogonal features, coefficients from raw inner products are not automatically orthogonal projections, and frame or Gram-matrix analysis is needed.

M067 · 2023-09-01 · Functional analysis · historical evidence A

Let 1<p<∞ and q=p/(p−1), so 1/p+1/q=1. Norms are ||f||_p=(∫|f|^p)^(1/p) and the analogous q-norm, on one fixed measure space.

For a,b≥0, ab≤a^p/p+b^q/q, with equality exactly when a^p=b^q. Consequently ∫|fg|≤||f||_p||g||_q. For nonzero finite norms, equality holds exactly when |f|^p/||f||_p^p=|g|^q/||g||_q^q almost everywhere.

Fix a and minimize h(b)=b^q/q−ab+a^p/p over b≥0. Its derivative is b^(q−1)−a, with its unique minimum at b=a^(p−1), and the minimum equals zero. Normalize nonzero f,g to unit p- and q-norms, apply the scalar inequality pointwise and integrate. Equality in the integrated nonnegative difference requires pointwise equality almost everywhere, which yields the normalized-power condition. To obtain equality for |∫fg| as well, the product must also have an almost-everywhere constant phase or sign.

Choose p=3, q=3/2, a=2 and b=4.

Here a^p=b^q=8, so Young is exact: ab=8=8/3+8/(3/2). For a finite counting measure, proportional normalized powers supply equally explicit Hölder equality examples. Choosing disjointly supported nonzero functions makes the product integral zero while both norms are positive, showing a strict case.

For p=1, triangle inequalities bound each output coordinate and collecting each |x_j| gives the maximum column sum; choosing a coordinate vector at a maximizing column attains it. The infinity case uses a maximizing row and matching signs. Orthogonal or unitary invariance reduces the Euclidean claims to a diagonal singular-value matrix, where the largest entry bounds their squared sum above and below. The rank-zero case has both norms zero.

Let A=[[1,2],[0,1]].

Its induced 1- and infinity-norms are both three. Its Frobenius norm is √6. The eigenvalues of AᵀA=[[1,2],[2,5]] are 3±2√2, so ||A||₂=√(3+2√2)=1+√2. These are distinct measures of the same operator. A claim of amplification three is sharp for a 1-norm or infinity-norm question, but overestimates the sharp Euclidean factor.

Track the factors before inserting the answer.

Write the first row as S_00,S_01,S_02,S_03 and the remaining rows with S_10=S_01 and the corresponding symmetries.

Compare dust and radiation under a scale factor that doubles.

M074 · 2023-09-30 · Foundations · historical evidence A

Classical result developed and worked

Universe language is a relative-size discipline backed by a set-theoretic assumption. It is not a mechanism for eliminating every paradox without cost. The useful mathematical task is to state the closure axioms and show exactly which categorical constructions they permit.

Definitions and assumptions

A Grothendieck universe U is a transitive set closed under pairing, power sets and unions indexed by a set belonging to U, with the family’s members in U. To support ordinary infinite mathematics one asks ω∈U. A U-small set is an element of U, which differs from merely being a subset of U.

The inaccessible-cardinal construction of a universe

If κ is a strongly inaccessible cardinal, then V_κ is a Grothendieck universe containing ω. Consequently U-small sets, maps, finite products and function sets can be handled inside one fixed relative-size level. The existence of such an uncountable inaccessible cardinal is an additional assumption, not a theorem of bare ZFC.

Derivation or proof

Transitivity of the cumulative hierarchy is immediate. If x,y∈V_κ, their ranks are below κ, so pairing and power sets still have rank below κ because κ is a limit ordinal. For an indexed family (x_i)_{i∈I} with I∈V_κ, strong inaccessibility ensures every set in V_κ has cardinality below κ. Regularity then bounds the supremum of the fewer-than-κ ranks of x_i below κ, so their union remains in V_κ. For function sets X→Y, their graphs are subsets of X×Y and are therefore contained in a suitable iterated power-set construction inside U.

Worked example

Take two U-small sets X and Y.

Ordered pairs can be constructed by the Kuratowski definition, yielding X×Y∈U. Every function graph lies in P(X×Y), and the collection of all such graphs is a subset of that power set, hence U-small under the closure axioms. By contrast, the entire collection of all U-small sets is U itself; asserting U∈U would contradict foundation. It belongs to a larger universe only when another size assumption is made.

The construction makes size bookkeeping precise while retaining a visible logical boundary.

Scope of the result

This treatment proves the conditional construction, not consistency or existence of inaccessible cardinals. Degenerate finite universes and conventions excluding or including ω must be distinguished. Different foundational treatments can avoid universe axioms for specific constructions.

Further development

Rebuild one category-of-structures construction using a fixed cardinal bound instead, then compare its smallness guarantees with the universe-based version.

First take N=4,k=2, then a constant total twist Θ.

Use the exact rotation with cosθ=3/5 and sinθ=4/5.

Take t₁=2,t₂=1 and compare an unrelated rescaled two-state model.

Take r=(1,2) and Σ=diag(1,4).

The raw residual is E=1+4=5. Whitening gives Z=(1,1), so Q=2. If both coordinates are expressed in ten times larger numerical units, r becomes (10,20) and Σ becomes diag(100,400); E becomes 500, whereas Q remains 2.
