Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis Lqᵢ=λᵢqᵢ and write x=Σcᵢqᵢ. Continuous coefficients are cᵢ(t)=e^(−λᵢt)cᵢ(0). For the step, cᵢ⁺=(1−ηλᵢ)cᵢ. Thus ||x⁺||²−||x||²=Σ[(1−ηλᵢ)²−1]cᵢ². This is nonpositive for every coefficient vector precisely when every factor has magnitude at most one. Multiplying each term by λᵢ/2 proves the energy version. Also 1ᵀx⁺=1ᵀx, so mass is preserved independently of decay.

Worked example

Use the four-cycle Laplacian with eigenvalues 0,2,2,4.

For η=0.4, the update factors are 1,0.2,0.2,−0.6, hence every nonconstant mode contracts. For η=0.6, the largest-frequency factor is −1.4 and that mode grows. The equilibrium constant mode remains unchanged in both cases.

A large time step can turn a dissipative differential equation into an unstable numerical scheme. Continuous dissipation alone cannot certify the discretization.

Scope of the result

Energy monotonicity does not imply positivity of each coordinate. Positivity of forward Euler is governed by entrywise update weights and can require a smaller bound. Nonsymmetric operators require a different argument.

Further development

Compare forward, backward and exponential steps for a common graph, recording preservation of mass, positivity and decay separately.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M081 · 2023-10-07 · Arithmetic · historical evidence A

Exact exponent arithmetic before approximation

Developed classical result with worked example

Very large magnitudes are best handled by separating an exact exponent from a modest mantissa. That separation avoids overflow and makes errors in scale immediately visible.

Definitions and assumptions

Scientific notation writes a positive number as a×10ᵏ with 1≤a<10.

Relative error for an approximation ỹ to y≠0 is |ỹ−y|/|y|. A decimal logarithm adds log₁₀a to the exponent.

Square-root normalization

For an integer m and a>0, √(a×10^(2m))=√a×10ᵐ. For the recovered expression, √(5×10^54004)=√5×10^27002 exactly.

Derivation or proof

Both factors on the right are positive, and squaring gives 5×10^(2×27002), which is the original radicand. Uniqueness of the positive square root completes the proof. If an exponent is odd, move one factor of 10 into the mantissa before taking the square root; there is no need to evaluate the enormous number itself.

Worked example

Approximate the exact answer by 10^27002, or instead retain eleven significant mantissa digits.

The exact logarithm is 27002+(log₁₀5)/2. Omitting √5 gives relative error 1−1/√5≈0.5527864045, over 55 percent. Keeping 2.2360679775 as mantissa gives a small rounding error whose size can be bounded by squaring rational decimal endpoints around √5. The old comparison with 25,000×10^50,000 differs by tens of thousands of decimal orders.

An order-of-magnitude summary and a numerical approximation answer different questions. Stating the exact exponent costs essentially no extra computation.

Scope of the result

Exponent manipulations assume the usual positive real square root. Complex powers require a branch convention, and expressions with uncertain exponents need interval propagation rather than a single rounded exponent.

Further development

Use rational interval endpoints for the mantissa and retain an integer exponent in all later products, quotients and roots. This gives a small certificate that can be replayed without arbitrary-precision libraries.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M082 · 2023-10-07 · Mathematical modeling · historical evidence A

Competing response laws and identifiable parameters

Developed classical result with worked example

A named empirical law is a family of fitted functions with a domain and an error model. A rigorous mathematical comparison first asks whether the parameters and competing shapes can be distinguished at all.

Definitions and assumptions

For x>0, a power response is y=axᵇ with a>0. Its logarithm is log y=α+b log x, α=log a.

An additive Gaussian model for y and an additive Gaussian model for log y imply different likelihoods. Hick-type logarithmic response models use a different independent variable and cannot be substituted without defining the experiment.

Two-point identifiability in the noiseless power family

For two distinct positive inputs x₁≠x₂ and positive outputs, there is a unique power-law interpolant: b=log(y₂/y₁)/log(x₂/x₁) and a=y₁/x₁ᵇ. This identifies a family member, not the truth of the family.

Derivation or proof

Taking logarithms makes the problem a two-equation linear system with design rows (1,log x₁) and (1,log x₂). Its determinant log(x₂/x₁) is nonzero, so the solution is unique. A third input is therefore already an opportunity to reject the noiseless family rather than simply refit its two parameters. Under noise, a likelihood and uncertainty model are needed; logging observations changes the effective error structure.

Worked example

Consider synthetic observations at x=1,2,4 with y=3,12,48.

The first two pairs give b=2 and a=3. The third output predicted by the same parameters is 3×4²=48. If the third output were 45, the exact interpolation claim would fail. A measurement error model would decide whether that discrepancy is tolerable; the name of the law cannot decide it.

The example supplies a clear algebraic diagnostic without asserting any real psychophysical mechanism.

Scope of the result

Three agreeing points do not establish extrapolation, uniqueness among all functional families, or a causal explanation. Fitting and evaluating on the same observations measures interpolation.

Further development

Compare out-of-sample log likelihoods or explicitly bounded approximation errors for power, logarithmic and saturating families, with the same observation protocol and parameter accounting.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M083 · 2023-10-07 · Tensor algebra · historical evidence T

Tensor order and matrix rank are different invariants

Developed classical result with worked example

A second-order tensor may be represented by a matrix, but its order is not the number of nonzero eigenvalues. A dyadic decomposition adds a third meaning of rank that needs a stated field and symmetry convention.

Definitions and assumptions

For a real matrix A, rank(A) is the dimension of its image. A rank-one dyad uvᵀ maps x to u(vᵀx).

For a real symmetric A, the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis and A=Σλᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ. Negative coefficients are permitted in this signed decomposition.

Minimal dyadic count for a symmetric matrix

The minimum number of unrestricted real rank-one matrix summands is rank(A). A symmetric matrix has a signed symmetric dyadic representation with exactly that many nonzero terms. A decomposition into positive-weight vvᵀ terms exists only for positive-semidefinite A.

Derivation or proof

The image of a sum of r rank-one maps is contained in the span of their r output vectors, so its rank is at most r. Therefore at least rank(A) summands are necessary. The spectral theorem supplies exactly rank(A) nonzero signed symmetric dyads. Finally every sum Σcᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ with cᵢ≥0 has nonnegative quadratic form, so an indefinite matrix cannot possess such a decomposition.

Worked example

Let A=diag(−2,0,3).

Its tensor order is two, its matrix rank is two, and its signed dyadic decomposition is −2e₁e₁ᵀ+3e₃e₃ᵀ. At e₁ the quadratic form equals −2, excluding any sum of positive dyads. Replacing the zero entry by ε≠0 changes rank to three even when ||A_ε−A||₂=|ε| is arbitrarily small.

Exact rank is discontinuous at a rank-deficient matrix; numerical effective rank requires a declared threshold and noise scale.

Scope of the result

These conclusions concern matrices. Higher-order tensor rank, symmetric rank and border rank are different problems, and a matrix spectral decomposition does not solve them.

Further development

Study a noisy matrix through singular-value intervals and separate exact algebraic rank from a tolerance-dependent approximation rank.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M084 · 2023-10-07 · Harmonic analysis · historical evidence T

Directional cancellation as a limited shearlet illustration

Developed classical result with worked example

A useful entry point to shearlets is to show why a directional high-pass filter can avoid wasting coefficients along a straight edge. This finite calculation illustrates a mechanism, not a theorem of universal representation superiority.

Definitions and assumptions

An anisotropic dilation can be A_a=diag(a,√a), and a shear S_s=[[1,s],[0,1]]. A normalized analyzing function has form a^(−3/4)ψ(A_a⁻¹S_s⁻¹(x−t)).

The factor a^(−3/4) preserves the L² norm because det A_a=a^(3/2). A full shearlet frame additionally requires a designed generator, sampling and frame bounds.

Exact cancellation along a discrete straight edge

For the finite binary image F(i,j)=1[j≥i], the tangent difference F(i+1,j+1)−F(i,j) vanishes wherever both samples exist. The horizontal difference F(i+1,j)−F(i,j) is nonzero on the diagonal.

Derivation or proof

Adding one to both i and j preserves the inequality j≥i, so the tangent statement follows pointwise. Holding j fixed while increasing i by one changes the truth value exactly when j=i. Thus a coordinate direction aligned with the edge recognizes a coherent geometric feature that an unaligned difference repeatedly crosses. The normalization formula follows separately from a change of variables in the L² integral.

Worked example

Use a 16×16 sample grid and compare valid interior differences.

All 225 tangent differences are zero. Among the 240 valid horizontal differences, 15 are nonzero. Reversing or rotating the edge changes which directional operator cancels, so the favorable orientation is part of the setup. A separable wavelet can itself be extremely sparse for an axis-aligned edge.

The calculation validates an orientation mechanism and its restrictions. It does not compare complete reconstruction errors, coefficient budgets or full shearlet and wavelet systems.

Scope of the result

Nearly optimal approximation theorems concern specified cartoon-like regularity classes and particular frames. They are not established by this image experiment and do not extend to every signal.

Further development

Implement matched complete transforms and plot best-N-term reconstruction errors under a declared edge model, coefficient budget and boundary convention.

M085 · 2023-10-07 · Quantum mathematics · historical evidence T

A fully normalized spin one-half Wigner representation

Developed classical result with worked example

The spin phase space is a sphere, and its kernel and measure must be chosen together. For a qubit the complete reconstruction can be derived from elementary spherical moments, including the appearance of negative quasiprobabilities.

Definitions and assumptions

Write A=a₀I+a·σ, with Pauli matrices σ=(σ_x,σ_y,σ_z). For Hermitian A, the four coefficients are real.

Choose Δ(n)=(I+√3 n·σ)/2 for unit n∈S² and measure dμ=dΩ/(2π), whose total mass is two. Define W_A(n)=Tr(AΔ(n)).

Self-dual reconstruction and trace pairing

W_A(n)=a₀+√3a·n, A=∫W_A(n)Δ(n)dμ and Tr(AB)=∫W_AW_Bdμ. For a density matrix ρ=(I+r·σ)/2, ∫W_ρdμ=1 even though W_ρ need not be nonnegative.

Derivation or proof

Use Trσ_i=0 and Tr(σ_iσ_j)=2δ_ij. The spherical moments are ∫1dμ=2, ∫n_idμ=0 and ∫n_in_jdμ=(2/3)δ_ij. Substitution gives the symbol immediately. Expanding W_AΔ and integrating leaves a₀I+a·σ. Expanding W_AW_B gives 2a₀b₀+2a·b, exactly Tr(AB). These calculations also fix the measure normalization; using dΩ/(4π) without changing other factors would break reconstruction.

Worked example

Take the pure spin-up state r=(0,0,1).

Its symbol is W(n)=(1+√3n_z)/2, with minimum (1−√3)/2<0 at the south pole. The six directions ±e_x,±e_y,±e_z with weights 1/3 each reproduce all required spherical moments exactly, so the reconstruction and trace identity can be checked by a six-point sum.

Negativity is compatible with reconstruction because Δ(n) is not a positive measurement effect. Treating W as an ordinary probability density would lose this distinction.

Scope of the result

This derivation concerns spin one-half and a specific self-dual convention. Higher-spin kernels have more multipoles, and changing conventions changes constants and symbol products.

Further development

Derive the induced star product from matrix multiplication and study its finite spherical-harmonic content before comparing it with a flat Moyal product.

M086 · 2023-10-07 · Mathematical physics · historical evidence T

Exact polynomial Moyal products

Developed classical result with worked example

On polynomial symbols the Moyal exponential terminates, so one can verify noncommutativity and associativity with exact arithmetic rather than relying on an informal infinite series.

Definitions and assumptions

For canonical coordinates (q,p), let B=←∂_q→∂_p−←∂_p→∂_q and define f⋆g=Σₙ≥₀(iℏ/2)ⁿBⁿ(f,g)/n!.

For polynomials only finitely many differentiated terms survive. The corresponding formal-series definition can be used beyond polynomials without claiming analytic convergence.

Canonical commutator and classical limit

q⋆p−p⋆q=iℏ. More generally the antisymmetrized product divided by iℏ equals the Poisson bracket plus terms of formal order ℏ². The product is associative in the polynomial or formal setting.

Derivation or proof

At first order q⋆p=qp+iℏ/2 and p⋆q=pq−iℏ/2; higher derivatives vanish. Interchanging f and g changes the sign of B, so only odd n contribute to the commutator. After division by iℏ, the n=1 term is the Poisson bracket and the next possible term has order ℏ². For associativity, introduce three tensor factors. The constant-coefficient bidifferential operators B₁₂, B₁₃ and B₂₃ commute. Either parenthesization is ordinary multiplication after exp[(iℏ/2)(B₁₂+B₁₃+B₂₃)], establishing equality.

Worked example

Set ℏ=1 and take f=q², g=p².

The finite expansion gives q²⋆p²=q²p²+2iqp−1/2, while p²⋆q²=q²p²−2iqp−1/2. Their commutator is 4iqp, agreeing with i times {q²,p²}=4qp. The verifier also compares both parenthesizations for a family of low-degree monomials with rational complex coefficients.

The example checks a finite, exact algebra. It requires no discretized phase-space grid and therefore has no grid-resolution error.

Scope of the result

Formal associativity does not prove convergence of the Moyal series for arbitrary smooth functions. Trace-integral identities require integrability and boundary conditions; polynomial symbols on the full plane are usually not integrable.

Further development

Specify a Schwartz-class or other analytic symbol space and prove continuity or trace properties there, keeping that analysis separate from the formal calculation.

M087 · 2023-10-07 · Operator theory · historical evidence T

A spectral definition of fractional quantum evolution

Developed classical result with worked example

A fractional differential symbol becomes a definite evolution only after specifying its self-adjoint operator, domain and boundary convention. A periodic box gives an explicit example with no ambiguous boundary prescription.

Definitions and assumptions

On the circle of length 2π, use normalized Fourier modes e_n(x)=e^(inx)/√(2π). For α>0, define (−Δ)^(α/2)e_n=|n|^αe_n.

Take ℏ=1 and H=D_α(−Δ)^(α/2) with D_α>0. Its domain consists of coefficients satisfying Σ|n|^(2α)|c_n|²<∞.

Unitary fractional evolution on the circle

The solution of iψ_t=Hψ is ψ(t)=Σc_ne^(−itD_α|n|^α)e_n. It preserves the L² norm and the spectral energy wherever that expectation is finite. The case α=2 recovers the usual quadratic dispersion with D₂=1/(2m) in ℏ=1 units.

Derivation or proof

The Fourier transform is unitary from L² of the circle to ℓ²(Z). Under it H is multiplication by the real nonnegative sequence D_α|n|^α on its maximal domain, hence self-adjoint. Exponentiation multiplies each coefficient by a complex number of modulus one. Parseval therefore gives ||ψ(t)||²=Σ|c_n|². Multiplying by the same unchanged spectral weights proves energy conservation for states in the form domain.

Worked example

Choose D_α=1, α=3/2 and ψ(0)=(e₀+e₁+e₂)/√3.

The three energies are 0,1,2√2. The coefficients at time t are (1,e^(−it),e^(−i2√2t))/√3, so their squared magnitudes still sum to one. At α=2 the energies become 0,1,4; this is a change in dispersion, not a change of normalization.

The finite-mode example can be replayed exactly at the spectral level and numerically in physical space.

Scope of the result

On an interval, spectral, restricted and regional fractional Laplacians are generally different operators. This periodic calculation does not choose among them or validate a physical interpretation for every α.

Further development

Compare two explicitly defined bounded-domain operators using the same initial data and observable, and distinguish operator-domain effects from fractional-order effects.

Mathematical references: R067

M088 · 2023-10-07 · Linear algebra · historical evidence T

Lagrange identity and its equality geometry

Developed classical result with worked example

The finite-dimensional identity is an exact decomposition of the Cauchy–Schwarz deficit. An operator boundary identity sharing the same historical name is a separate theorem with separate domains.

Definitions and assumptions

For a,b∈Rⁿ, define the antisymmetric coordinate minors m_ij=a_i b_j−a_j b_i.

The exterior product a∧b has squared norm Σ_{i<j}m_ij² in the orthonormal exterior basis.

Lagrange identity

||a||²||b||²−(a·b)²=Σ_{i<j}(a_i b_j−a_j b_i)². Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz holds exactly when all these minors vanish, equivalently when the two vectors are linearly dependent.

Derivation or proof

Expand the right-hand side and rewrite the sum over i<j as one half of the sum over all ordered pairs. The squared terms contribute Σ_i a_i²Σ_j b_j². The cross terms contribute −Σ_ij a_i a_j b_i b_j=−(a·b)². If a≠0 and every minor vanishes, select an index i with a_i≠0. The identities a_i b_j=a_j b_i give b=(b_i/a_i)a. If a=0, dependence is immediate.

Worked example

Let a=(1,2,3), b=(2,−1,4).

Their squared norms are 14 and 21, and their dot product is 12, giving 294−144=150. The three minors are −5,−2,11, whose squares sum to 25+4+121=150. In three dimensions this is also ||a×b||².

The identity quantifies the area spanned by two vectors; it does not itself introduce a field equation or an elasticity model.

Scope of the result

For complex vectors the Hermitian inner product and absolute squares must be used. Green or Lagrange identities for differential operators introduce integration by parts, boundary traces and domain assumptions not present here.

Further development

For a stated PDE operator, derive its own boundary pairing and use the finite-dimensional inequality only at the particular algebraic step where it is applicable.

M089 · 2023-10-12 · Topology · historical evidence A

Winding number and Gauss–Bonnet with boundaries explicit

Developed classical result with worked example

Topological charges are attached to specified spaces and deformation classes. Winding number and Euler characteristic are both invariant quantities, but they are not interchangeable measurements of a generic defect.

Definitions and assumptions

For a closed C¹ loop z:[0,2π]→C∖{0}, the winding number is w=(1/(2πi))∫z′(t)/z(t)dt.

For a closed oriented smooth surface, Gauss–Bonnet states ∫K dA=2πχ. A surface with boundary needs a boundary-geodesic-curvature term and possible corner contributions.

Integer winding and homotopy stability

The displayed winding integral is an integer and remains unchanged during a continuous homotopy of loops that avoids zero. Passing through zero removes the hypothesis that protects the invariant.

Derivation or proof

Lift the argument along the parameter interval: z(t)=r(t)e^(iθ(t)) with r>0 and continuous θ. Then z′/z=r′/r+iθ′ wherever derivatives exist. The radial integral vanishes because r has equal endpoints. Since the loop closes, θ(2π)−θ(0) is an integer multiple of 2π. Under a zero-avoiding homotopy, the resulting winding is continuous in the homotopy parameter and integer-valued, hence constant. Smooth approximation extends the argument to continuous loops.

Worked example

Use z(t)=e^(3it), and separately use a round sphere of radius R.

For the loop, z′/z=3i and the winding is three. For the sphere, K=R⁻² and area=4πR², so the curvature integral is 4π and χ=2. A flat disk has zero interior curvature but χ=1; its circular boundary contributes 2π, demonstrating why the closed-surface formula cannot simply be reused.

Each calculation answers a specific topological question and exhibits its own necessary boundary condition.

Scope of the result

Winding depends on a chosen omitted point or target circle. Gauss–Bonnet requires sufficient regularity and the correct boundary terms. Neither invariant completely classifies arbitrary spaces or dynamical defects.

Further development

Construct a one-parameter family that crosses a zero and calculate the jump in winding; separately examine a surface family where a topology change destroys smooth-manifold hypotheses.

M090 · 2023-10-12 · Complex geometry · historical evidence A

An explicit marked-torus deformation

Developed classical result with worked example

A torus supplies a complete elementary setting in which deformation parameters, marking, Beltrami coefficient and dilatation can all be written down. This replaces the old undefined sum of named geometric quantities.

Definitions and assumptions

For τ in the upper half-plane, the marked complex torus is C/(Z+τZ). The marking identifies the two chosen lattice generators with a fixed reference basis.

A quasiconformal map has f_z̄=μf_z with |μ|<1 almost everywhere. For a real-linear orientation-preserving map its maximal dilatation is K=(1+|μ|)/(1−|μ|).

Rectangular torus stretch

The map F(x+iy)=x+iby from the square marked torus to the rectangular marked torus of parameter ib has μ=(1−b)/(1+b) and K=max(b,1/b), for b>0. It realizes the classical torus Teichmüller distance |log b|/2.

Derivation or proof

Since x=(z+z̄)/2 and iy=(z−z̄)/2, F=((1+b)/2)z+((1−b)/2)z̄. Thus F_z=(1+b)/2, F_z̄=(1−b)/2 and the coefficient follows. The real singular values are 1 and b, giving the same K as their ratio. For optimality among maps in the marking class, the standard extremal-length distortion bound applied to horizontal and vertical curve families gives K at least max(b,1/b); this affine map attains it. The extremal-length bound is the classical geometric input, not a consequence merely of the algebraic derivative calculation.

Worked example

Set b=2.

The map doubles the vertical period, has μ=−1/3 and K=2. Its Teichmüller distance is (log2)/2. Replacing b by 1/2 reverses the stretch and has the same distance. Changing the marking by an integer modular transformation is a separate quotient operation.

Every number in this example has a defined geometric role, unlike an arbitrary linear combination of unrelated invariants.

Scope of the result

The affine torus formula does not classify extremal maps of higher-genus surfaces. Teichmüller space and the moduli-space quotient should not be identified.

Further development

For a specified higher-genus surface, choose a quadratic differential and formulate the associated deformation with its normalization and marking retained.

M091 · 2023-10-16 · Dynamics · historical evidence A

Certified first logistic-map period doublings

Developed classical result with worked example

The first two bifurcation parameters can be obtained algebraically, so they provide exact calibration points before any numerical Feigenbaum-ratio experiment.

Definitions and assumptions

Let f_r(x)=rx(1−x), with r in [0,4] and x in [0,1]. A period-k orbit is stable when the absolute value of the derivative of f_r^k along it is less than one.

A flip bifurcation is detected when this multiplier passes through −1, subject to the usual nondegeneracy conditions.

First two flip thresholds

The nonzero fixed point x*=1−1/r loses linear stability at r₁=3. The genuine two-cycle, existing for r>3, has multiplier m₂=−r²+2r+4 and is stable for 3<r<1+√6. At r₂=1+√6 the multiplier crosses −1 transversely; the classical flip theorem applies and produces the standard supercritical period-four branch.

Derivation or proof

At the fixed point, f′_r(x*)=r−2r(1−1/r)=2−r, so its stability interval is 1<r<3. Dividing f_r²(x)−x by the fixed-point factor leaves the two-cycle quadratic r²x²−r(r+1)x+(r+1). Its roots are x_±=(r+1±√((r−3)(r+1)))/(2r), giving multiplier −r²+2r+4 by their sum and product. The equation m₂=−1 selects r₂=1+√6, with derivative −2√6≠0. To check the flip nondegeneracy rather than infer birth from the multiplier alone, let g=f_r² near one cycle point. The logistic Schwarzian is Sf=−6/(1−2x)², and Sg=(Sf∘f)(f′)²+Sf<0 on the threshold cycle, where both first derivatives are nonzero. At g′=−1, the cubic normal-form coefficient is g‴/6+(g″)²/4=−Sg/6>0. Transversality and this positive coefficient are the hypotheses of the classical supercritical flip theorem. The algebra verifies those hypotheses; the local bifurcation theorem is classical input.

Worked example

Certify the second threshold using rational decimal endpoints.

Squaring 2.449489742783178 and 2.449489742783179 as exact fractions brackets six. Therefore 3.449489742783178<r₂<3.449489742783179. At r=3.2 the multiplier is 0.16; at r=3.5 it is −1.25, independently locating stability and instability.

The first low-order thresholds are now exact benchmarks, not points inferred from a bifurcation picture.

Scope of the result

Two thresholds do not estimate the asymptotic Feigenbaum constant reliably. Universality is a theorem with hypotheses, not an inference from any finite list of ratios. Higher-period orbit equations require root isolation and exclusion of lower periods.

Further development

Isolate subsequent flip parameters with interval arithmetic, verify minimal period, and report rigorous intervals for successive scaling ratios rather than bare decimal limits.

M092 · 2023-10-16 · Dynamics · historical evidence A

Parameter loci, orbit closures and dissipative flows

Developed classical result with worked example

Pictures of the Mandelbrot set, a logistic bifurcation diagram and a Lorenz trajectory refer to different mathematical spaces. Defining the plotted object prevents geometric resemblance from being mistaken for a common theorem.

Definitions and assumptions

For z₀=0 and zₙ₊₁=zₙ²+c, the Mandelbrot set is the set of parameters c whose critical orbit remains bounded.

The Lorenz vector field is ẋ=σ(y−x), ẏ=x(ρ−z)−y, ż=xy−βz. Its state space is R³; σ,ρ,β are separate parameters.

Escape and volume contraction are different tests

For the quadratic family, an orbit point with |z|>max(2,|c|) grows without bound. For positive Lorenz parameters the divergence is the constant −σ−1−β<0, so volume transported by a smooth local flow contracts exponentially. Volume contraction alone does not prove chaos.

Derivation or proof

The triangle inequality gives |z²+c|≥|z|²−|c|. If |z|>max(2,|c|), then |z|²−|c|>|z|²−|z|>|z|. The same inequality persists and gives eventual unbounded growth. For the flow, the diagonal derivatives are −σ,−1,−β. Liouville’s formula for the derivative flow gives det DΦ_t=exp(−(σ+1+β)t) while the solution exists. This controls transported volume, not orbit separation in every direction.

Worked example

Compare c=0, c=−1 and c=1, and compare the Lorenz divergence at σ=10,β=8/3.

The critical orbit for c=0 stays zero. For c=−1 it alternates 0,−1. For c=1 it begins 0,1,2,5 and then escapes by the criterion. The Lorenz volume factor is exp(−41t/3), regardless of ρ; this cannot alone distinguish periodic from chaotic parameter regimes.

A bounded critical orbit and a contracting state-space volume are statements about different objects and require different evidence.

Scope of the result

A finite run without detected escape does not certify Mandelbrot membership. Negative divergence does not imply a strange attractor, positive Lyapunov exponent or a complete global existence theorem.

Further development

Use rigorous escape certificates or validated trapping regions for individual questions, and label parameter space separately from state space in every visualization.

M093 · 2023-10-21 · Convex analysis · historical evidence A

Convex conjugates with their actual domains

Developed classical result with worked example

A Legendre–Fenchel transform is a supremum over a declared domain. Solving a derivative equation is sufficient only after boundary and finiteness cases are checked.

Definitions and assumptions

For an extended-real function f:R→R∪{+∞}, f*(p)=sup_x(px−f(x)). A domain restriction is encoded by f=+∞ outside the domain.

Fenchel’s inequality says f(x)+f*(p)≥px. Equality holds exactly when p is a subgradient of a closed proper convex f at x.

Quadratic and exponential conjugates

For k>0, f(x)=kx² on R gives f*(p)=p²/(4k). Restricting to x≥0 gives f*(p)=max(p,0)²/(4k). For f(x)=eˣ, f*(p)=p logp−p if p>0, f*(0)=0 and f*(p)=+∞ if p<0.

Derivation or proof

Complete the square: px−kx²=p²/(4k)−k(x−p/(2k))². On the half-line, the interior optimizer is feasible only if p≥0; otherwise the maximum is at x=0. For the exponential, differentiating gives eˣ=p, so p>0 has the unique maximizer x=logp. If p=0, the supremum of −eˣ is zero but is approached only as x→−∞. If p<0, sending x→−∞ makes px−eˣ diverge to +∞. These cases prove the complete extended-real formula.

Worked example

Take k=2 and p=−4.

On the full line the maximizer is x=−1 and the conjugate value is 2. On x≥0, the maximizer is x=0 and the value is zero. The same stationary equation cannot be used unchanged in both domains. For eˣ at p=0, no finite maximizer exists despite a finite conjugate value.

The example distinguishes finite supremum, attainment and an interior critical point.

Scope of the result

Biconjugacy f**=f requires f to be proper, lower semicontinuous and convex; otherwise f** gives the appropriate closed convex envelope rather than recovering arbitrary input data.

Further development

Develop a multivariable constrained example using normal cones and KKT conditions, recording both primal feasibility and dual equality as the certificate.

M094 · 2023-10-21 · Probability and foundations · historical evidence A

The CHSH bound and a finite-sample test

Developed classical result with worked example

The mathematical content of a Bell test begins with a probability model and a clear null hypothesis. A violation claim needs a sampling argument in addition to a formal inequality.

Definitions and assumptions

A deterministic local assignment specifies A₀,A₁,B₀,B₁∈{−1,1}. Shared randomness makes a convex mixture of such assignments when settings are independent of that randomness.

The CHSH expression is S=E[A₀B₀]+E[A₀B₁]+E[A₁B₀]−E[A₁B₁]. In its uniformly sampled game version, a trial wins when A_xB_y=(−1)^(xy).

Classical bound and an iid tail certificate

Every local model with measurement independence obeys |S|≤2, equivalently game success probability at most 3/4. For independent identically distributed trials under this null, P(ŵ≥3/4+ε)≤exp(−2nε²).

Derivation or proof

For a deterministic assignment, S=A₀(B₀+B₁)+A₁(B₀−B₁). Exactly one bracket is zero and the other is ±2, so S=±2. Convex averaging preserves the bound. Uniform setting probabilities give w=1/2+S/8. For the finite-sample statement, wins are independent variables in [0,1] with mean at most 3/4, and Hoeffding’s inequality supplies the displayed one-sided tail. Exhausting the sixteen deterministic assignments independently verifies the algebraic bound.

Worked example

Suppose n=1000 independent uniformly sampled trials have observed win fraction 0.80.

Here ε=0.05, so the upper bound on the null tail is exp(−5)≈0.00673795. This calculation uses the declared iid sampling and measurement-independence assumptions; it is not a p-value for an unspecified physical dataset.

The finite count, the null model and the test statistic are all explicit, making the strength and limitations of the evidence assessable.

Scope of the result

Adaptive devices, memory, nonuniform settings, missing detections or postselection require revised statistical reasoning and may alter the applicable null. Metaphysical conclusions do not follow from the probability algebra alone.

Further development

Replace the iid assumption by a clearly specified sequential local model and use a valid supermartingale test without discarding trials.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M095 · 2023-10-26 · Commutative algebra · historical evidence A

An exact free resolution and a separate geometric blowup

Developed classical result with worked example

A free resolution records relations among polynomial generators. A resolution of singularities changes a geometric space by a birational morphism. The two constructions can inform one another but their outputs and correctness criteria are different.

Definitions and assumptions

Let R=k[x,y] and I=(x²,xy,y²). Define d₀:R³→I by d₀(a,b,c)=ax²+bxy+cy².

Let d₁:R²→R³ have columns s₁=(−y,x,0) and s₂=(0,−y,x). With grading, the complex is 0→R(−3)²→R(−2)³→I→0.

A minimal graded free resolution of I

The displayed complex is exact, and its entries lie in the homogeneous maximal ideal, so it is minimal as a graded free resolution.

Derivation or proof

First d₀s₁=d₀s₂=0. Suppose ax²+bxy+cy²=0. Reducing modulo x gives c≡0 modulo x, so c=xc₁. Dividing by x gives ax+by+c₁y²=0. Reducing modulo y gives a≡0 modulo y; write a=−ya₁. Then b=xa₁−yc₁. Thus (a,b,c)=a₁s₁+c₁s₂, proving equality of image and kernel. If u s₁+v s₂=0, the first coordinate gives yu=0 and the last gives xv=0, so u=v=0 because R is a domain. This proves injectivity. The standard graded minimality criterion applies since no differential entry is a unit.

Worked example

Compare the plane cusp y²=x³ over a field of characteristic zero.

In the blowup chart y=xv, the total transform is x²(v²−x)=0. The strict transform v²−x=0 is smooth because its derivative with respect to x is −1. Its parametrization x=v²,y=v³ gives the familiar normalization map. It remains tangent to the exceptional divisor x=0; a normal-crossings embedded resolution requires further work.

The syzygy calculation proves exactness of a module complex. The blowup calculation proves smoothness of a strict transform in the relevant chart. Neither should be described as the other.

Scope of the result

The one-chart cusp example is not a general resolution algorithm or a completed embedded normal-crossings calculation. Schreyer methods do not automatically supply the geometric blowup data.

Further development

Construct a separate certificate for each stage of an embedded resolution, including exceptional multiplicities and intersection behavior.

M096 · 2023-10-26 · Algebraic geometry · historical evidence A

A complete two-dimensional toric subdivision

Developed classical result with worked example

A rational cone contains enough combinatorial data to detect and resolve a simple affine toric singularity. The lattice, primitive generators and subdivision must be specified rather than inferred from a picture.

Definitions and assumptions

Use N=Z² and the cone σ generated by v₀=(1,0),v₂=(1,2). A full-dimensional two-dimensional cone is regular when its primitive ray generators form a lattice basis.

The affine toric variety is Spec C[σ∨∩M], where M is the dual lattice. Subdividing a cone without changing its support defines a proper birational toric morphism.

Regular subdivision of an index-two cone

The original cone has determinant two and is singular. Adding the primitive ray v₁=(1,1) divides it into two determinant-one cones, giving a smooth toric surface mapping properly and birationally to the original affine surface.

Derivation or proof

The determinant det(v₀,v₂)=2 is the index of their generated sublattice. The adjacent determinants det(v₀,v₁)=det(v₁,v₂)=1, so both charts have ray bases of N and are smooth. The fan has the same support and agrees with the original torus, establishing properness and birationality by the standard toric fan criterion. The dual semigroup is generated by (0,1),(1,0),(2,−1), with the relation (0,1)+(2,−1)=2(1,0). Hence the original coordinate ring is C[u,v,w]/(uw−v²), whose gradient vanishes at the origin.

Worked example

Calculate the determinant and ring descriptions directly.

The defining polynomial F=uw−v² has gradient (w,−2v,u), so the only complex singular point is the origin. Each subdivided chart is a polynomial two-variable chart because its ray basis is unimodular. The exceptional curve records the new ray and is contracted by the toric morphism.

This supplies a full combinatorial smoothness certificate for this fan and a concrete algebraic model of the singular target.

Scope of the result

A determinant test at one cone does not establish smoothness of every cone in a larger fan. Properness depends on support and fan compatibility, not only local determinants.

Further development

Implement a two-dimensional subdivision certificate that checks primitive rays, angular ordering, unchanged support and determinant one for every resulting cone.

M097 · 2023-10-26 · Algebraic geometry · historical evidence A

Hodge numbers constrained by geometry

Developed classical result with worked example

A Hodge diamond is meaningful only after choosing a cohomology theory and geometric hypotheses. Smooth projective complex examples provide exact checks of both the numbers and their symmetries.

Definitions and assumptions

For a smooth projective complex variety X, h^(p,q)=dim H^q(X,Ω_X^p) and b_k=Σ_{p+q=k}h^(p,q).

For a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus g, the only nonzero Hodge numbers are h^(0,0)=h^(1,1)=1 and h^(1,0)=h^(0,1)=g.

Curve and product examples

A genus-g curve has Betti numbers (1,2g,1) and Euler characteristic 2−2g. For P¹×P¹ the nonzero Hodge numbers are h^(0,0)=h^(2,2)=1 and h^(1,1)=2, giving Euler characteristic four.

Derivation or proof

For curves, holomorphic one-forms have dimension g, and complex conjugation gives the antiholomorphic dimension g. Connectedness and orientation give the degree-zero and degree-two classes. Summing along diagonals proves the Betti numbers. For P¹, the Hodge polynomial is 1+uv. The Künneth formula for the product gives (1+uv)²=1+2uv+u²v², from which all displayed Hodge numbers follow. Their alternating total agrees with the product of the two sphere Euler characteristics.

Worked example

Use an elliptic curve and a smooth plane quintic.

At g=1, the elliptic curve has Betti numbers (1,2,1) and χ=0. A smooth plane curve of degree d has genus (d−1)(d−2)/2 by adjunction; at d=5 this gives g=6, hence Betti numbers (1,12,1) and χ=−10. This also independently diagnoses the earlier confusion between a plane quintic curve and a quintic Calabi–Yau threefold.

The numbers are linked by proven geometric structure, rather than predicted merely from a name or a numerical pattern.

Scope of the result

Singular, nonproper or non-Kähler examples require modified statements; ordinary pure Hodge symmetries cannot be assumed unchanged. Numerical estimates are not exact Hodge-number certificates.

Further development

For a specified smooth hypersurface, compute its relevant graded Jacobian pieces and reconcile the resulting Hodge numbers with independent Euler and symmetry checks.

M098 · 2023-10-26 · Arithmetic geometry · historical evidence A

A rational parametrization and a nonexistence certificate

Developed classical result with worked example

Finding many points and proving a point set complete are different achievements. Elementary conics already show how parametrization, integer constraints and local obstructions lead to distinct certificates.

Definitions and assumptions

For an equation X defined over Q, X(Q) is the rational point set, X(Z) the integral point set and X(F_p) a reduction over a finite field when defined.

Clearing denominators in a rational point yields a primitive integer tuple; primitivity must be retained in divisibility arguments.

Two conic certificates

Every rational point of x²+y²=1 except (−1,0) is x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), y=2t/(1+t²) for t∈Q. The conic x²+y²=3 has no rational point.

Derivation or proof

For the circle, draw the line y=t(x+1) through (−1,0). Substitution factors out the known intersection and yields the displayed second point. Conversely, for a rational circle point with x≠−1, t=y/(x+1) is rational and reconstructs the point, proving completeness. For x²+y²=3, a rational point would yield primitive integers a,b,c with a²+b²=3c². Modulo three, squares are zero or one; their sum can be zero only when a and b are divisible by three. Substituting a=3a₁,b=3b₁ gives c²=3(a₁²+b₁²), so c is also divisible by three, contradicting primitivity.

Worked example

Set t=2 for the parametrized circle.

This gives x=−3/5,y=4/5 and verifies the equation exactly. By contrast no finite search is needed for the second conic: the divisibility contradiction rules out every rational denominator at once. Its lack of integer points also follows from squares modulo four, but that easier integer argument alone would not automatically prove the rational statement.

A complete parametrization and a nonexistence proof are both finite certificates, though of different kinds.

Scope of the result

Local solvability is not a general guarantee of global rational solvability for arbitrary varieties. A bounded search with no point is not itself a nonexistence theorem.

Further development

Choose a higher-degree curve and state exactly which global theorem or height bound would turn a point search into a complete result.

M099 · 2023-10-09 · Notation · historical evidence A

A typed glossary that prevents invalid compositions

Developed classical result with worked example

A useful glossary is attached to one mathematical argument. Recording domains, codomains, fields and adjoints prevents expressions that look symbolic but cannot be composed or interpreted consistently.

Definitions and assumptions

Use F:R²→R, g:R³→R², DF(g(x)):R²→R and Dg(x):R³→R². Their composition DF(g(x))Dg(x):R³→R is well typed.

Over C, Aᵀ denotes transpose and A† conjugate transpose. They serve different bilinear and Hermitian pairings.

Type correctness and positivity are substantive conditions

The matrix product rule requires the inner dimensions to match. A complex squared norm is z†z, not zᵀz. The latter can vanish for a nonzero vector, so substituting transpose for adjoint can invalidate a positivity argument.

Derivation or proof

An m×n matrix represents a map from n-dimensional coordinate vectors to m-dimensional vectors. Composition A∘B is represented by AB when B has matching output dimension n; coordinate expansion proves the familiar summation over the shared index. For positivity, z†z=Σ|z_i|² is real and nonnegative, and equals zero only at z=0. In contrast zᵀz is a complex bilinear expression whose terms can cancel. These are algebraic differences, not stylistic notation choices.

Worked example

Take z=(1,i) and a derivative composition with DF=[2,3], Dg=[[1,0,4],[0,1,5]].

Here zᵀz=1+i²=0 although z is nonzero, whereas z†z=2. The derivative product is [2,3,23], a 1×3 row representing a map R³→R. Reversing the factors is not even dimensionally defined. The checker verifies the legal product and rejects incompatible dimensions.

A short typed glossary can therefore expose a false proof before any sophisticated theorem is invoked.

Scope of the result

Matching dimensions is necessary but not sufficient: boundedness, differentiability, measurability, convergence and geometric compatibility may also be required. A formal type checker cannot silently supply them.

Further development

Attach assumptions and units to the same signatures, then propagate them through a complete worked calculation so every invoked theorem has a visible hypothesis ledger.

M100 · 2023-11-01 · D-modules · historical evidence A

Bernstein–Sato certificates and a minimality proof

Classical result developed and example checked

The original broad application question becomes an exact operator identity with a lower-bound argument. A certificate proves that a polynomial works; minimality proves that it is the b-function. Both steps can be completed for monomials, and a linear coordinate change supplies a nonmonomial example.

Definitions and assumptions

Work over C in the Weyl algebra generated by x and ∂ with ∂x−x∂=1. The parameter s commutes with both generators.

A Bernstein–Sato relation is P(s)f^(s+1)=b(s)f^s in the formal localization module. The global b-function is the monic polynomial of least degree satisfying such a relation.

Exact monomial b-function

For m≥1, b_(x^m)(s)=∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), with certificate P(s)=m^(−m)∂^m.

Derivation or proof

Differentiate x^(m(s+1)) exactly m times. The coefficient is ∏_(k=0)^(m−1)(m(s+1)−k)=m^m∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), proving the certificate. To prove minimality, put an arbitrary polynomial-coefficient operator in normal order Σ a_ij(s)x^i∂^j. Its action contributes the Laurent monomial x^(ms+m+i−j). The coefficient of x^(ms) can only receive terms with j=m+i. Every such falling-factorial coefficient contains all m factors from the displayed certificate. The other Laurent powers are independent over C(s), so any possible b(s) is divisible by that monic product. Thus the candidate is minimal, not merely an annihilating multiple.

Worked example

Take f=x²y³ and then the nonmonomial f=x²+y².

For x²y³, P=(1/108)∂ₓ²∂ᵧ³ gives b(s)=(s+1/2)(s+1/3)(s+2/3)(s+1)². The same exponent-comparison argument in both variables proves minimality. Over C set u=x+iy and v=x−iy. Then x²+y²=uv and ∂ᵤ∂ᵥ=(1/4)(∂ₓ²+∂ᵧ²), so (1/4)Δf^(s+1)=(s+1)²f^s.

A polynomial automorphism preserves the defining differential-operator problem, so the nonmonomial quadratic has b(s)=(s+1)². Repeated roots carry actual multiplicity; they must not be discarded.

Scope of the result

These are global polynomial examples in characteristic zero. General singularities may require local rather than global b-functions, elimination in a Weyl algebra, or additional singularity theory. The derivation does not establish that every proposed physical or statistical application admits a useful b-function.

Further development

A worthwhile next calculation is to compute a local b-function for a chosen non-normal-crossing plane singularity, retaining the operator certificate and a separate minimality argument. An unverified candidate formula should be labeled as such.

M101 · 2023-11-21 · Projective geometry · historical evidence A

Conic polarity as a typed point-to-line map

Classical result developed and example checked

The corrected construction identifies the quadratic form first, then derives polarity, the dual conic and coordinate covariance. It removes the undefined polar-line formula and the invented idea that one point dualizes to a conic.

Definitions and assumptions

Let Q be an invertible symmetric 3×3 matrix over a field of characteristic different from two. Points are nonzero column vectors modulo scale; lines are nonzero covectors modulo scale.

The nonsingular conic is C={x:xᵀQx=0}. The polar line of p has covector ℓ=Qp, because its equation is pᵀQx=0.

Polarity and the dual quadratic form

The polarity p↦Qp is invertible, incidence is reciprocal, and the tangent-line locus in the dual projective plane is ℓᵀQ⁻¹ℓ=0.

Derivation or proof

At a conic point a, differentiating xᵀQx gives tangent covector 2Qa, which defines the same projective line as Qa. Conversely any ℓ has pole p=Q⁻¹ℓ. That line is tangent precisely when its pole lies on C, which is exactly ℓᵀQ⁻¹ℓ=0. Reciprocity follows from pᵀQq=qᵀQp. Under x′=Mx, Q′=M⁻ᵀQM⁻¹ and ℓ′=M⁻ᵀℓ; hence Q′p′=M⁻ᵀQp. The construction therefore respects projective coordinate changes rather than depending on one affine drawing.

Worked example

Use the real unit-circle conic x²+y²−z²=0 and p=(2,0,1).

Here Q=diag(1,1,−1), so the polar is 2x−z=0. Its intersections with the conic are a±=(1/2,±√3/2,1). The tangents at these points have covectors (1/2,±√3/2,−1), and each contains p because their pairing with p is zero. The polar itself is not tangent: its dual quadratic value is 2²−1²=3.

The polar joins the two contact points of tangents drawn from the exterior point. Applying Q⁻¹ to its covector returns p. This verifies the point-line correspondence and the dual-conic test separately.

Scope of the result

Invertibility of Q and the characteristic assumption matter. A degenerate quadratic form does not produce a global polarity. Real exterior/interior terminology has no direct analogue over every field; projective incidence survives, while real tangent counts may change.

Further development

For higher-dimensional quadrics the same matrix argument defines polar hyperplanes. A useful further problem is to classify how the construction degenerates as det Q tends to zero and which incidence statements remain valid.

Mathematical references: The elementary calculation is supplied in full above.

M102 · 2023-11-21 · Projective geometry · historical evidence A

Cross-ratio with a fixed ordering and homogeneous coordinates

Classical result developed and example checked

Cross-ratio becomes a precise projective invariant once the four-point order and convention are fixed. Harmonicity is then a concrete value of that invariant, not an order-free label.

Definitions and assumptions

For distinct projective points a,b,c,d on P¹, choose nonzero representatives v_a,…,v_d and write [u,v]=det(u,v).

Use CR(a,b;c,d)=[v_a,v_c][v_b,v_d]/([v_b,v_c][v_a,v_d]). In an affine chart this is ((c−a)(d−b))/((c−b)(d−a)).

Projective invariance and harmonic ordering

Every invertible 2×2 matrix preserves this ordered cross-ratio. Under permutations the possible values lie in {r,1/r,1−r,1/(1−r),r/(r−1),(r−1)/r}.

Derivation or proof

Rescaling any representative multiplies one numerator factor and one denominator factor by the same scalar. Applying M multiplies each bracket by det M; the two determinant factors above and below cancel. Thus CR is both projectively well defined and invariant. The permutation formulas follow by swapping arguments in the affine expression. In particular r=−1 can become 2 or 1/2 after a different ordering, so a harmonic assertion must retain its convention. Homogeneous representatives make the point at infinity routine rather than an exception requiring an invented formula.

Worked example

Take (a,b;c,d)=(−1,1;0,∞) and T(z)=(2z+3)/(z+2).

Using v∞=(1,0) gives CR=−1. The transformation has nonzero determinant one and sends the ordered tuple to (1,5/3;3/2,2). The transformed ratio is [(1/2)(1/3)]/[(-1/6)(1)]=−1, verified with rational arithmetic.

The example simultaneously checks infinity, ordering and projective invariance. A dual statement for four concurrent lines follows only after identifying their pencil with P¹; duality is not a license to replace undefined point coordinates by arbitrary line expressions.

Scope of the result

The four points must be distinct for the displayed nondegenerate ratio. Coinciding points require a limiting or compactified configuration-space interpretation. Over a general field, the listed six values can coincide more than they do over the real numbers.

Further development

Cross-ratio coordinates give a concrete entry into moduli of marked projective lines: normalize three points to 0,1,∞ and the fourth is the remaining parameter. Investigate degenerations by tracking this parameter toward 0,1 or ∞.

M103 · 2023-11-21 · Representation theory · historical evidence A

A Heisenberg field and its verified local algebra

Classical result developed and example checked

A worked Fock-space model supplies actual operators, a vacuum and a singular operator product. It shows what the abstract vertex-algebra vocabulary is organizing, without claiming that a few words or one OPE alone constitute the full theory.

Definitions and assumptions

Let F=C[x₁,x₂,…], with each polynomial involving finitely many variables. Set a₋ₙ=xₙ by multiplication and aₙ=n∂/∂xₙ for n>0; let a₀ act as zero.

The vacuum is 1. The current is J(z)=Σ_(n∈Z)aₙz^(−n−1), interpreted as a formal field. Normal ordering moves creation modes a₋ₙ to the left.

Fock commutator and current contraction

[a_m,a_n]=mδ_(m+n,0)I. The singular contraction of J(z)J(w) is 1/(z−w)², in the formal expansion associated with |z|>|w|.

Derivation or proof

For positive m,n, derivatives commute and multiplications commute. The only nonzero mixed commutator is [m∂ₓₘ,xₙ]=mδ_mn. Splitting the field into annihilation and creation parts gives [J₊(z),J₋(w)]=Σ_(n≥1)n z^(−n−1)w^(n−1). Differentiating the formal geometric series Σ_(n≥0)wⁿz^(−n−1)=1/(z−w) produces the claimed double pole. The normally ordered remainder has no additional singular contraction. This calculation is a complete local commutator derivation in a defined representation.

Worked example

Use the normally ordered stress tensor T(z)=(1/2):J(z)²: and vacuum states of low degree.

The mode L₋₂ sends 1 to x₁²/2. The only contribution of L₂ on this state is (1/2)a₁², giving L₂L₋₂1=1/2. With L₀1=0, the Virasoro convention [L₂,L₋₂]=4L₀+cI/2 yields c=1. Translation on generators is represented by T₀=Σ_(n≥1)n xₙ₊₁∂ₓₙ, so [T₀,a₋ₙ]=n a₋₍ₙ₊₁₎.

The example fixes normalization of the central term and makes the relation between formal fields and modes explicit. The verifier checks the displayed operator relations on a finite set of polynomial states.

Scope of the result

The finite checks do not prove all vertex-algebra axioms. The complete Heisenberg vertex algebra follows from the usual reconstruction construction, with vacuum, translation and locality stated on the full formal space. A coordinate-free chiral-algebra construction additionally needs a curve and coordinate transformation laws.

Further development

Develop conformal blocks for this explicit algebra on a chosen curve, or prove a stated reconstruction theorem. Such a continuation has concrete input data rather than a generic appeal to string theory.

M104 · 2023-11-22 · Integrable systems · historical evidence A

Classical result developed and example checked

The corrected Bethe equations are tied to one Hamiltonian normalization and checked against a finite matrix. The resulting calculation verifies a sector, while keeping singular-root and completeness questions explicit.

Definitions and assumptions

Take N=4 periodic spin-1/2 sites and H=Σ_(j=0)^3(I−P_(j,j+1)), where P swaps adjacent spins and the last edge wraps around.

In the one-down-spin sector, |j⟩ denotes the down spin at site j. A plane wave has coefficients exp(ipj), with p=2πm/4.

Exact one-magnon diagonalization

H|p⟩=(2−2cos p)|p⟩, so this four-dimensional sector has energies 0,2,4,2. The finite regular Bethe roots are λ=1/2,0,−1/2, giving energies 1/(λ²+1/4)=2,4,2.

Only the two bonds incident on the down spin act nontrivially, giving H|j⟩=2|j⟩−|j−1⟩−|j+1⟩. Substitution of the plane wave yields the dispersion. In the periodic XXX convention the regular roots obey ((λ_j+i/2)/(λ_j−i/2))^N=∏_(k≠j)(λ_j−λ_k+i)/(λ_j−λ_k−i). For one root the right side is one. Writing exp(ip)=(λ+i/2)/(λ−i/2) gives λ=(1/2)cot(p/2), and the energy agrees with the plane-wave dispersion. The p=0 state corresponds to the infinite-root limit.

Worked example

Use real vectors in the ordered basis |0⟩,…,|3⟩.

The vectors (1,1,1,1), (1,0,−1,0), (0,1,0,−1) and (1,−1,1,−1) form a basis with eigenvalues 0,2,2,4. Exact integer matrix multiplication verifies all four. For λ=1/2,0,−1/2 the complex Bethe ratio is i,−1,−i respectively; its fourth power is one.

This establishes agreement between a direct operator calculation and the regular Bethe description of the nonuniform one-magnon states. It also demonstrates why omitting the infinite-root state would lose an actual eigenvector.

Scope of the result

The calculation does not prove completeness in other magnetization sectors or for arbitrary N. Roots at ±i/2 and coincident roots need a regularization or a carefully specified admissibility convention. Including the self-index k=j would add a spurious factor and changes the equations.

Further development

For the two-magnon sector, diagonalize the six-dimensional matrix first, then match admissible Bethe solutions and explicitly account for singular solutions and descendants. The matrix spectrum supplies an independent target.

M105 · 2023-11-22 · Representation theory · historical evidence A

Classical result developed and example checked

A concrete spectral bridge replaces the unsupported Fourier-to-automorphic-form slogan. In the smallest nontrivial sl₂ example, the Bethe vector, Hamiltonian eigenvalues, Miura potential and cancellation of the apparent singularity can all be computed exactly. A rational three-site continuation also gives a complete eight-dimensional joint eigenbasis and two additional scalar-oper certificates.

Definitions and assumptions

On each C² take h=diag(1,−1), e|↓⟩=|↑⟩, f|↑⟩=|↓⟩ and Ω=(1/2)h⊗h+e⊗f+f⊗e. Choose marked points z₁=0,z₂=1.

Let H₁=Ω/(z₁−z₂)=−Ω and H₂=Ω. For weights (1,1), one Bethe root obeys 1/w+1/(w−1)=0.

The root w=1/2 yields a singlet with (H₁,H₂) eigenvalues (3/2,−3/2). Define u(x)=1/(2x)+1/(2(x−1))−1/(x−1/2). Then (∂−u)(∂+u)=∂²−V, where V=u²−u′=3/[4x²(x−1)²].

The Bethe vector is w⁻¹|↓↑⟩+(w−1)⁻¹|↑↓⟩=2|↓↑⟩−2|↑↓⟩. Direct use of Ω gives eigenvalue −3/2, hence the Hamiltonian pair above. Near a root w, write u=−1/(x−w)+a₀+O(x−w). The double pole cancels in u²−u′, and its simple residue is −2a₀. Here a₀=(1/2)(1/w+1/(w−1))=0 precisely by the Bethe equation. Expanding at the physical points gives V=3/(4x²)+3/(4(x−1)²)+(3/2)/x−(3/2)/(x−1). Its simple residues match H₁ and H₂ in the declared normalization.

Worked example

Treat the scalar differential equation y″−V(x)y=0 on the punctured projective line.

The apparent point x=1/2 is absent from V. One solution is y₁=(x−1/2)/sqrt(x(x−1)). Reduction of order gives y₂=(x²−x/2+1/4)/sqrt(x(x−1)), with Wronskian one. Both are regular at x=1/2. Around x=0 or x=1 their common square-root factor changes sign, so monodromy is scalar and projectively trivial. The vacuum sector, with no root, instead has simple residues (−1/2,1/2), matching the triplet eigenvalues. For sites (0,1,8/3), the one-root equation reduces to 3w²−(22/3)w+8/3=0, with roots 2 and 4/9. Their eigenvalue triples are (−3/16,6/5,−81/80) and (25/16,−8/5,3/80). The highest vectors have one-down-spin coefficients (1/2,1,−3/2) and (9/4,−9/5,−9/20). Applying total lowering once to each gives two doublets; applying it zero through three times to the vacuum gives a quartet with eigenvalues (−11/16,1/5,39/80). All eight rational vectors are independent and satisfy all three full 8×8 Hamiltonians. For each regular root, with g=∏(x−z_i), u=g′/(2g)−1/(x−w) gives V=(3/4)Σ_i(x−z_i)^(−2)+Σ_iE_i/(x−z_i). Exact residual polynomials vanish. Since g′(w)=0, reduction of order has no logarithm: y₁=(x−w)/sqrt(g), y₂=[−g(w)+(g″(w)/2)(x−w)²+(x−w)³/2]/sqrt(g). Their Wronskian is one, and both ODE residuals vanish identically.

The calculation supplies an actual rank-one instance of the Gaudin–oper relationship: eigenvalues are encoded in coefficients of a scalar differential operator. The simple finite example is classical; its explicit replay is an exposition and verification result. The three-site continuation settles this complete finite joint-spectrum example, including its scalar equations, rather than leaving it as a proposed computation.

Scope of the result

This is an sl₂ example, not a proof of the full Gaudin-algebra spectrum theorem, a global automorphic correspondence or arbitrary Bethe completeness. Oper terminology and Langlands duality must retain the relevant group, singularity and monodromy conditions.

Further development

S010 develops the arbitrary-site one-magnon theorem, S013 completes the three-site exceptional-point analysis, and S014 classifies every distinct-complex-site one-magnon Jordan block with closed matrix and characteristic formulas. Remaining extensions concern multi-magnon sectors, higher representations or physical-site collisions; they require additional hypotheses and independent checks. This is separate from full Gaudin completeness.

M106 · 2023-11-06 · Probability · historical evidence A

Joint reliability is a dependence problem

Classical result developed and example checked

The arithmetic correction is only the first step. An all-success probability cannot be identified from marginal accuracies alone. Exact dependence constructions show the full gap between what the individual probabilities say and what independence adds.

Definitions and assumptions

Let A₁,…,A_n be success events with P(A_i)=p_i. The target is P(∩A_i), a joint probability.

Mutual independence means P(∩_(i∈S)A_i)=∏_(i∈S)p_i for every subset S. Pairwise independence checks only subsets of size two.

Fréchet bounds and an independence counterexample

max(0,Σp_i−(n−1))≤P(∩A_i)≤min_i p_i. If all 104 marginals are 0.95, these bounds are 0 and 0.95, whereas independence gives 0.95^104≈0.00482230805327.

Derivation or proof

The upper bound follows because the intersection is a subset of every A_i. For the lower bound apply the union bound to the failure events: P(∩A_i)=1−P(∪A_iᶜ)≥1−Σ(1−p_i). Probabilities are also nonnegative. The product formula follows only after imposing mutual independence. To see why pairwise independence is insufficient, let X,Y be independent fair bits and set Z=X xor Y. Any pair is independent, but P(X=Y=Z=1)=0 rather than 1/8.

Worked example

Construct joint laws for 104 events, each with success probability 0.95.

For the maximal case take every A_i={U≤0.95} for one uniform U; then all-success probability is 0.95. For a zero case let failures be arcs of length 0.05 on the unit circle, starting at i/104. Since adjacent starts are less than 0.05 apart, the arcs cover the circle, so at least one failure always occurs, although each event still succeeds with probability 0.95. Independent Bernoulli variables give the intermediate product.

The same individual accuracy is compatible with no chance of complete correctness, a 95 percent chance, or the independent-model value. Replacing a dependency model by repeated multiplication can therefore be a major modeling error even after arithmetic is repaired.

Scope of the result

The numerical examples are abstract probability constructions, not estimated properties of a genealogy or any real audit. Real dependence requires observations or structural assumptions. Pairwise correlations alone generally do not determine the required high-order intersection.

Further development

For a specified dependency graph, derive an interval using available joint moments or solve a finite linear program over atomic outcomes. Report the identified interval if the joint probability remains underdetermined.

M107 · 2023-11-24 · Dynamical systems · historical evidence A

Nonlinearity does not imply chaos or identifiability

Classical result developed and example checked

A rigorous counterexample is more informative than another catalogue of nonlinear applications. A simple nonlinear ODE has a fully solvable, globally convergent flow and an observation that permanently hides the sign of its initial state.

Definitions and assumptions

Consider ẋ=−x³ on the real line for t≥0. The state is x, and first choose the observable y=x².

An observation model is identifiable on a set if no two admissible initial states generate exactly the same observed time history. This is distinct from state stability.

Global convergence with an exact observation collision

For every initial x₀, x(t)=x₀/sqrt(1+2x₀²t). All trajectories converge to zero, while x₀ and −x₀ give identical y(t)=x₀²/(1+2x₀²t).

Derivation or proof

For x₀≠0, differentiate x⁻² to obtain d(x⁻²)/dt=2 and solve; x₀=0 gives the equilibrium. The denominator stays positive, giving a global forward solution. With V=x²/2, V̇=−x⁴≤0, and the explicit solution proves convergence. Squaring removes the initial sign for all times. Equivalently y satisfies ẏ=−2y² with the same initial y₀ for both states. Thus the nonlinear system is elementary and convergent, while the chosen observation remains structurally ambiguous.

Worked example

Compare x₀=1 and x₀=−1, recording y=x² at any finite or infinite collection of times.

At t=0,1,2 the common observations are 1,1/3,1/5. No increase in temporal sampling resolves the sign because the entire continuous histories coincide. Adding the observable z=x distinguishes the two immediately. The exact rational y values and the observation evolution equation are checked by the verifier.

Complexity of the evolution law, richness of sampling and distinguishability of states are separate questions. This example refutes a generic inference from nonlinear equations to chaos and a generic inference from many measurements to complete state reconstruction.

Scope of the result

This proof concerns one scalar system and one observation. It is not a general criterion for absence of chaos in higher dimensions. Nor does adding a sign-sensitive observation establish practical robustness when measurement noise is large.

Further development

Classify observation collisions under a symmetry group: if both dynamics and output are sign-equivariant or sign-invariant in the appropriate way, determine whether the output can at best recover a symmetry orbit. Then quantify the additional measurement needed to break it.

M108 · 2023-12-02 · Mathematical physics · historical evidence A

The Klein–Gordon dispersion relation and its massless limit

Classical result developed and example checked

The mathematical comparison starts with two explicitly normalized differential operators. Their plane-wave dispersions, propagation equations and interpretation can then be compared without confusing a classical field equation with the procedure of quantization.

Definitions and assumptions

Use coordinates (t,x), speed c and □=c⁻²∂_t²−Δ. The free Klein–Gordon equation is (□+(mc/ℏ)²)φ=0.

A plane wave is exp(i(k·x−ωt)). Its wave vector k has inverse-length units, while ω has inverse-time units.

Massive and massless plane-wave dispersions

Substitution gives ω²=c²|k|²+m²c⁴/ℏ². Setting m=0 gives the classical massless wave dispersion ω²=c²|k|².

Derivation or proof

The second time derivative multiplies the wave by −ω² and the Laplacian by −|k|². The PDE therefore reduces to −ω²/c²+|k|²+(mc/ℏ)²=0. Multiplying by ℏ² and writing E=ℏω and p=ℏk gives E²=c²|p|²+m²c⁴. For m>0, differentiating the positive branch gives group velocity v_g=c²k/ω with magnitude below c; at high frequency it approaches c. These are consequences of the chosen PDE and Fourier ansatz, not additional quantum postulates.

Worked example

In units c=ℏ=1 take m=2 and spatial mode k=(3,0,0).

The frequencies are ω=±sqrt(13), and each wave has zero PDE residual because −13+9+4=0. The positive-branch group speed is 3/sqrt(13). On a periodic box of side L, allowed wave vectors are 2πn/L, producing a countable family of uncoupled harmonic oscillators at the classical level.

Mass changes the relation between frequency and wave number. The periodic Fourier decomposition also identifies the finite-mode truncations that can be computed exactly; it does not by itself choose a Fock space or turn amplitudes into operators.

Scope of the result

Negative-frequency solutions do not by themselves establish a negative-probability theory. Quantization and the choice of conserved inner product require their own construction. Interactions, curved backgrounds and boundary conditions change the analysis.

Further development

For a specified potential or curved metric, determine whether a positive self-adjoint spatial operator supplies a stable mode expansion. Retain the operator domain and boundary conditions rather than transferring the flat-space dispersion unchanged.

M109 · 2023-12-02 · Mathematical physics · historical evidence A

A controlled formal route from Dirac to Pauli

Classical result developed and example checked

The nonrelativistic limit must preserve spin and the magnetic coupling. Removing the rest-energy phase and eliminating the small spinor component gives the leading Pauli equation, together with an explicit statement of the scale assumptions.

Definitions and assumptions

Let π=p−qA with p=−iℏ∇ and B=∇×A. Use H_D=cα·π+βmc²+qΦ and a four-spinor ψ=e^(−imc²t/ℏ)(ϕ,χ)ᵀ.

The nonrelativistic regime requires typical |π|/(mc)≪1 and energies and time variation small compared with mc², together with fields smooth enough for the expansion.

Leading spin-sensitive Hamiltonian

At leading order χ≈(σ·π)ϕ/(2mc), and iℏϕ̇=[π²/(2m)−(qℏ/(2m))σ·B+qΦ]ϕ.

Derivation or proof

After extracting the rest-energy phase, the two components satisfy iℏϕ̇=qΦϕ+cσ·πχ and iℏχ̇=(qΦ−2mc²)χ+cσ·πϕ. The large 2mc² denominator permits the stated leading elimination of χ when the remaining terms are small. Pauli-matrix multiplication gives (σ·π)²=π²+(i/2)Σε_ijkσ_k[π_i,π_j]. Since [π_i,π_j]=iqℏε_ijkB_k, the second term is −qℏσ·B. Inserting this identity into the first equation produces the Hamiltonian and fixes the sign convention.

Worked example

First take A=Φ=0 and a plane wave of momentum magnitude p.

The exact positive relativistic energy is sqrt(m²c⁴+c²p²)=mc²+p²/(2m)−p⁴/(8m³c²)+O(p⁶/(m⁵c⁴)). Removing mc² leaves the Schrödinger kinetic term at leading order. For a magnetic field, the additional Pauli spin term survives at that same effective order; a scalar wave equation would miss it.

The result specifies both the limiting equation and the leading neglected kinetic correction. Its small parameter is p/(mc), not simply the statement that an experiment looks classical.

Scope of the result

This is a formal asymptotic derivation for a prescribed background field. A uniform error theorem over long times needs operator estimates and additional regularity. Strong fields and pair-production regimes invalidate the elementary elimination.

Further development

Choose a bounded momentum sector and smooth bounded fields, then derive a finite-time norm estimate comparing projected Dirac dynamics with the effective Pauli evolution. That is the appropriate next step toward a controlled approximation theorem.

M110 · 2023-12-02 · Mathematical physics · historical evidence A

Maxwell equations as field equations and identities

Classical result developed and example checked

Differential forms separate what follows from a potential from what must be imposed as a sourced equation. Gauge redundancy becomes a precise kernel of the map from potentials to field strength, with topology supplying an important qualification.

Definitions and assumptions

On an oriented spacetime with a fixed metric, A is a one-form and F=dA is a two-form. The Hodge star depends on that metric and orientation.

Use normalization dF=0 and d⋆F=J, where J is a source three-form. Constants can be restored according to electromagnetic unit conventions.

Gauge invariance and current closure

A↦A+dχ leaves F unchanged. Whenever d⋆F=J holds, dJ=0. Locally, every closed F is a potential field on a contractible coordinate patch.

Derivation or proof

The identity d²=0 gives d(A+dχ)=dA. Applying d to the sourced equation gives dJ=d²⋆F=0, so source conservation is a compatibility condition. The local converse dF=0⇒F=dA is the Poincaré lemma under the contractibility assumption. It is not a global theorem on arbitrary manifolds: nontrivial degree-two cohomology can obstruct a single globally defined potential. The coordinate form of dF=0 is the homogeneous Maxwell system; the Hodge-star equation contains the metric-dependent dynamical content.

Worked example

On flat coordinates (t,x,y,z), choose A=a cos(kx−ωt)dy and use units c=1.

Then F=−ak sin(kx−ωt)dx∧dy+aω sin(kx−ωt)dt∧dy. Direct exterior differentiation gives dF=0 because the two mixed terms cancel. The vacuum sourced equation requires ω²=k². Adding dχ for χ=λtx changes components of A but contributes no change to F.

The example distinguishes the automatic homogeneous identity, the dispersion imposed by the vacuum field equation and a gauge change of the potential. It also shows why covariant notation alone is not a quantization procedure.

Scope of the result

Global potentials, boundary conditions and gauge fixing require separate analysis. A flat connection can have nontrivial global holonomy while being locally pure gauge. A globally exact potential A=dχ with single-valued χ has no such loop holonomy; these cases must not be conflated.

Further development

Develop the same problem on a torus or a punctured domain and calculate closed forms that are not exact. This makes the topology of gauge data explicit before introducing a quantum theory.

M111 · 2023-12-02 · Quantum field theory · historical evidence A

Ward–Takahashi constrains a vertex without determining it

Classical result developed and example checked

The identity is made concrete by verifying it at tree level, constructing a longitudinal vertex for a prescribed inverse propagator, and displaying the remaining transverse freedom. This explains both the power and the limitation of the constraint.

Definitions and assumptions

Factor the charge from the full electromagnetic vertex Γ^μ. With consistent momentum assignments, the identity is q_μΓ^μ(p+q,p)=S⁻¹(p+q)−S⁻¹(p).

A transverse addition T^μ satisfies q_μT^μ=0. Such an addition cannot be detected by this contracted identity alone.

An explicit longitudinal construction

For a differentiable matrix-valued inverse propagator K(p)=S⁻¹(p), Γ_L^μ=∫₀¹(∂K/∂p_μ)(p+tq)dt satisfies the difference identity on any regular path. It is not the unique satisfying vertex.

Derivation or proof

Contract with q and use the chain rule: q_μ∂K(p+tq)/∂p_μ=dK(p+tq)/dt. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives K(p+q)−K(p). Adding any transverse T preserves the contraction. At tree level K(p)=slash(p)−m and Γ^μ=γ^μ, reducing the identity to slash(q)=slash(p+q)−slash(p). These are direct algebraic checks of the kinematic relation; they do not assert that an arbitrarily chosen K and Γ arise from a complete interacting quantum field theory.

Worked example

For an illustrative polynomial matrix function, take K(p)=slash(p)−m−αp²I.

The construction gives Γ_L^μ=γ^μ−α(2p^μ+q^μ)I. Contracting yields slash(q)−α(2p·q+q²)I, exactly K(p+q)−K(p). One may add κ(q²p^μ−(p·q)q^μ)I, whose contraction is zero. The verifier checks this example in a two-coordinate Euclidean Clifford representation with rational inputs.

The identity constrains differences of inverse propagators and the longitudinal vertex. It leaves dynamical transverse information undetermined. The polynomial example tests the logic without making a false renormalization claim.

Scope of the result

In QED the full identity is a statement about regularized and renormalized correlation functions. A symmetry-breaking regulator, inconsistent counterterms or an anomalous symmetry can require additional terms or restoration conditions. The algebraic construction above does not settle those issues.

Further development

Specify an actual perturbative action and regulator, calculate the one-loop self-energy and vertex in the same convention, and check the renormalized identity including counterterms. Retain transverse form factors as independent output.

M112 · 2023-12-02 · Quantum field theory · historical evidence A

A complete finite-dimensional perturbation calculation

Classical result developed and example checked

A zero-dimensional quartic model permits an exact derivation of propagator contractions, vacuum normalization, connected coefficients and a rigorous asymptotic remainder. It supplies a fully checkable model of perturbative logic without claiming to construct a continuum field theory.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X be a real standard Gaussian and define Z(g)=E[exp(−gX⁴/24)] for g≥0. The normalized two-point function is G₂(g)=E[X²exp(−gX⁴/24)]/Z(g).

Gaussian moments are E[X^(2r)]=(2r−1)!! and odd moments vanish. Wick pairings count those double factorials.

Quartic coefficients and a controlled remainder

Z(g)=1−g/8+35g²/384+O(g³), log Z(g)=−g/8+g²/12+O(g³), and G₂(g)=1−g/2+2g²/3+O(g³) as g↓0.

Derivation or proof

Expand the interaction exponential to a fixed order and integrate each Gaussian moment. The nth coefficient of Z is a_n=(−1)^n(4n−1)!!/(24^n n!). Multiplying and dividing the resulting formal series gives the displayed connected and normalized coefficients. For g≥0, Taylor’s integral remainder for exp(−y) has magnitude at most y^(N+1)/(N+1)!; taking y=gX⁴/24 and integrating bounds the partition-function remainder by the next absolute coefficient times g^(N+1). This proves a finite-order asymptotic statement without exchanging an infinite series and the integral.

Worked example

Calculate through second order using integer Gaussian moments.

E[X⁴]=3, E[X⁸]=105 and E[X¹⁰]=945. Thus the numerator of G₂ is 1−5g/8+105g²/128+O(g³); division by Z gives 1−g/2+2g²/3. Meanwhile |a_(n+1)/a_n|=(4n+3)(4n+1)/(24(n+1)), which grows without bound.

The perturbative series has zero radius of convergence although the original integral exists for every g≥0. Correct finite-order coefficients and an explicit asymptotic bound are therefore stronger and more honest deliverables than a claim that the infinite diagram sum converges.

Scope of the result

This toy integral has no spacetime ultraviolet divergences, locality or scattering theory. It does not replace renormalization of a continuum model. Its value is the exact separation of algebraic combinatorics, normalization and asymptotic control.

Further development

Add several Gaussian variables with a stated covariance and derive connected cumulants. For a continuum problem, introduce a cutoff and identify which bounds survive its removal rather than assuming the finite-dimensional argument is uniform.
